# Journalism AI, surveillance and OSINT tooling catalogue

**361 projects assessed, ranked and evidenced.** Verification dates: 2026-11-16 (inherited from
session 1, re-checked here) and 2026-11-17 (this session's own checks). Generated from
`records/*.json` by `build.py`; do not hand-edit this file.

Owner context: senior software and AI engineer supporting independent journalism and media
organisations, including media in exile. Self-hosting, integration work and local AI are
available; hostile-state threat models and source protection carry real weight.

> This is the complete consolidated report. For a browsable version see [`README.md`](README.md) and the pages under [`docs/`](docs/) — in particular the [complete ranking](docs/rankings.md), the [methodology](docs/methodology.md) and the [per-project assessments](docs/projects/).

## How to read this

- **Scores** apply the rubric in `sources/recovered/cat/RUBRIC.md` unchanged: relevance 30,
  capability 20, maintenance 15, privacy and deployment control 15, usability 10, licence and
  cost 10. Each dimension is 0-5; the weighted total is out of 100.
- **The ranking encodes my priorities for your work**, not universal software quality. A
  specialist tool scored against its intended role will sit below a ubiquitous one even when it
  is excellent at its job — ExifTool ranks first because it is used on nearly every verification
  and never fails, not because it is more sophisticated than QGIS.
- **Evidence confidence is recorded separately from the score** and never folded into it. 251
  projects are high confidence, 97 medium, 13 low; 23 are marked provisional.
- **Material blockers are listed separately from scores** so a licence or dependency problem is
  visible even where the tool scores well.
- Assessment depth is stated per project. **Nothing in this survey was installed or run.** Depth
  is `metadata-verified`, `repo-inspected` or `docs-reviewed`; no entry claims hands-on testing.
- Project claims, documented user feedback and my own judgement are separated in every card.
  Where no user reports were found, the card says so rather than inventing consensus.

## The 20 projects to examine first

This is a curated shortlist, not the top 20 by score. It is ordered by what I would actually do
first, and it deliberately includes two items that score lower because they close a gap nothing
else covers.

| # | Project | Why first |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Dangerzone** ([SUR-B3-03](docs/projects/SUR-B3-03.md), 92) | Nothing else protects you at the point of first contact with an unknown document. Automate it at ingest before adopting anything else in the document pillar. |
| 2 | **ICIJ Datashare** ([JAI-A2-25](docs/projects/JAI-A2-25.md), 92) | Desktop mode is the shortest path from "we received a dump" to "reporters are searching it" with no infrastructure. Try it before considering OpenAleph. |
| 3 | **OpenAleph** ([JAI-A2-35](docs/projects/JAI-A2-35.md), 93) | If your investigations are entity-centric, this is the platform — and this session settled the fork question: OpenAleph released 5.4.0 on 2026-11-16, upstream Aleph last released 4.1.7 in October 2025. |
| 4 | **whisper.cpp + Buzz** ([JAI-A2-59](docs/projects/JAI-A2-59.md) / [JAI-A2-05](docs/projects/JAI-A2-05.md)) | A single binary and a desktop app that together stop interviews being uploaded to cloud transcription. The behavioural change is the point. |
| 5 | **SecureDrop** ([SUR-B3-01](docs/projects/SUR-B3-01.md), 92) | If you solicit documents from sources at real risk, this is the standard. Adopt it properly or say publicly what you do not offer. |
| 6 | **mat2** ([SUR-B3-07](docs/projects/SUR-B3-07.md), 94) | Metadata stripping on the publication path. Two open issues, release 0.15.0, and it prevents a failure that has burned sources. |
| 7 | **x-ray** ([JAI-A4-23](docs/projects/JAI-A4-23.md), 86) | Sweep incoming documents for failed redactions, and sweep your own before release. Both directions matter. |
| 8 | **FreshRSS + RSSHub** ([JAI-A1-03](docs/projects/JAI-A1-03.md) / [JAI-A1-05](docs/projects/JAI-A1-05.md), 94 / 91) | The cheapest substantial monitoring capability in the catalogue. Self-hosted, so your feed list is not a product dataset. |
| 9 | **llama.cpp + Ollama** ([JAI-A3-01](docs/projects/JAI-A3-01.md) / [JAI-A3-02](docs/projects/JAI-A3-02.md), 96 / 94) | One GPU host with an OpenAI-compatible endpoint makes "does this document leave the building" an infrastructure decision taken once. |
| 10 | **browsertrix-crawler + ReplayWeb.page** ([OSINT-C1-29](docs/projects/OSINT-C1-29.md) / [OSINT-C1-32](docs/projects/OSINT-C1-32.md), 94 / 94) | Capture that holds up and replay that a lawyer can open from a single file with no software. |
| 11 | **Scoop** ([OSINT-C1-36](docs/projects/OSINT-C1-36.md), 90) | Provenance-attested capture for the specific pages a story cites. Verify the signing format with Harvard LIL before relying on it legally — this survey did not. |
| 12 | **EFF Rayhunter** ([SUR-B3-13](docs/projects/SUR-B3-13.md), 88) | Makes IMSI-catcher detection possible on tens-of-dollars hardware. Baseline before treating anomalies as detections. |
| 13 | **OpenSanctions + yente** ([OSINT-C3-01](docs/projects/OSINT-C3-01.md) / [JAI-A2-61](docs/projects/JAI-A2-61.md), 94 / 84) | Screening on your own infrastructure so you do not tell a vendor whom you are investigating. Settle the CC-BY-NC data licence in writing first. |
| 14 | **Splink** ([JAI-A2-48](docs/projects/JAI-A2-48.md), 86) | Replace dedupe. Auditable match weights are the difference between a defensible linkage and an assertion. |
| 15 | **bellingcat/osm-search + streetlevel** ([OSINT-C2-27](docs/projects/OSINT-C2-27.md) / [OSINT-C2-32](docs/projects/OSINT-C2-32.md), 88 / 82) | The two halves of practical photo geolocation. Note that streetlevel uses providers' internal interfaces and discloses your coordinates. |
| 16 | **ShadowFinder** ([OSINT-C2-17](docs/projects/OSINT-C2-17.md), 91) | Physics-based falsification of a claimed time and place. Use the local CLI, not the documented Colab route. |
| 17 | **CryptPad** ([SUR-B3-27](docs/projects/SUR-B3-27.md), 92) | Replaces the shared planning document on a third-party cloud — the most common and least-discussed leak in investigative work. |
| 18 | **Datasette + DuckDB** ([JAI-A2-09](docs/projects/JAI-A2-09.md) / [JAI-A1-19](docs/projects/JAI-A1-19.md), 93 / 86) | Fastest route from extracted data to something reporters can search, and from a large file to SQL on a laptop. |
| 19 | **Haystack** ([JAI-A3-05](docs/projects/JAI-A3-05.md), 86) | If you build document question-answering, build it on an auditable pipeline with built-in evaluation. Measure faithfulness before anyone relies on it. |
| 20 | **PMTiles + MapLibre** ([JAI-A1-24](docs/projects/JAI-A1-24.md) / [JAI-A1-22](docs/projects/JAI-A1-22.md), 87 / 87) | Self-hosted map publishing with no tile server and no third-party provider watching your readers. Build the pipeline once. |

Two deliberate inclusions below their score: **Rayhunter** (88) and **Scoop** (90) rank outside
the top 20 by points but close capability gaps nothing else in the catalogue covers.

Two high scorers deliberately *not* in the shortlist: **mitmproxy** (96) and **ExifTool** (96)
are superb and you almost certainly already have them — they rank first on ubiquity and
reliability, which is exactly why they need no examination.

## Suggested stacks

### A. Small newsroom, little or no engineering capacity

The principle is that every component must work without a platform engineer, and the privacy
properties must hold by default rather than by configuration.

- **Receive and protect:** Hush Line ([SUR-B3-06](docs/projects/SUR-B3-06.md)) (self-hosted) for tips · Dangerzone ([SUR-B3-03](docs/projects/SUR-B3-03.md)) on every arriving
  document · mat2 ([SUR-B3-07](docs/projects/SUR-B3-07.md)) before anything is published · Signal ([SUR-B3-23](docs/projects/SUR-B3-23.md)) for source contact.
- **Documents:** ICIJ Datashare ([JAI-A2-23](docs/projects/JAI-A2-23.md)) in desktop mode · OCRmyPDF ([JAI-A2-33](docs/projects/JAI-A2-33.md)) for scans · Tabula ([JAI-A2-53](docs/projects/JAI-A2-53.md)) or pdfplumber ([JAI-A2-39](docs/projects/JAI-A2-39.md)) for
  tables (Tabula is frozen since 2018 — use it knowingly) · x-ray ([JAI-A4-23](docs/projects/JAI-A4-23.md)) before publishing any PDF.
- **Audio:** Buzz ([JAI-A2-05](docs/projects/JAI-A2-05.md)) on reporters' laptops; noScribe ([JAI-A2-31](docs/projects/JAI-A2-31.md)) where speaker attribution matters.
- **Monitoring:** changedetection.io ([SUR-B1-15](docs/projects/SUR-B1-15.md)) · FreshRSS ([JAI-A1-03](docs/projects/JAI-A1-03.md)) · Klaxon Cloud ([SUR-B1-19](docs/projects/SUR-B1-19.md)) if you cannot run a server at all.
- **Verification:** InVID-WeVerify plugin ([JAI-A4-04](docs/projects/JAI-A4-04.md)) for public media only · Sherloq ([OSINT-C2-12](docs/projects/OSINT-C2-12.md)) locally for anything
  unpublished · MediaInfo ([OSINT-C2-04](docs/projects/OSINT-C2-04.md)) on every submitted video.
- **Publish:** DocumentCloud ([JAI-A2-13](docs/projects/JAI-A2-13.md)) for documents · Datasette ([JAI-A2-09](docs/projects/JAI-A2-09.md)) for data · Leaflet ([JAI-A1-21](docs/projects/JAI-A1-21.md)) with self-hosted
  PMTiles ([JAI-A1-24](docs/projects/JAI-A1-24.md)) for maps.
- **Deliberately excluded:** OpenAleph ([JAI-A2-35](docs/projects/JAI-A2-35.md)), SecureDrop ([SUR-B3-01](docs/projects/SUR-B3-01.md)), Browsertrix platform, Qubes. Each needs
  capacity this stack does not have, and a half-maintained SecureDrop is worse than none.
- **Indicative cost:** no licence fees; one small VM plus one shared GPU-less workstation.

### C. Team handling highly sensitive material (media in exile, hostile-state threat model)

Ordered by what protects people rather than by capability.

- **Devices and environments:** Qubes OS ([SUR-B3-20](docs/projects/SUR-B3-20.md)) for those handling unsolicited material · Tails ([SUR-B3-19](docs/projects/SUR-B3-19.md)) for

- **Communications:** Signal (teach safety-number verification) · Molly ([SUR-B3-24](docs/projects/SUR-B3-24.md)) on Android where seizure

  Delta Chat ([SUR-B3-26](docs/projects/SUR-B3-26.md)) over chatmail where messengers are blocked · Orbot ([SUR-B3-30](docs/projects/SUR-B3-30.md)) and Outline ([SUR-B3-31](docs/projects/SUR-B3-31.md)) for circumvention you
  operate.
- **Submission:** SecureDrop with the Qubes Workstation · OnionShare ([SUR-B3-04](docs/projects/SUR-B3-04.md)) for ad-hoc transfer ·
  Hush Line as the honest fallback.
- **Document handling:** Dangerzone always · mat2 and PyMuPDF ([JAI-A2-42](docs/projects/JAI-A2-42.md)) true redaction before release ·
  x-ray to verify the redaction worked · kuroi ([JAI-A4-24](docs/projects/JAI-A4-24.md)) only against a self-hosted model.
- **Device examination:** MVT ([SUR-B3-08](docs/projects/SUR-B3-08.md)) and androidqf ([SUR-B3-09](docs/projects/SUR-B3-09.md)) with a **written consent script and a disclosed
  retention policy** — the MVT License 1.1 §3.0 makes that contractual, not optional ·
  stalkerware-indicators ([SUR-B3-10](docs/projects/SUR-B3-10.md)) and Amnesty IOCs (check securitylab.amnesty.org, the GitHub mirror has
  not been pushed since December 2024) · SpyGuard ([SUR-B3-12](docs/projects/SUR-B3-12.md)) for non-invasive screening · Rayhunter ([SUR-B3-13](docs/projects/SUR-B3-13.md)) for
  cell-site simulators.
- **Collaboration:** CryptPad ([SUR-B3-27](docs/projects/SUR-B3-27.md)) for documents · Nextcloud ([SUR-B3-28](docs/projects/SUR-B3-28.md)) for files, understanding that server-side
  encryption does not protect against the server · Tella ([OSINT-C3-06](docs/projects/OSINT-C3-06.md)) for field documentation.
- **AI:** local only, no exceptions. llama.cpp or Ollama, never a hosted API, and audit the
  simonw/llm log store because it holds full document content.
- **Rules that matter more than tools:** never use the InVID plugin on unpublished media (it
  uploads) · never run `datasette publish` on source-derived data · never create a Perma link
  during an investigation (it publishes the URL and date) · never request an ArchiveBot crawl of
  a target (the request is public IRC).

## Significant findings

### Licensing — the ones that will actually bite

1. **MVT and androidqf are not OSI-licensed.** MVT License 1.1 §3.0 requires the Data Owner's
   explicit, uncoerced, fully informed consent *including disclosure of your data-retention and
   disposal policy*. Quoted verbatim in `sources/evidence/leads.md`. Build the consent script.
2. **SuperGlue is academic/non-profit noncommercial only** (Magic Leap agreement, read this
   session). It is the most-cited matcher in geolocation pipelines, GitHub reports NOASSERTION so
   scanners miss it, and hloc's default pipelines can pull its weights. Use LoFTR (Apache-2.0).
3. **Marker and Surya weights are OpenRAIL-M** with a commercial threshold of **$5M revenue OR
   funding** ($2M for Chandra) — verified on datalab.to/pricing. Docling is the licence-clean
   alternative.
4. **Do No Harm licence** on Forensic Architecture's timemap and mtriage: clause 4 bars use by
   organisations deriving majority income from a listed set of activities, and clause 5 makes it
   viral on redistribution. Both repositories are also dormant.
5. **OpenSanctions: code MIT, data CC-BY-NC-4.0.** The data is the restricted layer and
   commercial use needs a paid licence (quote only). "OpenSanctions is open source" is true of
   the code only.
6. **Tracker Radar is CC-BY-NC-SA-4.0 data**, not software — NonCommercial plus ShareAlike, and
   GitHub reports NOASSERTION.
7. **CC-BY-NC on model weights** where you would not expect it: GLiNER v0/v1 checkpoints (the
   ones most tutorials link to), NVIDIA Sortformer diarisation, DeepfakeBench. The Apache-2.0
   code licence never cures a restricted weights licence.
8. **Non-OSI "open" tools:** n8n is Sustainable Use Licence (fair-code); MinerU is Apache-2.0
   *plus unread restrictive additional terms*; TruFor, Noiseprint, SBI and LAA-Net are all
   academic or non-profit-only.
9. **OnionShare is GPL-3.0** — session 1's error came from reading a bundled third-party licence.
   Corrected with primary evidence.
10. **AGPL network copyleft** matters in exactly one place people miss: embedding wabac.js in a
    public newsroom web application. Take advice before shipping that.

### Maintenance — what died, and why

Of 361 projects: 228 actively maintained, 72 stable with low activity, 18 declining, 25 dormant,
6 archived, 12 uncertain.

**Archived (confirmed `archived=true`):** Telethon (MIT, 12k stars — Telegram collection
pipelines inherit the risk) · Kùzu (embedded graph DB, final release 2025-10-10) ·
news-please (still widely recommended in data-journalism material) · pagodo · Whoogle ·
CooRnet · meedan/fetch.

**The pattern:** almost everything that died in 2024-2026 died because a **platform API or
scraping path was withdrawn**, not because maintainers lost interest. CrowdTangle killed CooRnet;
Google's anti-scraping killed Whoogle and automated dorking. Design collection layers so the data
source is replaceable without rewriting the analysis — CooRTweet versus CooRnet is the model.

**Declining but undeprecated, which is the dangerous state:** alephdata/aleph (use OpenAleph) ·
alephdata/followthemoney 3.x (use opensanctions/followthemoney 4.x — the old URL does *not*
redirect) · dedupe (no push since 2025-07-29; use Splink) · olmOCR (no activity since March 2026)
· Klaxon self-hosted (README warns it may miss changes) · Hyphe · Overview · Atlos (no release in
14 months, holding investigation-critical data).

**22 repository transfers verified by redirect**, including faster-whisper → SYSTRAN,
marker/surya → datalab-to, sentence-transformers → huggingface, DVC → **treeverse**,
Presidio → data-privacy-stack, NVIDIA/NeMo → NVIDIA-NeMo/Speech, Ragas → vibrantlabsai.
Pinned git URLs keep working; SBOMs and provenance records should be updated.

**17 session-1 candidate paths were genuine 404s** — bad discovery guesses, each resolved to its
real home in `sources/evidence/leads.md`.

### Pricing — verified, and deliberately unpriced

Verified from vendor pages with currency, period and basis: Transkribus (EUR0-449/yr plus credits)
· Datalab ($5M threshold; hosted Free/$400/mo Team) · Maltego (EUR3,000-7,500/yr per seat) ·
pyannote.ai (EUR0.035-0.198 per audio-hour) · Neo4j (Community free GPL-3; AuraDB from
$0.09/GB/hour; Enterprise quote-only) · Gemini API per-million-token rates with dated increases.

**Sentinel Hub / Planet: not publicly listed — quote required.** Re-verified twice: the
sentinel-hub pricing page returns only a redirect to planet.com/pricing, which renders no prices.
Treat commercial satellite imagery as an unpriced dependency and build on openly licensed
Sentinel/Landsat via pystac wherever the story allows.

**Have I Been Pwned figures are LOW confidence** — from secondary sources, not verified on the
vendor page. Do not budget against them.

**Deliberately not asserted:** DocumentCloud, Browsertrix hosted, Perma.cc, MuckRock, Shodan,
Censys, FOFA, Hunter, ZoomEye, Serper, OpenAI, Google Programmable Search, Carrot Search Lingo3G,
Artifex's PyMuPDF commercial licence, OpenCellID, Global Fishing Watch. Each is recorded as
unknown rather than estimated.

### Dependency and operational-security findings

- **Tools that upload by default and are easy to use anyway:** InVID-WeVerify plugin (media to
  AFP/vera.ai plus Google/Baidu/Yandex) · `datasette publish` · Perma.cc link creation ·
  ArchiveBot requests (public IRC) · OpenRefine reconciliation · Marker's LLM-enhancement mode ·
  Surya's configurable remote inference endpoint · webchanges' AI summaries · kuroi against a
  hosted model. Each is one click or one config line from disclosing an investigation.
- **Queries that disclose your targets to commercial vendors:** uncover and Mihari (scan
  databases) · streetlevel (Google/Apple/**Yandex**) · Maltego transforms · OpenCellID API.
- **The worst irony in the catalogue:** kuroi exists to find and remove source-identifying data
  and, pointed at a hosted LLM, transmits the unredacted documents to that provider.
- **Three tools whose own presence endangers the user** in a hostile jurisdiction: Tails (the
  USB), Orbot (the app), Tella (the camouflaged app). Brief people honestly.
- **Two dependency traps worth naming:** `alephdata/followthemoney` is two major versions behind
  with no redirect; grab-site depends on wpull, dormant since April 2024, so both layers stalled.

## Remaining evidence gaps and provisional conclusions

23 projects are marked **provisional** and 13 are **low confidence**. The substantive gaps:

1. **Unresolved licences** (treat reuse as legally unclear): AVeriTeC, ClaimsKG extractor,
   ASVspoof 2021 baselines, Deepfake-Eval-2024, dorks_hunter, stalkerware-indicators,
   AmnestyTech/investigations. Indicator repositories without licences are a systemic problem.
2. **MinerU's additional terms were recorded as restrictive in session 1 but not characterised.**
   Get a legal reading before any commercial use.
3. **Stanza's model archives have no stated licence** while the code is Apache-2.0. Unresolved
   commercial-use risk for derived published datasets.
4. **Hosted-service maintenance cannot be evidenced like a repository's.** Google Fact Check
   Tools API, Internet Society Pulse, DataIndex.us, Microsoft Planetary Computer, OpenCellID and
   the Senate LDA database are classified Uncertain on purpose, not by omission.
5. **Bot protection is not evidence of removal.** OpenSecrets and lda.senate.gov returned 403 to
   `curl`; both are recorded as live-but-unverified. The **EU Transparency Register** is the one
   genuinely unresolved source URL — the old ec.europa.eu path 404s.
6. **Scoop's cryptographic signing format was not independently verified** beyond the
   maintainers' description. Confirm with Harvard LIL before relying on it in a legal filing.
7. **Model weights not individually verified** for Docling, PaddleOCR, Alegre's bundled
   checkpoints, RAGFlow's parsing models, Kraken's Zenodo models and several spaCy and Stanza
   language packs. In each case the code licence is clear and the weights are not.
8. **No project was installed or run.** Every capability claim rests on documentation, repository
   inspection and API metadata. The three I would want hands-on before committing budget are
   OpenAleph (Elasticsearch sizing), RAGFlow (whether reporters trust it appropriately) and
   Rayhunter (false-positive rate on your actual networks).
9. **Feedback is thin by design.** Where I found no documented user reports, the card says so.
   Issue-to-star ratios and release cadence are used as *maintenance* evidence, never as proxies
   for quality or for user satisfaction.

**Recovered versus new.** Session 1's consolidation reported 185 unique projects. That count was
**one too high**: ThreatExchange appeared twice because A4 recorded it as `meta/ThreatExchange`
and C2 as `facebook/ThreatExchange`, and session 1's RENAMES map lacked that transfer. The GitHub
API confirms the redirect, so **184 recovered projects** carry into this catalogue, all of them
assessed. The remaining **177 are new work** in this session: the four segments session 1 never
reached (A1 32, A3 20, B2 20, B3 31 new of 33) plus 32 new C2 records filling the truncated
geospatial, satellite, aviation and maritime coverage, and 42 new C3 records.

**Segment totals:** A1 32 · A2 61 · A3 20 · A4 31 · B1 27 · B2 20 · B3 33 · C1 45 · C2 50 · C3 42.
**Pillars:** Journalism and AI 144 · Surveillance and journalist protection 80 · OSINT 137.

**Segment re-homing.** Each project appears in exactly one segment. Where session 1's assignment
did not match a project's primary role it was moved and the move recorded in `STATE.md`:
Dangerzone and mat2 to B3; yt-dlp to C1; ExifTool, PyExifTool, ImageHash, MediaInfo,
PySceneDetect, Sherloq, GeoCLIP, ShadowFinder and SunCalc to C2. No project is counted twice.

# Assessment of every project

All 361 projects in overall rank order. Every assessment carries the same fourteen fields; project claims, documented feedback and the author's judgement are kept separate. Each heading links to the project's own page.

## 1. ExifTool — 96/100

`OSINT-C2-01` · C2 · Image/video verification, geolocation, satellite, aviation and maritime · Metadata extraction · **cli** · bucket `verified-oss` · maintainer Phil Harvey
[Project page](docs/projects/OSINT-C2-01.md) · [repository](https://github.com/exiftool/exiftool) · [docs](https://exiftool.org/)

**Scores** — relevance 5/5 · capability 5/5 · maintenance 5/5 · privacy 5/5 · usability 4/5 · licence+cost 4/5 → **weighted 96/100** (pillar rank 1, segment rank 1)

### 1. Purpose

Perl library and command-line tool that reads, writes and edits metadata in several hundred file formats, covering EXIF, IPTC, XMP, GPS, maker notes and embedded thumbnails.

### Journalism / investigative use case

First step on almost every image verification: dump the full metadata block to read capture time, GPS coordinates, device and lens, software history and embedded thumbnails. An embedded thumbnail that disagrees with the main image is a classic indicator that the visible picture was edited after capture.

### 2. Audience

journalist, newsroom analyst, specialist investigator

### 3. Project type

cli · bucket `verified-oss`

### 4. Pros

- Unmatched format and maker-note coverage — it reads proprietary camera fields no other tool parses, which is often where the useful capture detail lives
- The embedded-thumbnail extraction is a genuine forensic technique, not just metadata reading, and it has broken real cases
- Entirely local with no dependencies beyond Perl, so it runs on an air-gapped evidence machine and nothing is transmitted
- Exceptionally maintained for a single-maintainer project: release 13.64 and a near-empty tracker (19 open issues against 5,268 stars)

### 5. Cons

- Metadata is evidence about a file, not about reality: every field can be written or stripped — by ExifTool itself — so a plausible EXIF block is corroboration, never authentication
- Most social platforms strip metadata on upload, so for the majority of circulating images there is simply nothing to read, and reporters misread that absence as suspicious
- The output is dense and expert-oriented; a non-specialist will not know which of 400 fields matter
- Perl dependency is unusual in a modern stack, and the write capability makes it easy to alter evidence accidentally if used carelessly

### 6. Feedback (documented)

No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 5,268 stars with only 19 open issues and a current tag (13.64), pushed 2026-11-16 — extraordinary maintenance consistency over two decades. ExifTool is the de facto standard underneath most other metadata tooling, verifiable from PyExifTool, Sherloq and ArchiveBox all depending on it.

### 7. Assessment

Adopt unconditionally: it is the baseline instrument for image and document files and there is no substitute. For your profile two disciplines matter. First, work on copies — ExifTool can write, and an accidental write destroys the evidential value of the original. Second, train reporters that stripped metadata is the normal case for social media, so 'no EXIF' is not a finding. Pair with MediaInfo for video containers, where ExifTool is weaker.

### 8. Maintenance

**Actively maintained** — GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-16, latest tag 13.64, no GitHub release objects (releases are published on exiftool.org), 5,268 stars, 19 open issues. Continuous releases over twenty years from a single maintainer with near-zero backlog — the strongest issue-throughput record in the catalogue.

### 9. Licensing

**Licence:** GPL-3.0 _(SPDX verified)_

**Model / data licence:** n/a

**Restrictions:** GPL-3.0 (the upstream distribution is also offered under the Artistic Licence — check the distribution you obtain). Embedding in a closed-source newsroom product would trigger copyleft; calling the CLI as a subprocess does not.

**Licence evidence:** https://github.com/exiftool/exiftool/blob/master/LICENSE

### 10. Costs

No fee, no infrastructure, no paid dependencies. Among the cheapest high-value capabilities here.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

Entirely local; nothing is transmitted, which makes it safe for source-sensitive material. The inverse risk matters more: ExifTool reveals GPS and device data in files you may intend to publish, so it is also the tool that tells you what to strip.

### 12. Verdict

**Adopt**

### 13. Alternatives

- [PyExifTool](docs/projects/OSINT-C2-02.md) to drive it from a Python pipeline
- [Exiv2](docs/projects/OSINT-C2-03.md) for a C++ library embedding path
- [MediaInfo](docs/projects/OSINT-C2-04.md) for video container and encoder analysis
- [mat2](docs/projects/SUR-B3-07.md) for removing rather than reading metadata

### 14. Evidence

Verified **2026-11-17** · confidence **high** · assessment depth `metadata-verified`

- https://github.com/exiftool/exiftool
- https://exiftool.org/
- https://github.com/exiftool/exiftool/blob/master/LICENSE

## 2. llama.cpp — 96/100

`JAI-A3-01` · A3 · RAG, research agents, knowledge graphs, provenance and AI evaluation · Local LLM inference · **library** · bucket `verified-oss` · maintainer Georgi Gerganov / ggml-org
[Project page](docs/projects/JAI-A3-01.md) · [repository](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp) · [docs](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp#readme)

**Scores** — relevance 5/5 · capability 5/5 · maintenance 5/5 · privacy 5/5 · usability 3/5 · licence+cost 5/5 → **weighted 96/100** (pillar rank 1, segment rank 1)

### 1. Purpose

C/C++ inference engine for large language models using the ggml/GGUF format, with quantisation, CPU and GPU backends across many platforms, and an OpenAI-compatible server.

### Journalism / investigative use case

The foundation of any newsroom AI capability that must not send documents to a vendor: run a capable instruction model on your own hardware for summarisation, claim extraction, translation assistance or redaction detection, with leaked material never leaving the building.

### 2. Audience

engineer

### 3. Project type

library · bucket `verified-oss`

### 4. Pros

- Makes local inference genuinely practical on ordinary hardware through aggressive quantisation — which is what turns 'we should process this locally' into something that finishes
- OpenAI-compatible server means tools written against hosted APIs (kuroi, Loki-style pipelines, your own code) can be pointed at your own model with a configuration change rather than a rewrite
- MIT licensed with extraordinary activity (135,527 stars, v1.0.0 released 2026-11-13, pushed 2026-11-17) and backends for CPU, CUDA, Metal, Vulkan and more
- Single binary with no Python dependency, so it deploys on a hardened or air-gapped machine where a framework install is impractical

### 5. Cons

- Fast-moving with frequent breaking changes in quantisation formats and server APIs, so pinning is essential and upgrades need testing — the 1.0.0 release is recent and the history before it was volatile
- Quantisation costs quality in ways that vary by model and task, and the loss is rarely measured by the people deploying it — a quantised model that summarises badly will do so plausibly
- Engineer-facing: you supply the model, choose the quantisation and operate the server, and model selection has more effect on output quality than anything the engine does
- Running a local model does not make its output reliable: hallucination is a property of the model, and local deployment removes the privacy problem without touching the accuracy one

### 6. Feedback (documented)

No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 135,527 stars with release v1.0.0 (2026-11-13) and a push on 2026-11-17, MIT licence. Its role as the standard local-inference engine is verifiable from the ecosystem built on it, including Ollama and most desktop LLM applications.

### 7. Assessment

Adopt it as the inference layer for every AI capability you want without a vendor — this is the single component that makes local AI a realistic newsroom choice. For your profile the right pattern is one GPU host running llama.cpp's OpenAI-compatible server, with every internal tool pointed at it, so the decision 'does this document leave the building' is made once in infrastructure rather than repeatedly by users. Pin the version, and evaluate your chosen quantisation on real tasks rather than assuming parity with the full model.

### 8. Maintenance

**Actively maintained** — GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release v1.0.0 (2026-11-13), 135,527 stars. Same-day commits at very high velocity with a newly reached 1.0; the maintenance concern is churn, not neglect.

### 9. Licensing

**Licence:** MIT _(SPDX verified)_

**Model / data licence:** n/a for the engine. Model weights carry their own licences, which vary enormously — this is where the licence risk in local AI actually sits.

**Restrictions:** Engine unrestricted. The engine licence does not launder a restricted model licence: running a non-commercial or restricted-weights model locally is still bound by those weights' terms.

**Licence evidence:** https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/LICENSE

### 10. Costs

No fee. The cost is hardware: a GPU with sufficient VRAM for your chosen model (or substantial RAM for CPU inference at lower speed). One shared GPU host serves a small newsroom. Estimate; assumes self-hosted.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

Entirely local inference with no telemetry and no external calls — the whole point. Model weights are downloaded once and can be pre-staged for air-gapped operation.

### 12. Verdict

**Adopt**

### 13. Alternatives

- [Ollama](docs/projects/JAI-A3-02.md) for a much easier operational wrapper around the same engine
- [vLLM](docs/projects/JAI-A3-03.md) where GPU throughput for many concurrent requests matters more than footprint
- Hosted model APIs — appropriate only for non-sensitive material

### 14. Evidence

Verified **2026-11-17** · confidence **high** · assessment depth `metadata-verified`

- https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp
- https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/LICENSE

## 3. mitmproxy — 96/100

`SUR-B2-06` · B2 · Investigating surveillance companies, infrastructure, procurement and tracking tech · Network traffic interception · **application** · bucket `verified-oss` · maintainer mitmproxy project
[Project page](docs/projects/SUR-B2-06.md) · [repository](https://github.com/mitmproxy/mitmproxy) · [docs](https://docs.mitmproxy.org/)

**Scores** — relevance 5/5 · capability 5/5 · maintenance 5/5 · privacy 5/5 · usability 3/5 · licence+cost 5/5 → **weighted 96/100** (pillar rank 1, segment rank 1)

### 1. Purpose

Interactive TLS-capable intercepting HTTP(S) proxy with a console UI, web interface and Python scripting API, allowing inspection, modification and recording of traffic.

### Journalism / investigative use case

Showing what an app or device actually sends and to whom: put a phone behind mitmproxy, use the app, and record the endpoints, payloads and identifiers transmitted. 'This app sent your contacts to this company's servers' is a story; 'this app requests contacts permission' is not.

### 2. Audience

engineer, specialist investigator

### 3. Project type

application · bucket `verified-oss`

### 4. Pros

- Observed transmission is the strongest form of evidence in app and device investigation — it documents conduct rather than capability, and that is what makes a publishable claim
- Python scripting API means you can automate capture and extraction across many apps or repeated sessions, turning a one-off demonstration into a survey
- MIT licensed with outstanding maintenance (v12.3.1, 2026-10-25; pushed 2026-11-14) and a very large community (47,047 stars)
- Local and self-contained: no cloud service, so the traffic you capture stays with you

### 5. Cons

- Requires installing a CA certificate on the device under test, which modern Android and iOS increasingly resist, and many apps use certificate pinning that defeats interception without further work (patching the app, which escalates the legal question)
- Captured traffic contains credentials, tokens and personal data of whoever used the device — treat captures as highly sensitive and keep them briefly
- Interception of a device you do not own, or of someone else's traffic, raises serious legal and ethical issues; this must be your own test device
- 560 open issues reflecting a broad feature surface; the learning curve for scripting is real

### 6. Feedback (documented)

No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 47,047 stars with 560 open issues, release v12.3.1 (2026-10-25), pushed 2026-11-14, MIT licence. mitmproxy is the standard tool for HTTP interception across security and development work, which is well established in its own documentation and ecosystem.

### 7. Assessment

Adopt it — the capability to show what an app transmits is the single most valuable technical input to surveillance-industry reporting, and nothing else does it as well. For your profile the operating rules are: use a dedicated test device you own, never intercept a colleague's or source's live traffic, destroy captures promptly because they contain credentials, and expect certificate pinning to block the most interesting apps, at which point the realistic options are a specialist partner or a rooted test device with the legal position checked.

### 8. Maintenance

**Actively maintained** — GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-14, latest release v12.3.1 (2026-10-25), 47,047 stars, 560 open issues. Frequent releases on a 12.x line with a broad contributor base and long-term stability.

### 9. Licensing

**Licence:** MIT _(SPDX verified)_

**Model / data licence:** n/a

**Restrictions:** None material. The constraints are legal rather than licensing: intercepting traffic you are not authorised to intercept is unlawful in most jurisdictions.

**Licence evidence:** https://github.com/mitmproxy/mitmproxy/blob/main/LICENSE

### 10. Costs

No fee. A test device and a workstation; negligible infrastructure.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

All capture is local. The sensitivity runs the other way: captures contain credentials and personal data from the test session, so storage, access and retention need the same care as source material.

### 12. Verdict

**Adopt**

### Material blockers

_Tracked separately from the score._

- Certificate pinning blocks interception for many apps; intercepting traffic you are not authorised to intercept is unlawful

### 13. Alternatives

- MobSF's dynamic analysis, which wraps interception into an app-analysis workflow
- Wireshark for lower-level packet capture where HTTP is not the layer of interest
- Frida for defeating certificate pinning — which escalates the legal and technical commitment

### 14. Evidence

Verified **2026-11-17** · confidence **high** · assessment depth `metadata-verified`

- https://github.com/mitmproxy/mitmproxy
- https://docs.mitmproxy.org/
- https://github.com/mitmproxy/mitmproxy/blob/main/LICENSE

## 4. Scrapy — 95/100

`OSINT-C1-16` · C1 · Web and social research, archives and evidence capture · Structured web scraping · **framework** · bucket `verified-oss` · maintainer Zyte and the Scrapy community
[Project page](docs/projects/OSINT-C1-16.md) · [repository](https://github.com/scrapy/scrapy) · [docs](https://docs.scrapy.org/)

**Scores** — relevance 5/5 · capability 5/5 · maintenance 5/5 · privacy 4/5 · usability 4/5 · licence+cost 5/5 → **weighted 95/100** (pillar rank 2, segment rank 1)

### 1. Purpose

Mature Python framework for building web crawlers that extract structured data, with built-in request scheduling, throttling, retry handling, item pipelines and export formats.

### Journalism / investigative use case

Build repeatable bulk collection of structured public records — court listings, corporate registries, planning applications, classifieds — into datasets for analysis. This is the workhorse behind most data-journalism collection that is not a one-off script.

### 2. Audience

engineer

### 3. Project type

framework · bucket `verified-oss`

### 4. Pros

- Handles the unglamorous parts properly: politeness delays, retries, deduplication, concurrency limits and resumable crawls — the things ad-hoc scripts get wrong and that determine whether a multi-day collection completes
- Enormous ecosystem and the best documentation in this category, so a new engineer can be productive in a day and the code is maintainable by the next person
- BSD-3-Clause and very actively maintained (release 2.20.0 on 2026-11-06, 65,442 stars) with a long track record of stability
- Item pipelines give you a clean place to validate and normalise records at collection time, which materially improves dataset quality

### 5. Cons

- Developer tool: no UI, no archiving or evidentiary output by default, so a Scrapy dataset is analysis input rather than evidence of what a page said
- No JavaScript rendering natively — dynamic sites need scrapy-playwright or a separate headless step, which adds complexity
- Learning the framework's conventions (spiders, items, middlewares) is an upfront cost that a simple requests script avoids for small jobs
- 176 open issues; large-site crawls still require hand-tuning of throttling to avoid blocking or harming the target

### 6. Feedback (documented)

No individual user reports verified in this survey, but Scrapy's use in data journalism is extensively documented in the field's teaching materials and in newsroom open-source repositories (openstates-scrapers, querido-diario and similar projects are Scrapy-based, which is verifiable from those repositories).

### 7. Assessment

Adopt as the standard for any collection you expect to run more than once. For your profile the decisive feature is resumability and throttling: a registry crawl that takes four days and can be paused is the difference between a dataset and a failed attempt. Always add a separate evidentiary capture for the specific pages a story will cite — Scrapy gives you data, not proof of what was published.

### 8. Maintenance

**Actively maintained** — GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-16, latest release 2.20.0 (2026-11-06), 65,442 stars, 176 open issues. Regular releases over more than a decade with commercial backing (Zyte) and a broad contributor base.

### 9. Licensing

**Licence:** BSD-3-Clause _(SPDX verified)_

**Model / data licence:** n/a. Collected content belongs to the source publishers.

**Restrictions:** None material for the framework. Scraping engages target sites' terms and, for personal data, data-protection law — both separate from the licence and both real considerations for a registry crawl.

**Licence evidence:** https://github.com/scrapy/scrapy/blob/master/LICENSE

### 10. Costs

No fee. Infrastructure: a VM for long crawls; optional paid proxy or headless-browser services if the target blocks you (vendor costs not priced here). Engineer time is the main cost.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

Requests go from your infrastructure to the targets, and data is stored locally. The target sees your IP and pattern. For personal data in registries, your own data-protection obligations attach to the collected dataset — treat it as regulated material, not just files.

### 12. Verdict

**Adopt**

### 13. Alternatives

- [Crawlee](docs/projects/OSINT-C1-17.md) for a JavaScript/TypeScript-native equivalent with browser support built in
- [katana](docs/projects/OSINT-C1-15.md) for URL discovery rather than structured extraction
- requests plus BeautifulSoup for genuinely one-off small jobs

### 14. Evidence

Verified **2026-11-17** · confidence **high** · assessment depth `metadata-verified`

- https://github.com/scrapy/scrapy
- https://docs.scrapy.org/

## 5. Signal (Android client) — 95/100

`SUR-B3-23` · B3 · Protecting journalists and sources · Secure communications · **application** · bucket `verified-oss` · maintainer Signal Foundation
[Project page](docs/projects/SUR-B3-23.md) · [repository](https://github.com/signalapp/Signal-Android) · [docs](https://support.signal.org/)

**Scores** — relevance 5/5 · capability 5/5 · maintenance 5/5 · privacy 4/5 · usability 5/5 · licence+cost 4/5 → **weighted 95/100** (pillar rank 2, segment rank 1)

### 1. Purpose

End-to-end encrypted messaging application for text, voice and video, with disappearing messages, sealed sender, safety numbers for key verification and encrypted group messaging.

### Journalism / investigative use case

The default channel for source communication where a phone number is acceptable: messages and calls are end-to-end encrypted, disappearing messages limit what a seized device reveals, and the protocol is the most scrutinised in the field. In practice it is the channel most sources already have.

### 2. Audience

journalist, newsroom analyst, specialist investigator

### 3. Project type

application · bucket `verified-oss`

### 4. Pros

- The most heavily analysed end-to-end encryption protocol in general use, with repeated independent cryptographic review — the strongest assurance basis of any communications tool here
- Disappearing messages and remote-deletion materially reduce what a seized or compromised device yields, which is the realistic threat for most journalists
- AGPL-3.0 client and server, actively maintained (v8.35.2, 2026-11-09; pushed 2026-11-16), with reproducible-build efforts and a non-profit operator
- Ubiquity matters: a protected channel the source already uses beats a better one they will not install

### 5. Cons

- Requires a phone number, which is an identifier the source must reveal to you and to Signal — a real limitation when the source must not be identifiable at all, and the reason SecureDrop exists
- Metadata minimisation is strong but not absolute: Signal knows when accounts registered and, to a limited degree, when they connect, and the operator is subject to legal process (its published transparency responses show it holds very little)
- Centralised service dependency: if Signal is blocked in a country, sources need censorship circumvention, and that adds operational burden exactly where it is hardest
- Safety-number verification is the step that makes end-to-end encryption meaningful against interception, and almost nobody does it — a training rather than a software problem

### 6. Feedback (documented)

No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 29,652 stars with 491 open issues, release v8.35.2 (2026-11-09), pushed 2026-11-16, AGPL-3.0; the server (signalapp/Signal-Server, AGPL-3.0, pushed 2026-11-16) is also published, which is unusual and supports the privacy claims. The protocol's cryptographic review record is extensively documented in published literature.

### 7. Assessment

Adopt as the default communication channel and train safety-number verification, because unverified end-to-end encryption protects against the wrong threat. For your profile the phone-number requirement is the decision point: use Signal for ongoing contact with sources whose identity you already know, and SecureDrop or Hush Line for first contact with sources who must stay anonymous. In exile contexts, plan for Signal being blocked — pre-arrange circumvention and a fallback channel before it is needed.

### 8. Maintenance

**Actively maintained** — GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-16, latest release v8.35.2 (2026-11-09), tag v8.36.2, 29,652 stars, 491 open issues. Frequent releases under a funded non-profit; the server component is separately published and equally current.

### 9. Licensing

**Licence:** AGPL-3.0 _(SPDX verified)_

**Model / data licence:** n/a

**Restrictions:** AGPL-3.0 on client and server. Note that running a modified client against Signal's servers is contrary to the service's terms regardless of the licence — relevant to forks like Molly.

**Licence evidence:** https://github.com/signalapp/Signal-Android/blob/main/LICENSE

### 10. Costs

Free to use. No infrastructure. Cost is training time and the operational work of maintaining circumvention where Signal is blocked.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

End-to-end encrypted content with strong metadata minimisation, backed by a published server implementation and a transparency record showing very little retained data. The irreducible disclosure is the phone number, which is an identifier linking source to journalist.

### 12. Verdict

**Adopt**

### Material blockers

_Tracked separately from the score._

- Requires a phone number — unsuitable where the source must not be identifiable

### 13. Alternatives

- [SimpleX Chat](docs/projects/SUR-B3-25.md) where no identifier at all can be exchanged
- [Molly](docs/projects/SUR-B3-24.md) for a hardened Signal-compatible Android client
- [SecureDrop](docs/projects/SUR-B3-01.md) or Hush Line for anonymous first contact

### 14. Evidence

Verified **2026-11-17** · confidence **high** · assessment depth `metadata-verified`

## 6. yt-dlp — 95/100

`OSINT-C1-45` · C1 · Web and social research, archives and evidence capture · Media capture · **cli** · bucket `verified-oss` · maintainer yt-dlp community
[Project page](docs/projects/OSINT-C1-45.md) · [repository](https://github.com/yt-dlp/yt-dlp) · [docs](https://github.com/yt-dlp/yt-dlp#readme)

**Scores** — relevance 5/5 · capability 5/5 · maintenance 5/5 · privacy 4/5 · usability 4/5 · licence+cost 5/5 → **weighted 95/100** (pillar rank 3, segment rank 2)

### 1. Purpose

Command-line media downloader supporting well over a thousand sites, retrieving video, audio, subtitles, thumbnails and uploader metadata at the highest available quality, with extensive format and post-processing control.

### Journalism / investigative use case

The workhorse for securing a copy of social video before deletion — pulling the highest available bitrate (crucial because compression destroys the artefacts forensic analysis relies on), plus uploader metadata, upload timestamps, subtitles and thumbnails. For verification work, the bitrate point is decisive: a re-encoded copy from a screen recording is forensically useless.

### 2. Audience

journalist, newsroom analyst, engineer, specialist investigator

### 3. Project type

cli · bucket `verified-oss`

### 4. Pros

- Highest-available-quality retrieval preserves the forensic signal that any re-encoding destroys, which makes it the correct first step before any media verification
- Captures uploader metadata, upload timestamps, subtitles and thumbnails alongside the media — often the evidentiary context that matters more than the video itself
- Unlicense (public domain) and extraordinarily active (208,589 stars, release 2026.10.26, pushed 2026-11-17), with extractors updated continuously as platforms change
- Covers over a thousand sites, so it works on the regional and niche platforms where much relevant material actually lives

### 5. Cons

- A capture tool with no verification logic and no authenticity judgement — it tells you nothing about whether the content is real
- Extractors break frequently when platforms change, so you must pin or update often and expect occasional silent format downgrades that quietly reduce quality
- Contacts the target platform directly from the operator's machine, so your IP and request pattern are visible to that platform — and for a high-volume capture campaign that is an identifiable footprint
- Downloading may breach platform terms of service and, depending on jurisdiction and purpose, raises copyright questions that are a legal rather than technical matter

### 6. Feedback (documented)

No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 208,589 stars with 2,790 open issues, release 2026.10.26, pushed 2026-11-17 — the largest community in this catalogue, with a backlog that reflects the constant churn of platform extractors rather than neglect. The project itself notes platform-specific constraints in its documentation.

### 7. Assessment

Adopt unconditionally as the media-capture step — the quality-preservation property alone makes it non-negotiable before verification work. For your profile the operational points are: capture from a dedicated egress rather than the newsroom address when the uploader should not know you are looking, record the yt-dlp version and the full metadata JSON alongside the media so the capture is documented, and update frequently because a stale extractor silently gives you a lower-quality file. Treat the terms-of-service and copyright questions as editorial decisions, taken knowingly.

### 8. Maintenance

**Actively maintained** — GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release 2026.10.26, 208,589 stars, 2,790 open issues. Continuous releases on a date-based scheme with same-day commits; the huge issue count is intrinsic to maintaining a thousand platform extractors against constant upstream change.

### 9. Licensing

**Licence:** Unlicense _(SPDX verified)_

**Model / data licence:** n/a. Downloaded content belongs to the original rights holders.

**Restrictions:** None from the licence — the Unlicense is a public-domain dedication. The real constraints are external: platform terms of service and copyright in the downloaded material, both of which are editorial and legal judgements rather than licence issues.

**Licence evidence:** https://github.com/yt-dlp/yt-dlp/blob/master/LICENSE

### 10. Costs

No fee. FFmpeg/FFprobe strongly recommended; yt-dlp-ejs with a JavaScript runtime for some sites. Storage for high-bitrate media is the real cost and grows quickly. Estimate.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

Contacts the target platform directly from the operator's machine, so IP and request pattern are visible to that platform. For sensitive subjects, capture from a dedicated egress. Downloaded metadata may include personal information about uploaders, which attracts your own data-protection obligations.

### 12. Verdict

**Adopt**

### 13. Alternatives

- gallery-dl for image-focused platform capture
- [browsertrix-crawler](docs/projects/OSINT-C1-29.md) or ArchiveWeb.page to capture the surrounding page as evidence of context
- Platform-specific archival tools where yt-dlp lacks an extractor

### 14. Evidence

Verified **2026-11-17** · confidence **high** · assessment depth `metadata-verified`

**Scores** — relevance 5/5 · capability 5/5 · maintenance 5/5 · privacy 5/5 · usability 3/5 · licence+cost 4/5 → **weighted 94/100** (pillar rank 4, segment rank 3)

### 1. Purpose

Dockerised browser-based crawler that drives Chromium to produce high-fidelity WARC/WACZ captures, with configurable scope, behaviours for dynamic pages and sitemap support.

### Journalism / investigative use case

Capture modern government portals, dashboards and interactive document viewers faithfully enough that the archived copy still behaves like the live page when a disputed change is later examined — the capture tool of record for anything built as a single-page application.

### 2. Audience

engineer, newsroom analyst

### 3. Project type

framework · bucket `verified-oss`

### 4. Pros

- Highest practical capture fidelity in this catalogue for dynamic content, because it records what a real browser actually fetched and rendered
- Single Docker image with declarative configuration, which makes it dramatically easier to operate than brozzler for comparable capability
- WACZ output is a single portable file that ReplayWeb.page can open with no server, so sharing a capture with an editor or lawyer is trivial

### 5. Cons

- No change detection or alerting — it is capture infrastructure, so monitoring must be built around it
- Resource-hungry: browser-based capture is far slower and more memory-intensive per page than static crawling, which caps throughput
- AGPL-3.0 has network-service implications if you expose a modified version, which is worth a legal check before building a capture service for partners
- Requires Docker familiarity and 152 open issues reflect the complexity of behaviours across many site types

### 6. Feedback (documented)

No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 1,197 stars with 152 open issues, release v1.15.4 (2026-11-11), pushed 2026-11-14. Webrecorder's tooling is the de facto standard in modern web archiving, verifiable from IIPC and institutional archive adoption.

### 7. Assessment

Adopt as your capture tool of record for anything dynamic or disputed. For your profile the combination that works is browsertrix-crawler for capture, WACZ as the artefact, and ReplayWeb.page for handing a capture to a colleague or lawyer who has no infrastructure. Write the capture configuration into version control alongside the investigation notes, so the methodology is reproducible — that is what makes the capture defensible rather than merely good.

### 8. Maintenance

**Actively maintained** — GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-14, latest release v1.15.4 (2026-11-11), 1,197 stars, 152 open issues. Frequent releases from a funded organisation whose core mission this is.

**Licence:** AGPL-3.0 _(SPDX verified)_

**Model / data licence:** n/a. Captured content belongs to the original publishers.

**Restrictions:** AGPL-3.0: offering a modified version as a network service obliges source publication. Running it internally to produce captures carries no obligation.

**Licence evidence:** https://github.com/webrecorder/browsertrix-crawler/blob/main/LICENSE

### 10. Costs

No fee. Infrastructure estimate: a Docker host with several GB of RAM per concurrent browser plus storage for WACZ output; capture throughput is low enough that large crawls need either patience or parallel workers. Assumptions: self-hosted, moderate crawl sizes.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

WARC/WACZ output is written to storage you control (local disk or S3-compatible); nothing is sent to Webrecorder unless you choose their hosted service. Note that captures of logged-in sessions will contain session material — treat output as sensitive.

**Adopt**

## 8. OpenSanctions (dataset) — 94/100

`OSINT-C3-01` · C3 · Public records, corporate ownership, finance, infrastructure, link analysis, collaboration · Sanctions and PEP data · **dataset** · bucket `source-available-restricted` · maintainer OpenSanctions Datenbanken GmbH
[Project page](docs/projects/OSINT-C3-01.md) · [repository](https://github.com/opensanctions/opensanctions) · [docs](https://www.opensanctions.org/docs/)

**Scores** — relevance 5/5 · capability 5/5 · maintenance 5/5 · privacy 5/5 · usability 4/5 · licence+cost 3/5 → **weighted 94/100** (pillar rank 5, segment rank 1)

### 1. Purpose

Continuously built dataset of sanctioned entities, politically exposed persons, companies of interest and related entities, assembled from hundreds of official sources and published in FollowTheMoney format with the build pipeline open-sourced.

### Journalism / investigative use case

The screening layer for any investigation involving money or power: check a leaked client list, shareholder register or property dataset against sanctions and PEP data to find the names that matter. It is the difference between a spreadsheet of 40,000 names and a shortlist of twelve.

### 2. Audience

newsroom analyst, specialist investigator, engineer

### 3. Project type

dataset · bucket `source-available-restricted`

### 4. Pros

- Breadth and currency: hundreds of official source lists consolidated and rebuilt continuously, which no newsroom could replicate and which commercial screening vendors charge heavily for
- Published in FollowTheMoney, so it joins directly to your own entity data through nomenklatura and yente without a mapping project
- Code is MIT and the build pipeline is public (pushed 2026-11-17), so the provenance of every entity is traceable to its source list — which matters when a screening hit informs a published allegation
- Self-hostable with yente, so screening happens on your infrastructure and your query targets stay private

### 5. Cons

- LICENCE BLOCKER for commercial use: the DATA is CC-BY-NC 4.0 and commercial use requires a paid licence, with the Screening Licence and Reseller/OEM options quote-only (verified on the vendor licensing page). A commercially operated newsroom cannot assume its use is non-commercial
- PEP designation is a status, not an allegation: a match means a person holds or held public office or is connected to someone who does, and reporting it as suspicion would be wrong
- Entity matching produces candidates requiring adjudication — name collisions are frequent, especially for common names in transliteration, so a hit is a question not a finding
- No GitHub releases (continuous build), so pinning a dataset state for a reproducible analysis means recording the build date yourself

### 6. Feedback (documented)

No individual user reports verified in this survey. The decisive documented facts: code licence MIT (licence blob read 2026-11-17, copyright OpenSanctions Datenbanken GmbH with earlier Friedrich Lindenberg and Journalism Development Network copyrights), and data CC-BY-NC 4.0 with commercial use requiring a paid licence and quote-only enterprise tiers (vendor licensing page, verified 2026-11-16). Recorded in sources/evidence/leads.md L6 and pricing.md.

### 7. Assessment

Adopt the capability and settle the data licence explicitly in writing — that is the whole decision. Self-host with yente so query targets stay internal, and resolve whether your outlet's use is non-commercial before building a workflow on it; if it is not, price the commercial licence rather than relying on an optimistic reading of CC-BY-NC. Editorially, treat every match as a lead requiring identity confirmation, and never publish a PEP match as an implication of wrongdoing.

### 8. Maintenance

**Actively maintained** — GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, no release objects (continuous build model), 878 stars, MIT code licence. Daily commits on the build pipeline with a commercial entity dependent on the dataset's currency — the strongest possible maintenance incentive.

### 9. Licensing

**Licence:** MIT (code) _(SPDX verified)_

**Model / data licence:** Data is CC-BY-NC 4.0; commercial use requires a paid licence (Screening Licence and Reseller/OEM are quote-only; the Screening API uses prepaid credit bundles with free credits on signup).

**Restrictions:** Material and the central consideration: NonCommercial bars commercial exploitation of the data, and NGO or journalism status does not automatically satisfy it. Publishing an article informed by the data is ordinary journalistic use; building a paid product or client-facing screening service on it is not. 'OpenSanctions is open source' is true of the code only.

**Licence evidence:** https://www.opensanctions.org/licensing/

### 10. Costs

Code and non-commercial data use free. Commercial data licence: quote required, not publicly listed (verified 2026-11-16). Self-hosting needs an Elasticsearch/OpenSearch node for yente. Hosted Screening API sold in prepaid credit bundles. Estimate for self-hosting: one 8-16GB VM.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

Self-hosting with yente keeps your screening queries entirely private — the decisive advantage over hosted screening APIs, which learn exactly whom you are investigating. The dataset itself concerns public figures and sanctioned entities.

### 12. Verdict

**Adopt**

### Material blockers

_Tracked separately from the score._

- Data is CC-BY-NC 4.0 — commercial-use licence required, price not publicly listed

### 13. Alternatives

- [yente](docs/projects/JAI-A2-61.md) for the self-hosted screening API over this data
- Official sanctions lists directly (OFAC, EU, UN) for a licence-free but far more laborious approach
- Commercial screening vendors, which are expensive and disclose your query targets

Python library extending pandas with geometry columns, providing spatial joins, overlays, buffering, dissolving, reprojection and plotting over vector data.

### Journalism / investigative use case

The scripted counterpart to QGIS for reproducible spatial analysis: join a leaked list of addresses to electoral boundaries to show which districts a scheme benefited, count incidents within a radius of military installations, or dissolve parcel data by owner to reveal concentrated land holdings.

### 2. Audience

engineer, newsroom analyst

### 3. Project type

library · bucket `verified-oss`

### 4. Pros

- Reproducibility is the decisive advantage over desktop GIS: a notebook documenting every spatial operation can be rerun, reviewed and published as methodology, which a sequence of QGIS clicks cannot
- Familiar pandas idioms mean a data journalist already comfortable with dataframes can do spatial joins without learning GIS software
- BSD-3-Clause with active maintenance (v1.2.0, 2026-09-28) and a 1.x stable API after a long pre-1.0 period
- Integrates with the whole Python data stack, so spatial results flow directly into charts, tables and further analysis

### 5. Cons

- Spatial joins on large datasets are memory-hungry and slow compared with a spatial database — above a few million geometries you want PostGIS or DuckDB spatial
- 437 open issues and a dependency chain (shapely, pyproj, GDAL bindings) that is a frequent source of installation pain, especially on Windows
- Reprojection correctness is the user's responsibility: geopandas will happily compute a wrong area if you forget to project out of degrees, and it is the single most common error in published spatial journalism
- No visualisation beyond basic matplotlib plots, so publication-quality maps need another tool

### 6. Feedback (documented)

No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 5,301 stars with 437 open issues, release v1.2.0 (2026-09-28), pushed 2026-11-14, BSD-3-Clause. Widely used in data journalism, reflected in its prominence in the field's teaching materials.

### 7. Assessment

Adopt as the default for any spatial analysis that will inform a published claim, precisely because the notebook is the methodology. For your profile I would pair it with one habit: assert the CRS explicitly at the top of every analysis and compute areas and distances only in a projected CRS appropriate to the region. That single discipline prevents the most common category of spatial error in journalism.

### 8. Maintenance

**Actively maintained** — GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-14, latest release v1.2.0 (2026-09-28), 5,301 stars, 437 open issues. Regular releases on a stable 1.x line with a broad contributor base and NumFOCUS-adjacent governance.

### 9. Licensing

**Licence:** BSD-3-Clause _(SPDX verified)_

**Model / data licence:** n/a. Datasets carry their own licences.

**Restrictions:** None material.

**Licence evidence:** https://github.com/geopandas/geopandas/blob/main/LICENSE.txt

### 10. Costs

No fee. CPU and RAM proportional to dataset size; memory is the binding constraint on large joins. Negligible infrastructure for typical newsroom datasets.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

Local processing. Note that some convenience functions can download basemaps or example datasets from external hosts — review before use on an isolated machine.

### 12. Verdict

**Adopt**

### 13. Alternatives

- DuckDB spatial or PostGIS for datasets too large for memory
- [QGIS](docs/projects/OSINT-C2-19.md) for interactive exploration and georeferencing
- [rasterio](docs/projects/OSINT-C2-22.md) for raster rather than vector analysis

### 14. Evidence

Verified **2026-11-17** · confidence **high** · assessment depth `metadata-verified`

## 12. mat2 — 94/100

`SUR-B3-07` · B3 · Protecting journalists and sources · Metadata removal · **cli** · bucket `verified-oss` · maintainer Julien Voisin (jvoisin)
[Project page](docs/projects/SUR-B3-07.md) · [repository](https://github.com/jvoisin/mat2) · [docs](https://0xacab.org/jvoisin/mat2)

**Scores** — relevance 5/5 · capability 4/5 · maintenance 5/5 · privacy 5/5 · usability 4/5 · licence+cost 5/5 → **weighted 94/100** (pillar rank 3, segment rank 2)

### 1. Purpose

Metadata removal tool supporting a wide range of file formats — images, documents, audio, video, archives — that strips identifying metadata and can report which formats are supported on the current system.

### Journalism / investigative use case

The counterpart to verification: strip identifying metadata from images and documents before publishing or sharing them, so a published photo does not burn the source's device, location or filesystem trail. This is the step that has repeatedly failed in real cases where published files carried GPS coordinates or author names.

### 2. Audience

journalist, newsroom analyst, engineer

### 3. Project type

cli · bucket `verified-oss`

### 4. Pros

- Breadth of format support means one tool covers the realistic range of files a newsroom publishes, rather than needing per-format handling
- Addresses a documented and recurring failure mode — published files leaking source-identifying metadata — with a simple, auditable intervention
- LGPL-3.0-or-later with exemplary maintenance: release 0.15.0 (2026-08-04), pushed 2026-11-15, and only 2 open issues against 394 stars
- Fully local processing, and `--check-dependencies` tells you honestly which formats your installation can actually clean

### 5. Cons

- Cleaning is best-effort and format-specific: unsupported formats may be refused or incompletely cleaned, so a silent partial clean is possible and you must check the tool's own report rather than assume success
- It cannot remove information in visible pixels — reflections, screen contents, identifiable surroundings, visible badges — which is a frequent and more serious disclosure route than metadata
- Per-format system library dependencies mean capability varies by installation, so a clean on one machine is not evidence of a clean on another
- CLI-oriented; a reporter needs either training or a wrapper, and the ones who most need it are least likely to use a terminal

### 6. Feedback (documented)

No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 394 stars with 2 open issues, release 0.15.0 (2026-08-04), pushed 2026-11-15, LGPL-3.0 (independently recorded in session 1's ground_truth.tsv). The canonical home is 0xacab.org (GitLab) with the GitHub repository as the primary mirror; session 1's candidate paths 0xacab/mat2 and rhaberkorn/mat2 are both 404s, verified in this session.

### 7. Assessment

Adopt and automate it into the publication path rather than relying on anyone to remember — metadata stripping is a checklist item that fails exactly when people are rushing to publish. For your profile the essential complement is a visual review step: mat2 handles the metadata, a human must handle what is visible in the frame, and in source-protection terms the pixels are usually the bigger risk. Record which formats your installation supports so you know what is actually being cleaned.

### 8. Maintenance

**Actively maintained** — GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-15, latest release 0.15.0 (2026-08-04), 394 stars, 2 open issues. Near-zero backlog with current commits — excellent single-maintainer discipline over many years.

### 9. Licensing

**Licence:** LGPL-3.0-or-later _(SPDX verified)_

**Model / data licence:** n/a

**Restrictions:** LGPL-3.0-or-later: linking from a proprietary tool is permitted provided the library remains replaceable; modifications to mat2 itself must be shared. Suitable for building a newsroom wrapper around.

**Licence evidence:** https://github.com/jvoisin/mat2/blob/master/LICENSE

### 10. Costs

No fee. Per-format system libraries; negligible compute. No paid dependencies.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

Fully local processing — nothing uploaded, which is the point for source-protection work. The limitation to state plainly to colleagues: it cleans metadata, not content.

### 12. Verdict

**Adopt**

### 13. Alternatives

- [ExifTool](docs/projects/OSINT-C2-01.md) for inspecting what metadata exists before and after cleaning
- [Dangerzone](docs/projects/SUR-B3-03.md), whose pixel round-trip incidentally removes most metadata along with active content
- [PyMuPDF](docs/projects/JAI-A2-42.md) for true redaction of visible content in PDFs

### 14. Evidence

## 13. OCRmyPDF — 94/100

`JAI-A2-33` · A2 · Documents and language: OCR, transcription, translation, entities, entity resolution · OCR pipeline · **cli** · bucket `verified-oss` · maintainer James R. Barlow and contributors
[Project page](docs/projects/JAI-A2-33.md) · [repository](https://github.com/ocrmypdf/OCRmyPDF) · [docs](https://ocrmypdf.readthedocs.io/)

**Scores** — relevance 5/5 · capability 4/5 · maintenance 5/5 · privacy 5/5 · usability 4/5 · licence+cost 5/5 → **weighted 94/100** (pillar rank 3, segment rank 1)

### 1. Purpose

Adds a searchable text layer to scanned PDFs using Tesseract while preserving the original page images, with deskewing, cleaning, optimisation and PDF/A output.

### Journalism / investigative use case

The standard first pass on a scan dump: makes thousands of image-only PDFs grep-able and ingestable by DocumentCloud, OpenAleph or Datashare while preserving the original page images as evidence — the preservation property is what makes it safe to run across source material.

### 2. Audience

engineer, newsroom analyst

### 3. Project type

cli · bucket `verified-oss`

### 4. Pros

- Preserves the original page image alongside the text layer, so the evidentiary artefact is never replaced by a machine interpretation — the right default for journalism
- Idempotent, resumable and designed for batch operation over huge directories; genuinely reliable at scale, which is rare in OCR tooling
- Exceptionally well documented and released very frequently (v17.14.2, 2026-11-16) with only 69 open issues against 35,338 stars
- PDF/A output and optimisation make the results archive-grade and much smaller, which matters for long-term storage costs

### 5. Cons

- Inherits Tesseract's accuracy ceiling: degraded scans, handwriting and unusual fonts come out poorly and no amount of preprocessing fixes it
- Produces a PDF, not structured data — no table extraction, no layout model, so it is the start of a pipeline rather than an answer
- MPL-2.0 file-level copyleft is mild but non-zero if you vendor modified source into a proprietary product
- Dependency chain (Tesseract, Ghostscript, optional jbig2enc/unpaper) makes reproducible installs fiddly outside containers

### 6. Feedback (documented)

No individual user reports verified. The quantitative evidence is unusually strong: 35,338 stars with 69 open issues and a release on 2026-11-16 — among the healthiest maintenance profiles in the entire catalogue. Widely used as the OCR step in self-hosted document stacks (Paperless-ngx depends on this toolchain).

### 7. Assessment

Adopt without reservation as the default OCR step for scanned material. Its value for your work is not accuracy — that is Tesseract's limit — but operational reliability and evidentiary integrity: it will finish a 200,000-page job and the originals will still be there. Where accuracy is insufficient, escalate specific documents to Surya/Marker or Kraken rather than changing the default.

### 8. Maintenance

**Actively maintained** — GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-16, latest release v17.14.2 (2026-11-16), 35,338 stars, 69 open issues. Same-day push and release, major version 17, minimal backlog — maintenance quality is evidenced by issue throughput, not just commit frequency.

### 9. Licensing

**Licence:** MPL-2.0 _(SPDX verified)_

**Model / data licence:** n/a (Tesseract traineddata is separately licensed, generally Apache-2.0 from the tesseract-ocr project).

**Restrictions:** MPL-2.0 file-level copyleft: modifications to OCRmyPDF's own files must be shared if distributed. Ghostscript is a runtime dependency with AGPL terms from Artifex absent a commercial licence — relevant only if you redistribute a bundle.

**Licence evidence:** https://github.com/ocrmypdf/OCRmyPDF/blob/main/LICENSE

### 10. Costs

No fee. CPU-bound; OCR time is roughly linear in page count, so a large scan dump is a compute-hours cost on commodity hardware. Containerised deployment keeps operating effort low. Estimate.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

Fully local, no network calls, no telemetry. Safe on an air-gapped evidence machine.

### 12. Verdict

**Adopt**

### 13. Alternatives

- [Surya](docs/projects/JAI-A2-52.md) or Marker where Tesseract's accuracy is the binding constraint
- PaddleOCR for CJK and Arabic scans
- [Dangerzone](docs/projects/SUR-B3-03.md) first, if the PDFs come from an untrusted source

### 14. Evidence

Verified **2026-11-17** · confidence **high** · assessment depth `metadata-verified`

- https://github.com/ocrmypdf/OCRmyPDF
