## 14. Ollama — 94/100

`JAI-A3-02` · A3 · RAG, research agents, knowledge graphs, provenance and AI evaluation · Local LLM inference · **application** · bucket `verified-oss` · maintainer Ollama
[Project page](docs/projects/JAI-A3-02.md) · [repository](https://github.com/ollama/ollama) · [docs](https://docs.ollama.com/)

**Scores** — relevance 5/5 · capability 4/5 · maintenance 5/5 · privacy 5/5 · usability 5/5 · licence+cost 4/5 → **weighted 94/100** (pillar rank 4, segment rank 2)

### 1. Purpose

Application that packages local model serving behind a simple CLI and HTTP API, handling model download, quantisation selection, memory management and concurrent requests, with an OpenAI-compatible endpoint.

### Journalism / investigative use case

The practical way to give a newsroom local AI: one command installs it, one command pulls a model, and every internal tool has an OpenAI-compatible endpoint on the local network — which is the difference between local AI being a project and being available.

### 2. Audience

engineer, newsroom analyst

### 3. Project type

application · bucket `verified-oss`

### 4. Pros

- Removes essentially all operational friction from local inference: model management, memory handling and serving are automatic, which is why it has become the default
- OpenAI-compatible API means existing tools work unchanged, so you can redirect a pipeline from a hosted provider to local inference by changing a base URL
- MIT licensed with enormous adoption (187,366 stars) and a very fast release cadence (v0.40.16, 2026-11-09; pushed 2026-11-17)
- Cross-platform desktop and server support, so a reporter can run a model on a laptop and the newsroom can run one on a server with the same interface

### 5. Cons

- Abstracts away quantisation and model-variant choices, which is convenient and means teams often do not know which quantisation they are running — and that affects output quality materially
- Model library convenience encourages pulling models without checking their licences: the library includes weights with restrictive terms alongside permissive ones, and the pull command does not make you read them
- Fast release cadence with occasional behavioural changes, so pin the version for anything production
- Defaults are tuned for convenience rather than for maximum throughput or minimum memory; a heavily used server benefits from vLLM or direct llama.cpp tuning

### 6. Feedback (documented)

No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 187,366 stars with release v0.40.16 (2026-11-09) and a push on 2026-11-17, MIT licence. Its position as the default local-model runner is evident from adoption scale.

### 7. Assessment

Adopt it — the usability gain is what actually gets local AI deployed, and deployment is the point. For your profile two governance items matter more than the technology. First, record which model and quantisation each workflow uses, because 'we summarised with a local model' is not a reproducible methodology. Second, check the licence of every model you pull: the convenience of `ollama pull` is exactly how a non-commercial-weights model ends up behind a published story.

### 8. Maintenance

**Actively maintained** — GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release v0.40.16 (2026-11-09), 187,366 stars, MIT licence. Same-day commits with near-weekly releases and commercial backing.

### 9. Licensing

**Licence:** MIT (application) _(SPDX verified)_

**Model / data licence:** VARIES AND MATTERS: models in the library carry their own licences, from Apache-2.0 and MIT through to restrictive community licences with usage conditions. Verify each model you pull.

**Restrictions:** Application unrestricted. The real exposure is model licences, which `ollama pull` does not surface prominently — a commercially operated newsroom must check each model's terms before output reaches publication.

**Licence evidence:** https://github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/main/LICENSE

### 10. Costs

No fee. Hardware is the cost: a GPU host for useful speed on larger models, or a capable laptop for small ones. One shared server serves a small newsroom. Estimate.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

Local inference with no document content leaving your infrastructure. Model pulls contact Ollama's registry, which discloses which models you fetch (not your data) and can be pre-staged for air-gapped use.

### 12. Verdict

**Adopt**

### Material blockers

_Tracked separately from the score._

- Model licences in the library vary and are easy to overlook — verify before publishing work derived from a pulled model

### 13. Alternatives

- [llama.cpp](docs/projects/JAI-A3-01.md) directly for control over quantisation and server behaviour
- [vLLM](docs/projects/JAI-A3-03.md) for high-throughput GPU serving
- Hosted APIs for non-sensitive work only

## 15. PySceneDetect — 94/100

`OSINT-C2-10` · C2 · Image/video verification, geolocation, satellite, aviation and maritime · Video shot detection · **cli** · bucket `verified-oss` · maintainer Brandon Castellano (Breakthrough)
[Project page](docs/projects/OSINT-C2-10.md) · [repository](https://github.com/Breakthrough/PySceneDetect) · [docs](https://www.scenedetect.com/)

**Scores** — relevance 5/5 · capability 4/5 · maintenance 5/5 · privacy 5/5 · usability 4/5 · licence+cost 5/5 → **weighted 94/100** (pillar rank 8, segment rank 3)

### 1. Purpose

Python library and CLI that detects shot boundaries in video using content, threshold, adaptive and histogram detectors, and can split video or export keyframes per scene.

### Journalism / investigative use case

First step in video verification: fragment an unknown clip into shots and pull one keyframe per shot so each frame can be reverse-image-searched, geolocated or compared against earlier uploads — the InVID/WeVerify keyframes workflow, runnable locally without uploading the video anywhere.

### 2. Audience

engineer, newsroom analyst

### 3. Project type

cli · bucket `verified-oss`

### 4. Pros

- Reproduces the single most useful verification workflow (keyframes for reverse search) entirely locally, which the InVID plugin cannot
- Multiple detector algorithms with tunable thresholds, so you can handle both hard cuts and gradual transitions
- Very actively maintained (v0.7.3, 2026-11-08; pushed 2026-11-17) with a large community (5,526 stars) and good documentation
- BSD-3-Clause and scriptable, so it drops into a batch pipeline over an archive of collected video

### 5. Cons

- Detects cuts, not manipulation: it produces no authenticity judgement and no proof of anything — a point worth stating because shot-boundary anomalies get over-read
- Content-based detection is threshold-sensitive and can over- or under-segment heavily compressed, low-light or shaky footage, which is most citizen video
- Requires ffmpeg or mkvmerge for splitting, so deployment has an external dependency
- 61 open issues; tuning for a specific footage type takes experimentation

### 6. Feedback (documented)

No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 5,526 stars with 61 open issues, release v0.7.3 (2026-11-08), pushed 2026-11-17. The keyframe-per-shot workflow it enables is the documented basis of the InVID/WeVerify video-verification method.

### 7. Assessment

Adopt — it is the local foundation of video verification and the reason you do not need to upload a sensitive clip to a third-party keyframe service. For your profile the workflow to standardise: yt-dlp to capture at full bitrate, MediaInfo to establish whether it is an original, PySceneDetect for keyframes, then local reverse-image comparison via your ImageHash/PDQ index before resorting to any external search engine.

### 8. Maintenance

**Actively maintained** — GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release v0.7.3 (2026-11-08), 5,526 stars, 61 open issues. Same-day commits and a recent release from a long-standing single maintainer with consistent cadence.

### 9. Licensing

**Licence:** BSD-3-Clause _(SPDX verified)_

**Model / data licence:** n/a

**Restrictions:** None.

**Licence evidence:** https://github.com/Breakthrough/PySceneDetect/blob/main/LICENSE

### 10. Costs

No fee. CPU-bound; ffmpeg required for splitting. Negligible infrastructure.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

Fully local — no network calls or API keys in the documented workflow, so the video never leaves your machine.

### 12. Verdict

**Adopt**

### 13. Alternatives

- [Katna](docs/projects/OSINT-C2-11.md) for keyframe selection optimised for visual quality — but note its stalled maintenance
- ffmpeg scene-detection filters for a dependency-free approximation

### 1. Purpose

Browser-based, fully client-side viewer that opens WARC and WACZ archives and replays them without any server, using service workers.

### Journalism / investigative use case

Let editors, lawyers and readers open and inspect an archived page themselves, offline, from a single file — which is what converts a capture into usable evidence in an editorial or legal conversation, with no infrastructure between them and the material.

### 2. Audience

journalist, newsroom analyst, specialist investigator

### 3. Project type

application · bucket `verified-oss`

### 4. Pros

- Zero infrastructure and zero upload: hand someone a WACZ file and they can inspect it in a browser, which removes the single biggest practical barrier to using archived evidence

### 7. Assessment

Adopt — it is the piece that makes your captures socially useful. For your profile the highest-value application is legal and editorial review: a WACZ plus ReplayWeb.page lets counsel examine exactly what a page said without you building anything or exposing the archive. Embedding it in published stories is also worth considering where a source page is likely to change, since it lets readers verify your sourcing directly.

### 8. Maintenance

**Actively maintained** — GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release v2.5.4 (2026-10-22), 1,015 stars, 119 open issues. Same-day commits and current releases within the Webrecorder suite.

**Model / data licence:** n/a

**Restrictions:** AGPL-3.0: embedding a modified version in a distributed product triggers source obligations. Using the hosted viewer or an unmodified self-hosted copy is unaffected.

**Licence evidence:** https://github.com/webrecorder/replayweb.page/blob/main/LICENSE

### 10. Costs

Free. No infrastructure; optionally self-host the static viewer alongside your archives.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

Replay happens entirely client-side and archives are not uploaded — among the strongest privacy properties in this catalogue, and the reason it is safe to use for sensitive captures. If you use the hosted viewer, the page itself is loaded from Webrecorder but your archive file is not sent to them.

Document and entity management platform built for human-rights documentation, with customisable entity templates, relationships, multilingual interfaces, full-text search and public or private publishing.

### Journalism / investigative use case

Building a structured, publishable collection of documents and entities around a long-running investigation: court filings linked to defendants linked to incidents, with a custom data model, in several languages, publishable as a public resource when the reporting is done.

### 2. Audience

newsroom analyst, specialist investigator, engineer

platform · bucket `verified-oss`

Plain C/C++ implementation of Whisper inference using the ggml tensor library, with quantised GGUF models, no Python dependency, and backends for CPU, Metal, CUDA, Vulkan and OpenVINO.

### Journalism / investigative use case

Transcribing suspect audio and video locally so the words in a claimed 'leaked recording' can be checked, searched and quoted without uploading sensitive material to any service — and because it needs no Python, it runs on a hardened or borrowed machine where installing a toolchain is not an option.

engineer, journalist

library · bucket `verified-oss`

### 7. Assessment

The transcription runtime I would standardise on for anything that must run on arbitrary hardware — field laptops, hostile-environment machines, a reporter's borrowed computer. For server-side batch work faster-whisper is better. The combination of 'single binary, no network, MIT weights' is uniquely well matched to media-in-exile constraints, and it is worth packaging a known-good binary plus model internally so reporters never download anything at the moment of need.

## 22. SecureDrop — 92/100

`SUR-B3-01` · B3 · Protecting journalists and sources · Secure submission · **platform** · bucket `verified-oss` · maintainer Freedom of the Press Foundation
[Project page](docs/projects/SUR-B3-01.md) · [repository](https://github.com/freedomofpress/securedrop) · [docs](https://docs.securedrop.org/)

**Scores** — relevance 5/5 · capability 5/5 · maintenance 5/5 · privacy 5/5 · usability 2/5 · licence+cost 4/5 → **weighted 92/100** (pillar rank 5, segment rank 3)

### 1. Purpose

Whistleblower submission system where sources upload documents and messages over a Tor onion service to hardware controlled by the news organisation, with per-source codenames, no accounts and an air-gapped decryption model.

### Journalism / investigative use case

The reference system for receiving documents from a source who must not be identifiable, including by the news organisation itself: the source connects over Tor, receives a codename rather than an account, and submissions are decrypted on an air-gapped machine so a server compromise does not expose plaintext.

### 2. Audience

engineer, journalist

### 3. Project type

platform · bucket `verified-oss`

### 4. Pros

- Threat model is explicit and unusually honest: it is designed on the assumption that the server will be seized or compromised, which is why decryption is air-gapped rather than server-side
- Tor onion service means no IP address is exposed to the newsroom or its hosting provider, so the organisation cannot be compelled to produce what it never had
- Maintained by an organisation whose sole purpose is press freedom, with regular releases (2.16.2, 2026-10-29), published security audits and a documented support process
- Codename-based pseudonymity avoids collecting any source identifier at all — the strongest available posture against legal compulsion

### 5. Cons

- Heavy operational requirement: dedicated hardware (application server, monitor server, air-gapped Secure Viewing Station), physical security, and a maintenance routine — this is an institutional commitment, not a deployment
- Journalists must actually use the workstation discipline, and the system's security collapses if submissions are copied onto an ordinary laptop — the human failure mode dominates the technical one
- GitHub reports SPDX NOASSERTION (the project is AGPL-3.0 per its own licensing) and carries 479 open issues, reflecting a large, complex system
- Sources must find and trust the onion address, so publicising it safely is part of the work, and a source using Tor in a hostile country may itself attract attention

### 6. Feedback (documented)

No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 3,896 stars with 479 open issues, release 2.16.2 (2026-10-29), pushed 2026-11-14; session 1's ground_truth.tsv independently recorded AGPL-3.0 and the same release line. SecureDrop's deployment by major news organisations is publicly documented by FPF, and the project publishes independent security audits — the strongest assurance evidence in this catalogue.

### 7. Assessment

If your organisation intends to solicit documents from sources at real risk, this is the standard and I would adopt it — but only with the institutional commitment it requires, because a half-maintained SecureDrop is worse than none (it implies a protection it does not deliver). For an exile outlet the specific advantage is that it minimises what you hold: you cannot be compelled to produce source identities you never collected. If you cannot meet the operational bar, Hush Line or an OnionShare-based workflow is the honest fallback, and you should say publicly what protection you do and do not offer.

### 8. Maintenance

**Actively maintained** — GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-14, latest release 2.16.2 (2026-10-29), 3,896 stars, 479 open issues. Regular versioned releases, a dedicated institutional maintainer (FPF), published security audits and a documented vulnerability-disclosure process — maintenance assessed on security process, not commit count.

### 9. Licensing

**Licence:** AGPL-3.0 (project's own licensing; GitHub API reports NOASSERTION) _(SPDX not verified — resolved from the licence file or project documentation)_

**Model / data licence:** n/a

**Restrictions:** AGPL-3.0: a modified instance offered over a network obliges source publication. Running the released version for your own newsroom carries no obligation. Do not fork quietly — security-critical modifications should go upstream.

**Licence evidence:** https://github.com/freedomofpress/securedrop/blob/develop/LICENSE

### 10. Costs

No software fee. Real costs are hardware and staff: two servers plus an air-gapped Secure Viewing Station and a dedicated USB workflow (low four figures in hardware, estimate), a Tor-reachable hosting arrangement, and — dominantly — ongoing administrator time for updates and a journalist-training routine. Budget this as a permanent staffed service rather than a project.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

The strongest privacy design in this catalogue: Tor onion service (no source IP), no accounts (no identifiers), air-gapped decryption (no plaintext on a networked machine). Residual risks are real and must be managed: source-side risk from using Tor in a hostile network, metadata inside submitted documents (run Dangerzone and mat2), and the organisational discipline of never moving submissions onto ordinary devices.

### 12. Verdict

**Adopt**

### Material blockers

_Tracked separately from the score._

- Requires dedicated hardware, an air-gapped workstation and permanent administrator capacity — a partial deployment is actively misleading to sources

**Scores** — relevance 5/5 · capability 4/5 · maintenance 5/5 · privacy 5/5 · usability 4/5 · licence+cost 4/5 → **weighted 92/100** (pillar rank 6, segment rank 4)

### 1. Purpose

End-to-end encrypted collaborative office suite — documents, spreadsheets, kanban, forms, polls — where the server stores only ciphertext and encryption keys travel in the URL fragment.

### Journalism / investigative use case

Collaborative drafting and shared notes on a sensitive investigation where the hosting provider must not be able to read the material — replacing Google Docs for the planning document, the source list and the draft, which is where newsrooms most often leak their own investigations to a third party.

### 2. Audience

journalist, newsroom analyst, engineer

### 3. Project type

platform · bucket `verified-oss`

### 4. Pros

- Zero-knowledge server design means the operator — including you, if self-hosted — cannot read documents, which is a structural answer to the Google Docs problem rather than a policy promise
- Covers the formats a newsroom actually collaborates in (documents, sheets, kanban, forms), so it can genuinely replace a cloud suite for sensitive work rather than only for text
- AGPL-3.0 and self-hostable, very actively maintained (2026.10.1 released 2026-11-10; pushed 2026-11-16) with a substantial community (8,087 stars)
- Link-based access with no account requirement makes it usable by an external collaborator or source without onboarding

- Keys in the URL fragment means link handling IS key handling: a link pasted into Slack, email or a chat log hands over the document, and this is the dominant real-world failure mode

- Performance and feature depth are below commercial office suites, which creates pressure to revert to Google Docs for convenience — a social problem that will decide whether adoption sticks
- Self-hosting requires real operations care, and a misconfigured instance (or a compromised server serving modified JavaScript) can undermine the encryption model entirely

### 6. Feedback (documented)

No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 8,087 stars with 372 open issues, release 2026.10.1 (2026-11-10), pushed 2026-11-16, AGPL-3.0. CryptPad's zero-knowledge model is documented by the project and it operates a public instance; the key-in-URL design is inherent and openly documented.

### 7. Assessment

Adopt it for sensitive collaborative work and self-host it, with one rule drilled into the team: the link is the key, so links go only through a channel you would send the document itself through. For your profile this replaces the single most common and least-discussed leak in investigative work — the shared planning document on a third-party cloud. Expect to actively defend adoption against the convenience of commercial suites; that is the real implementation challenge, not the deployment.

### 8. Maintenance

**Actively maintained** — GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-16, latest release 2026.10.1 (2026-11-10), 8,087 stars, 372 open issues. Frequent dated releases under a commercial sponsor (XWiki SAS) with public-instance operation.

### 9. Licensing

**Licence:** AGPL-3.0 _(SPDX verified)_

**Model / data licence:** n/a

**Restrictions:** AGPL-3.0: a modified instance offered to users obliges source publication. Running the released version for your newsroom carries no obligation.

**Licence evidence:** https://github.com/cryptpad/cryptpad/blob/main/LICENSE

### 10. Costs

No software fee. Infrastructure estimate: a single VM with modest resources serves a small newsroom; storage grows with document history. Operating effort is moderate — it is a web application with a cryptographic front end, so updates matter. The public CryptPad instance has free and paid tiers whose prices were not verified here.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

The server stores only ciphertext, so a hosting compromise or legal demand yields nothing readable — the strongest property available for collaborative documents. The two residual risks are link disclosure (keys in URLs) and browser compromise, both of which are user-side and must be addressed by practice rather than configuration.

### 12. Verdict

**Adopt**

### Material blockers

_Tracked separately from the score._

- Document keys travel in URLs — link handling is key handling

### 13. Alternatives

- [Nextcloud](docs/projects/SUR-B3-28.md) with server-side or end-to-end encryption for a broader self-hosted suite with weaker confidentiality
- Etherpad self-hosted for simple shared text without encryption
- Local files plus encrypted transfer for the most sensitive documents, accepting the collaboration cost

## 24. Dangerzone — 92/100

`SUR-B3-03` · B3 · Protecting journalists and sources · Document sanitisation · **application** · bucket `verified-oss` · maintainer Freedom of the Press Foundation
[Project page](docs/projects/SUR-B3-03.md) · [repository](https://github.com/freedomofpress/dangerzone) · [docs](https://dangerzone.rocks/)

**Scores** — relevance 5/5 · capability 4/5 · maintenance 5/5 · privacy 5/5 · usability 4/5 · licence+cost 4/5 → **weighted 92/100** (pillar rank 7, segment rank 5)

### 1. Purpose

Desktop application that converts potentially malicious PDFs, Office documents and images into safe PDFs by rendering them to pixels inside an isolated container and rebuilding a clean file, with optional OCR to restore a text layer.

### Journalism / investigative use case

The step before any other tool in this catalogue touches a document from an unknown source: a file is sanitised so opening it cannot execute an exploit or beacon out to the sender. That protects the reporter's machine and, just as importantly, prevents a document from signalling to its originator that it has been opened — which can expose that a leak is being investigated.

### 2. Audience

journalist, newsroom analyst, engineer

### 3. Project type

application · bucket `verified-oss`

### 4. Pros

- Addresses a threat that is real and routinely ignored: weaponised documents sent to journalists are a documented attack vector, and ordinary antivirus does not reliably stop a targeted exploit
- The pixel round-trip is a structural rather than detection-based defence — it does not need to recognise the exploit to neutralise it, which is why it works against unknown attacks
- Fully local by design: the whole premise is that nothing is uploaded and the conversion is isolated from the host, which distinguishes it from cloud sanitisation services
- Actively maintained (v0.11.1, 2026-10-22; pushed 2026-11-09) by FPF with a journalism-specific threat model and installable builds for all desktop platforms

### 5. Cons

- The pixel round-trip destroys the text layer unless OCR is enabled, and the OCR'd text is then only as accurate as Tesseract — so sanitised documents are worse for search and quotation than originals, and teams are tempted to skip it
- Conversion is slow on large documents, which again creates pressure to bypass it on exactly the big leaked set where it matters most
- Container runtime dependency (Docker or Podman) complicates installation on managed or locked-down machines
- AGPL-3.0 affects redistribution of a modified version; 193 open issues reflect the breadth of document formats in the wild

### 6. Feedback (documented)

No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 5,850 stars with 193 open issues, release v0.11.1 (2026-10-22), pushed 2026-11-09, AGPL-3.0 (independently recorded in session 1's ground_truth.tsv). FPF builds it specifically for journalists, and the threat it addresses — malicious documents targeting newsrooms — is documented in published threat reporting.

### 7. Assessment

Adopt it as a mandatory first step and automate it so the choice is not left to a tired reporter at midnight: ingest pipelines should sanitise on arrival, keeping the original in a quarantined store for later forensic examination. For your profile the detail that matters most is preserving both artefacts — the sanitised copy for reading and the untouched original for analysis — because the original is evidence about the sender and discarding it loses that. Enable OCR, and accept the accuracy cost rather than skipping sanitisation.

### 8. Maintenance

**Actively maintained** — GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-09, latest release v0.11.1 (2026-10-22), 5,850 stars, 193 open issues. Regular releases from an institutional maintainer with a security-focused mission; session 1 independently verified the same licence and release line.

### 9. Licensing

**Licence:** AGPL-3.0 _(SPDX verified)_

**Model / data licence:** n/a

**Restrictions:** AGPL-3.0: distributing a modified version or offering it as a service obliges source publication. Desktop use is unaffected.

**Licence evidence:** https://github.com/freedomofpress/dangerzone/blob/main/LICENSE

### 10. Costs

No fee. A container runtime and CPU time — conversion is the cost, measured in minutes per large document. No paid dependencies. For a large leak, budget compute time in the ingest plan.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

Fully local — nothing is uploaded and the conversion is isolated from the host. This is the correct architecture and the direct contrast with commercial document-sanitisation services, which would receive your source documents.

### 12. Verdict

**Adopt**

### 13. Alternatives

- Opening documents inside a disposable Qubes VM or a Tails session for equivalent isolation without the text-layer loss
- A dedicated offline examination machine, which is slower but preserves fidelity
- Commercial sanitisation services — avoid, since they require uploading source documents

### 14. Evidence

Verified **2026-11-17** · confidence **high** · assessment depth `metadata-verified`

- https://github.com/freedomofpress/dangerzone
- https://dangerzone.rocks/
- https://github.com/freedomofpress/dangerzone/blob/main/LICENSE

## 25. ICIJ Datashare — 92/100

`JAI-A2-23` · A2 · Documents and language: OCR, transcription, translation, entities, entity resolution · Leak analysis platform · **platform** · bucket `verified-oss` · maintainer International Consortium of Investigative Journalists
[Project page](docs/projects/JAI-A2-23.md) · [repository](https://github.com/ICIJ/datashare) · [docs](https://icij.gitbook.io/datashare/)

**Scores** — relevance 5/5 · capability 4/5 · maintenance 5/5 · privacy 5/5 · usability 4/5 · licence+cost 4/5 → **weighted 92/100** (pillar rank 8, segment rank 5)

### 1. Purpose

Self-hosted document-analysis platform that extracts text and entities from a document collection and gives journalists a search, tagging and review interface, available as a desktop application or a multi-user server deployment.

### Journalism / investigative use case

The reference end-to-end newsroom stack for a leaked document set: one journalist can run it as a desktop app over 50,000 files, or a cross-border team can run it in server mode and share tags and saved searches across an investigation — the architecture ICIJ built for its own cross-border projects.

### 2. Audience

journalist, newsroom analyst, engineer

### 3. Project type

platform · bucket `verified-oss`

### 4. Pros

- Built by the organisation that runs the largest cross-border leak investigations, so the workflow assumptions (tagging, batch search, team sharing) match how reporting actually happens
- Desktop mode is the standout feature: a journalist with no infrastructure gets OCR plus NER plus search on their own laptop, with the documents never leaving it
- Explicitly designed so no external cloud services are required — the README states sensitive material stays under your control, which is the correct architecture for source protection
- Very active: pushed 2026-11-17 with release 21.24.2 on 2026-11-16, and multiple NER backends (CoreNLP, Ixa Pipes, MITIE) bundled

### 5. Cons

- Server mode needs real infrastructure — Elasticsearch, PostgreSQL, Redis — and the operational capacity to run them; this is where small newsrooms stall
- Entity types are limited to person/organisation/location, so it indexes and surfaces rather than resolving entities; cross-document identity work needs nomenklatura or manual effort
- AGPL-3.0 obligations apply if you modify it and host it for others, which constrains building a customised newsroom service on top
- Elasticsearch dependency carries the Elastic licensing question that Solr/OpenSearch avoid — relevant if you redistribute a bundled deployment

### 6. Feedback (documented)

No individual user reports verified. The strongest documented signal is institutional: ICIJ builds and uses Datashare for its own investigations, and the release cadence (21.24.x in November 2026) reflects a tool under continuous internal use. 783 stars, 76 open issues.

### 7. Assessment

For a small newsroom I would recommend Datashare desktop over almost anything else in this pillar — it is the shortest path from 'we received a dump' to 'reporters are searching it' without an engineer. In server mode the choice between Datashare and OpenAleph is close: Datashare has the better reporter UI and institutional backing; OpenAleph has the stronger entity model and cross-referencing against sanctions and registry data. If your investigations are document-centric, choose Datashare; if they are entity-centric, choose OpenAleph.

### 8. Maintenance

**Actively maintained** — GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release 21.24.2 (2026-11-16), 783 stars, 76 open issues. Daily-scale commits, releases within the week, and an institutional owner that depends on the tool operationally — the strongest form of maintenance evidence available.

### 9. Licensing

**Licence:** AGPL-3.0 _(SPDX verified)_

**Model / data licence:** n/a for the platform; bundled NER models carry their own terms and were not individually verified.

**Restrictions:** AGPL-3.0 network copyleft: modifying Datashare and offering it over a network to third parties obliges you to publish your modified source. Running it unmodified for your own newsroom is unaffected.

**Licence evidence:** https://github.com/ICIJ/datashare/blob/master/LICENSE

### 10. Costs

No software fee. Desktop mode: zero infrastructure. Server mode estimate: an Elasticsearch node with 8-16GB RAM, PostgreSQL, Redis and worker capacity — realistically one well-provisioned VM for a few hundred thousand documents, scaling with OCR load. Assumptions: self-hosted, no managed Elasticsearch. Operating effort is the dominant cost in server mode.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

Designed for local custody: no third-party services are required, documents remain on your hardware, and desktop mode keeps everything on one machine. Residual risks: Elasticsearch must not be exposed, and in server mode the index becomes a high-value target that needs encryption at rest and strict access control.

### 12. Verdict

**Adopt**

### 13. Alternatives

- [OpenAleph](docs/projects/JAI-A2-35.md) where entity cross-referencing against sanctions and registries is the priority
- [Uwazi](docs/projects/OSINT-C3-05.md) for public-facing document collections
- [Paperless-ngx](docs/projects/JAI-A2-38.md) for a small internal archive with far lower operational cost

### 14. Evidence

## 26. OnionShare — 92/100

`SUR-B3-04` · B3 · Protecting journalists and sources · Secure file transfer · **application** · bucket `verified-oss` · maintainer Micah Lee and contributors
[Project page](docs/projects/SUR-B3-04.md) · [repository](https://github.com/onionshare/onionshare) · [docs](https://docs.onionshare.org/)

**Scores** — relevance 5/5 · capability 4/5 · maintenance 5/5 · privacy 5/5 · usability 4/5 · licence+cost 4/5 → **weighted 92/100** (pillar rank 8, segment rank 6)

### 1. Purpose

Desktop and CLI tool that uses Tor onion services to share files, receive files, host a static website or run an ephemeral chat room directly between participants, with no intermediary server.

### Journalism / investigative use case

Direct, serverless transfer between a reporter and a source who are already in contact: the source runs OnionShare and sends a one-time onion address, the reporter downloads, and no third-party service ever holds the file or the metadata. The receive mode also gives a lightweight drop box without SecureDrop's infrastructure.

### 2. Audience

journalist, specialist investigator

### 3. Project type

application · bucket `verified-oss`

### 4. Pros

- No intermediary at all — the file goes device to device over Tor, so there is no provider to subpoena, no account, and no retained copy
- Receive mode provides a usable drop box in minutes, which is the right tool when a source materialises and you have no SecureDrop
- Licence corrected in this survey: the project's own LICENSE.txt is GPL-3.0 (GitHub's NOASSERTION is caused by a prepended note pointing to bundled third-party licences, which is what produced session 1's incorrect reading)
- Very actively maintained (v2.7.2, 2026-11-07; pushed 2026-11-16) with 7,238 stars and a small backlog (63 open issues)

### 5. Cons

- Both parties must be online simultaneously for a transfer, which is a real coordination problem across time zones and for sources with intermittent connectivity
- Requires the source to install and run software and to understand onion addresses — a meaningful barrier for a non-technical source under stress
- Using Tor may itself be conspicuous on a monitored network, so in some countries the act of running OnionShare carries risk even though the transfer is protected
- Nothing protects against metadata inside the transferred documents, so mat2 and Dangerzone remain necessary afterwards

### 6. Feedback (documented)

No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 7,238 stars with 63 open issues, release v2.7.2 (2026-11-07), pushed 2026-11-16. The licence question is resolved with primary evidence: LICENSE.txt opens with '(Note: Third-party licenses can be found under licenses/.)' followed by the OnionShare copyright and the full GPL-3.0 text — recorded in sources/evidence/leads.md as lead L8.

### 7. Assessment

Adopt as the standard answer for ad-hoc secure transfer, and specifically teach reporters the receive mode — it is the fastest route from 'a source has documents' to 'we have them, with no intermediary'. For your profile the operational caveats to brief are the simultaneity requirement and the conspicuousness of Tor in some networks; where the latter matters, a bridge or a pre-arranged time window helps. Always follow a transfer with Dangerzone and mat2 before the documents touch anything else.

### 8. Maintenance

**Actively maintained** — GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-16, latest release v2.7.2 (2026-11-07), 7,238 stars, 63 open issues. Frequent releases with a clean tracker; long-standing project with a security-literate maintainer base.

### 9. Licensing

**Licence:** GPL-3.0 (project's own LICENSE.txt read directly 2026-11-17; GitHub reports NOASSERTION because a note about bundled third-party licences is prepended to the GPL text) _(SPDX not verified — resolved from the licence file or project documentation)_

**Model / data licence:** n/a. Third-party components under licenses/ have their own terms and must not be read as the project licence — this was the cause of session 1's misidentification.

**Restrictions:** GPL-3.0 on the project's own code; immaterial for ordinary use.

**Licence evidence:** https://github.com/onionshare/onionshare/blob/main/LICENSE.txt

### 10. Costs

Free. No infrastructure — the point is that there is no server. Bandwidth only.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

Among the strongest in the catalogue: no intermediary, no account, ephemeral onion address, nothing retained after the transfer. Residual risks are the conspicuousness of Tor on a monitored network and document metadata, neither of which OnionShare addresses.

### 12. Verdict

**Adopt**

### 13. Alternatives

- [SecureDrop](docs/projects/SUR-B3-01.md) where sources must be protected from the newsroom itself and cannot coordinate live
- [Hush Line](docs/projects/SUR-B3-06.md) for asynchronous encrypted tips
- Signal for messages and small files between parties who can both install it

## 27. Orbot — 92/100

`SUR-B3-30` · B3 · Protecting journalists and sources · Anonymous networking (mobile) · **application** · bucket `verified-oss` · maintainer Guardian Project
[Project page](docs/projects/SUR-B3-30.md) · [repository](https://github.com/guardianproject/orbot-android) · [docs](https://orbot.app/)

**Scores** — relevance 5/5 · capability 4/5 · maintenance 5/5 · privacy 5/5 · usability 4/5 · licence+cost 4/5 → **weighted 92/100** (pillar rank 9, segment rank 7)

### 1. Purpose

Android application that provides Tor connectivity for the device, either as a VPN-mode tunnel for selected applications or system-wide, with bridge support for censored networks.

### Journalism / investigative use case

Routing a reporter's phone traffic through Tor in a country where the network is monitored or specific services are blocked — including selectively tunnelling only the applications that matter, so a messaging app works while ordinary traffic looks normal.

### 2. Audience

journalist, specialist investigator

### 3. Project type

application · bucket `verified-oss`

### 4. Pros

- Per-application tunnelling is the practically important feature: routing everything through Tor is slow and conspicuous, while tunnelling just the messaging or browsing app is usable daily
- Bridge support addresses the case that actually matters — networks where Tor itself is blocked — which is common in the jurisdictions exile media report on
- Very actively maintained (release 17.9.8-RC-1 with Tor 0.4.9.17 on 2026-11-16; pushed the same day) by Guardian Project, which has a long record in this field
- Repository transfer guardianproject/orbot → guardianproject/orbot-android verified by redirect, so the canonical path is current

### 5. Cons

- VPN-mode Tor on Android is visible to anyone inspecting the device, and in some jurisdictions the presence of Orbot is itself incriminating — a risk the app cannot mitigate
- Tor over mobile networks is slow and battery-hungry, so users disable it exactly when they are travelling and most at risk
- GitHub reports SPDX NOASSERTION so the licence must be read from the repository, and the release/tag structure is confusing (RC releases against a v15-beta-2 tag)
- Mobile Tor does not protect against application-level identifiers: an app that transmits an account identity over Tor is still identified

### 6. Feedback (documented)

No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 3,711 stars with 87 open issues, release 17.9.8-RC-1-tor-0.4.9.17 (2026-11-16) with same-day push, SPDX NOASSERTION; the repository is mirrored from Guardian Project's GitLab. Transfer confirmed by API redirect 2026-11-17.

### 7. Assessment

Adopt for reporters working in censored or monitored networks, with per-app tunnelling rather than system-wide so it stays usable. For your profile the briefing that matters is twofold: configure bridges before travel rather than on arrival, and be clear that Tor hides the network path, not the account you log into — a journalist signing into an identified account over Tor has protected very little. In jurisdictions where Orbot's presence is itself risky, consider whether a clean device is the better answer.

### 8. Maintenance

**Actively maintained** — GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-16, latest release 17.9.8-RC-1-tor-0.4.9.17 published the same day, 3,711 stars, 87 open issues. Same-day release and push, tracking current Tor versions, under a long-established maintainer.

### 9. Licensing

**Licence:** Not detected by the GitHub API — read the repository licence file (Guardian Project projects are predominantly BSD/GPL-family) _(SPDX not verified — resolved from the licence file or project documentation)_

**Model / data licence:** n/a

**Restrictions:** Unverified in this survey; confirm from the repository before redistribution.

**Licence evidence:** https://github.com/guardianproject/orbot-android

### 10. Costs

Free. No infrastructure. Cost is battery life and connection speed for the user.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

Provides network-level anonymity for tunnelled applications, with bridges for censored networks. Residual risks: app presence is visible on the device, application-level identifiers defeat network anonymity, and mobile-network metadata (that the phone connected at all, and from which cell) is unaffected.

### 12. Verdict

**Adopt**

### Material blockers

_Tracked separately from the score._

- Presence of the app may itself be incriminating in some jurisdictions

- Tor Browser for Android where only browsing needs protection

## 28. Tails — 92/100

`SUR-B3-19` · B3 · Protecting journalists and sources · Amnesic operating system · **application** · bucket `verified-oss` · maintainer Tails project (Tor Project affiliated)
[Project page](docs/projects/SUR-B3-19.md) · [repository](https://gitlab.tails.boum.org/tails/tails) · [docs](https://tails.net/doc/)

**Scores** — relevance 5/5 · capability 4/5 · maintenance 5/5 · privacy 5/5 · usability 3/5 · licence+cost 5/5 → **weighted 92/100** (pillar rank 10, segment rank 8)

### 1. Purpose

Live operating system booted from a USB stick that routes all network traffic through Tor, leaves no trace on the host computer by default, and bundles encryption, secure deletion and anonymity tooling.

### Journalism / investigative use case

The standard tool for working on sensitive material on a machine you do not trust, or for a source who must contact you without leaving evidence on their own computer: boot Tails, work, shut down, and the computer retains nothing. Also the historical environment for handling the most sensitive leaks.

### 2. Audience

journalist, specialist investigator

### 3. Project type

application · bucket `verified-oss`

### 4. Pros

- Amnesia by default is a structural protection no application can provide: nothing written to the host disk means nothing to find in a later device search
- All traffic forced through Tor removes the commonest operational-security mistake — a single application leaking outside the tunnel
- Actively maintained with a visible release cadence (Tails 7.17 announced on the project's news page, verified 2026-11-17) and a long institutional track record in press-freedom contexts
- Optional encrypted persistent storage lets a journalist keep keys and documents across sessions when amnesia is inconvenient, as an explicit choice

### 5. Cons

- Developed on the project's own GitLab rather than GitHub, so it is invisible to GitHub-based discovery and dependency tooling; the GitHub path TAILS-Project/TAILS is an unrelated stub (1 star, last push 2017) and must not be mistaken for it
- Booting from USB requires access to firmware settings, which managed, corporate or locked-down laptops often prevent — and in some countries carrying a Tails USB is itself incriminating
- Tor-only networking is slow and breaks many ordinary web services, so it is a dedicated-session tool rather than a daily environment
- Persistent storage, if enabled, reintroduces exactly the forensic trace that amnesia removes — a configuration choice with serious consequences that users make casually

### 6. Feedback (documented)

No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: Tails 7.17 is the most recent release announced on tails.net/news (retrieved 2026-11-17), and the project's own GitLab instance is the development home — the GitLab API on that host is not publicly queryable, so maintenance was verified from the release announcements instead. Tails's role in high-profile leak handling is extensively documented publicly.

### 7. Assessment

Adopt as a standard capability: keep prepared Tails USB sticks and train reporters to use them for first contact with unknown material and for work on untrusted machines. For your profile, two points matter particularly in exile contexts. First, possession can be a risk in itself — think about where sticks are stored and how they look. Second, decide a policy on persistence: amnesia is the protection, and a persistent volume full of documents on a USB stick in a journalist's bag is a different and worse threat model than they imagine.

### 8. Maintenance

**Actively maintained** — Release announcements on tails.net/news retrieved 2026-11-17 show Tails 7.17 as the current release, with the 7.x line in active development. Development occurs on gitlab.tails.boum.org (API not publicly queryable, so repository-level metrics are unavailable). The unrelated GitHub stub TAILS-Project/TAILS (1 star, pushed 2017-10-20) is NOT the project and should not be cited.

### 9. Licensing

**Licence:** GPL-3.0-or-later (project licensing; the distribution aggregates many components under their own licences) _(SPDX not verified — resolved from the licence file or project documentation)_

**Model / data licence:** n/a. The distribution bundles software under many licences.

**Restrictions:** Aggregate free-software licensing; immaterial for use. Redistribution of a modified Tails image would require attention to the component licences.

**Licence evidence:** https://tails.net/doc/about/license/

### 10. Costs

No fee. A USB stick per user (negligible) plus the time to prepare and verify images. Verification of the download signature is an essential, non-optional step and takes a few minutes.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

The strongest privacy posture available in a general-purpose environment: no host disk writes, all traffic over Tor, memory wiped on shutdown. Residual risks are physical (possession of the stick), firmware-level compromise of the host, and user error in enabling persistence.

### 12. Verdict

**Adopt**

### Material blockers

_Tracked separately from the score._

- Requires firmware access to boot from USB; possession may itself carry risk in hostile jurisdictions

### 13. Alternatives

- [Qubes OS](docs/projects/SUR-B3-20.md) for a compartmentalised daily-use system rather than an amnesic session
- A dedicated air-gapped laptop for the most sensitive material
- Whonix for Tor-routed virtual machines on an existing host

`OSINT-C2-19` · C2 · Image/video verification, geolocation, satellite, aviation and maritime · Geospatial analysis (desktop) · **application** · bucket `verified-oss` · maintainer QGIS.org (OSGeo project)
[Project page](docs/projects/OSINT-C2-19.md) · [repository](https://github.com/qgis/QGIS) · [docs](https://docs.qgis.org/)

**Scores** — relevance 5/5 · capability 5/5 · maintenance 5/5 · privacy 4/5 · usability 3/5 · licence+cost 4/5 → **weighted 91/100** (pillar rank 11, segment rank 4)

### 1. Purpose

Full desktop geographic information system for viewing, editing, analysing and publishing spatial data, with hundreds of processing algorithms and a large plugin ecosystem.

### Journalism / investigative use case

The workbench for any story with a spatial claim: overlay satellite imagery against a conflict incident's coordinates, measure distances and areas from imagery for damage assessment, join a leaked contracts dataset to administrative boundaries, or georeference a scanned historical map to compare land use over decades.

### 2. Audience

newsroom analyst, specialist investigator

### 3. Project type

application · bucket `verified-oss`

### 4. Pros

- The only tool here that lets a non-programmer do serious spatial analysis — georeferencing, measurement, raster algebra, buffer and overlay operations — which is the difference between a mapped story and a guessed one
- Georeferencing scanned maps and imagery is a distinctive investigative capability: it turns a photographed or leaked map into something you can measure against satellite data
- Enormous plugin ecosystem including satellite-imagery loaders, OSM downloaders and Sentinel Hub integration, so acquisition and analysis happen in one place
- Actively maintained under OSGeo governance with a long-term-release track (final-3_44_15, 2026-09-25) and daily commits

### 5. Cons

- Steep learning curve and a dense interface: a reporter will need training, and a bad projection choice silently produces wrong distances and areas — the most common and most consequential mistake
- 5,500 open issues (the largest in the catalogue), reflecting both scale and a long accumulated backlog; expect to encounter rough edges in less-used algorithms
- Heavy desktop application, awkward on low-powered machines and unsuitable for scripted pipelines (use GDAL/geopandas for that)
- GPL-2.0 means plugin and derivative distribution carries copyleft obligations — immaterial for internal analysis, relevant if you ship a tool

### 6. Feedback (documented)

No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 14,853 stars with 5,500 open issues, release final-3_44_15 (2026-09-25), pushed 2026-11-17, GPL-2.0. QGIS is the standard open GIS in both the geospatial and data-journalism communities, reflected in its adoption across OSGeo and in journalism training curricula.

### 7. Assessment

Adopt it as the newsroom's spatial workbench and invest in training one or two analysts properly — the capability-per-trained-analyst is very high, and spatial claims are where investigations get challenged. ## 35. ShadowFinder — 91/100

`OSINT-C2-17` · C2 · Image/video verification, geolocation, satellite, aviation and maritime · Chronolocation · **cli** · bucket `verified-oss` · maintainer Bellingcat
[Project page](docs/projects/OSINT-C2-17.md) · [repository](https://github.com/bellingcat/ShadowFinder) · [docs](https://github.com/bellingcat/ShadowFinder#readme)

**Scores** — relevance 5/5 · capability 4/5 · maintenance 4/5 · privacy 5/5 · usability 4/5 · licence+cost 5/5 → **weighted 91/100** (pillar rank 14, segment rank 5)

### 1. Purpose

Tool that computes the set of possible locations consistent with an observed shadow length and a known timestamp, or the set of possible times consistent with a shadow at a known location, producing a map of candidate bands.

### Journalism / investigative use case

Classic chronolocation and geolocation: given a photo with a visible shadow and a claimed timestamp, narrow the possible latitudes and longitudes — or run it in reverse to test whether a claimed location and time are physically consistent with the shadow in the image. The reverse test is the stronger journalistic move, because it can falsify a claim outright.

### 2. Audience

specialist investigator, newsroom analyst

### 3. Project type

cli · bucket `verified-oss`

### 4. Pros

- Grounded in astronomy rather than machine learning, so the result is a deterministic physical constraint rather than a probabilistic guess — qualitatively stronger evidence than any model output here
- The reverse mode (test a claimed location and time for consistency) can falsify a claim, which is rarer and more valuable than narrowing a search
- MIT licensed, actively released (0.7.1 on 2026-09-03, same-day push), built by Bellingcat for practising investigators
- The Python/CLI route runs entirely locally and takes measurements as input, not the image itself — so nothing sensitive leaves the machine

### 5. Cons

- Output is a probabilistic band of candidate locations, not a point and not proof, and is only as good as its inputs: object height and shadow length must be estimated from the image, and that estimation is usually the dominant error source
- Requires a visible, measurable shadow with a known or estimable object height — a minority of photographs qualify
- The recommended Google Colab route executes in Google's cloud, which means the measurements (and potentially the image, if uploaded there) leave your control — use the local CLI instead for sensitive cases
- Narrow applicability and 13 open issues on a small project (628 stars)

### 6. Feedback (documented)

No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 628 stars with 13 open issues, release 0.7.1 on 2026-09-03 with same-day push, MIT licence; the Colab-based workflow is documented by the project. Shadow-based chronolocation is an established technique in open-source investigation practice.

### 7. Assessment

Adopt, and prefer the local CLI over the documented Colab route — that is the single most important operational point, because Colab puts your measurements and possibly the image into Google's infrastructure. For your profile the highest-value use is falsification: when a government or a propaganda account claims a video was shot at a given place and time, shadow geometry can show it was not, and that is a publishable finding grounded in physics rather than in a model's opinion. Document your height and length estimates, since they carry the error.

### 8. Maintenance

**Actively maintained** — GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-09-03, latest release 0.7.1 published the same day, 628 stars, 13 open issues. Recent release from an institutional maintainer (Bellingcat) with a clean tracker.

### 9. Licensing

**Licence:** MIT _(SPDX verified)_

**Model / data licence:** n/a — astronomical computation, no trained model. Depends on suncalc and timezone grid data.

**Restrictions:** None.

**Licence evidence:** https://github.com/bellingcat/ShadowFinder/blob/main/LICENSE

### 10. Costs

No fee. Negligible compute; runs on a laptop. The Colab route is free within Google's limits but is the option to avoid for sensitive work.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

The Python/CLI route runs entirely locally and takes measurements rather than the image itself — an excellent privacy position. The recommended Colab route executes in Google's cloud and should be avoided for unpublished material.

The extraction layer under any news-monitoring or narrative-tracking pipeline: fetch thousands of articles from a list of outlets and get clean text plus a reliable publication date, which is what makes 'how did this claim propagate across these fifty sites' answerable at all.

engineer, newsroom analyst

library · bucket `verified-oss`

Adopt it as your default article extractor — and specifically in place of news-please, which is archived and still widely recommended. For your profile the combination that works is a feed reader or sitemap crawl for discovery, trafilatura for extraction, and a stored raw copy alongside the extracted text so you can re-extract when the heuristics improve or a failure is discovered. ### 1. Purpose

Python library that inspects PDFs for bad redactions — text that remains in the content stream beneath a drawn black rectangle — and reports the recoverable text.

### Journalism / investigative use case

Triaging FOIA releases, court filings and leaked document sets for failed redactions that reveal names, figures or passages the releasing body intended to withhold. This is a recurring source of scoops, and also the routine check you run before relying on a document being genuinely redacted.

### 2. Audience

engineer, newsroom analyst

### 3. Project type

library · bucket `verified-oss`

### 4. Pros

- Automates a check that is otherwise accidental: failed redactions are found when someone happens to copy-paste, and x-ray turns that into a systematic sweep over thousands of documents
- Built by Free Law Project against a very large corpus of real court filings, so the heuristics are tuned on the documents that actually exhibit the failure
- BSD-2-Clause, pure Python, fully local — appropriate for sensitive leaked documents
- Dual value: offensive (find what others hid) and defensive (check your own publications before release)

### 5. Cons

- Detection is heuristic: outputs are candidate bad redactions, not conclusive findings, and both false positives and missed redactions occur
- Finds text-layer failures only — an image-based redaction that is merely a low-opacity overlay, or a scan of a poorly redacted page, is outside its scope
- GitHub release metadata lags the tag line (release v0.3.5 from 2025-12-08 versus tag v0.4.0), so pinning requires care
- 44 open issues against 837 stars with a small maintainer team

### 6. Feedback (documented)

No individual user reports verified in this survey. The institutional context is strong and checkable: Free Law Project operates CourtListener over millions of filings and built x-ray for that corpus, which is credible production provenance. Failed redactions in court and government documents are a well-documented recurring phenomenon.

### 7. Assessment

Adopt it twice over: as a sweep on every document set you receive, and as a mandatory pre-publication check on every document you release. The second use is the one newsrooms skip and the one that protects sources — publishing a 'redacted' PDF whose text layer is intact has burned sources before. Pair it with PyMuPDF for applying true redactions, and remember x-ray cannot see image-based failures, so visual spot-checks remain necessary.

### 8. Maintenance

**Actively maintained** — GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-16, latest release v0.3.5 (2025-12-08), latest tag v0.4.0, 837 stars, 44 open issues. Current commits with a tag ahead of the published release; maintained by a functioning non-profit that uses it operationally.

**Model / data licence:** n/a

**Licence evidence:** https://github.com/freelawproject/x-ray/blob/main/LICENSE

### 10. Costs

No fee, negligible compute. No paid dependencies.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

Local processing with no third-party service — essential, since the documents you run it over are by definition ones containing information someone tried to withhold.

**Adopt**

## 38. MVT (Mobile Verification Toolkit) — 90/100

`SUR-B3-08` · B3 · Protecting journalists and sources · Device forensics · **cli** · bucket `source-available-restricted` · maintainer MVT Project (Amnesty International Security Lab lineage)
[Project page](docs/projects/SUR-B3-08.md) · [repository](https://github.com/mvt-project/mvt) · [docs](https://docs.mvt.re/)

**Scores** — relevance 5/5 · capability 5/5 · maintenance 5/5 · privacy 5/5 · usability 2/5 · licence+cost 3/5 → **weighted 90/100** (pillar rank 11, segment rank 9)

### 1. Purpose

Forensic toolkit that acquires and analyses iOS backups and filesystem dumps and Android device data, checking them against indicators of compromise for mercenary spyware such as Pegasus and Predator.

### Journalism / investigative use case

The standard tool for answering 'has this journalist's phone been targeted?' — running a consensual check on a reporter's or source's device against published spyware indicators, which is how most publicly confirmed Pegasus infections of journalists have been established.

### 2. Audience

specialist investigator, engineer

### 3. Project type

cli · bucket `source-available-restricted`

### 4. Pros

- The reference implementation in this field, with direct lineage to the Amnesty Security Lab work that exposed Pegasus targeting of journalists — provenance no alternative matches
- Works against standard iOS backups, so a check can be run without jailbreaking or specialist hardware, which makes consensual checks practical in the field
- Very actively maintained (v2026.11.2, 2026-11-02; pushed 2026-11-17) with 16,096 stars and a modest backlog (66 open issues)
- Indicator-driven: pair it with Amnesty's published IOCs and stalkerware-indicators to extend coverage beyond mercenary spyware

### 5. Cons

- LICENCE BLOCKER, verified with primary evidence: MVT License 1.1 §3.0 imposes a Consensual Use Restriction requiring the Data Owner's explicit, uncoerced and fully informed consent, including disclosure of privacy implications and the data-retention policy. This is a contractual obligation, not merely ethics, and it is not an OSI licence
- A clean result is not evidence of safety: MVT finds known indicators, so a novel or well-cleaned implant is invisible, and reporting 'no infection found' as 'not targeted' would be wrong
- iOS coverage is substantially better than Android, where acquisition is harder and artefacts are fewer — so Android results are weaker and need androidqf plus more care
- Interpreting output requires forensic literacy; a false positive communicated badly to a journalist causes real distress, and a missed detection creates false confidence

### 6. Feedback (documented)

No individual user reports verified in this survey. The decisive documented fact is the licence, read in full from the repository: MVT License 1.1 §3.0 quoted verbatim in sources/evidence/leads.md with the full text saved at sources/recovered/cat/mvt.txt. 16,096 stars with 66 open issues; release v2026.11.2 (2026-11-02). MVT's role in confirmed Pegasus cases is publicly documented by Amnesty International.

### 7. Assessment

Adopt it, and build the licence obligation into your process rather than treating it as background: a written consent script that explains what is collected, what it reveals and how long you keep it, plus a retention policy you actually follow. That satisfies §3.0 and is good practice anyway. Two communication rules matter as much as the tooling: never describe a clean result as proof of safety, and never deliver a positive result to a journalist without a plan for what happens next — device replacement, account recovery, legal and psychological support.

### 8. Maintenance

**Actively maintained** — GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release v2026.11.2 (2026-11-02), 16,096 stars, 66 open issues. Same-day commits with date-versioned releases; institutional lineage and an active indicator-update cadence.

### 9. Licensing

**Licence:** MVT License 1.1 — NOT OSI-approved (MPL-2.0 derivative with a Consensual Use Restriction at §3.0); GitHub reports NOASSERTION _(SPDX not verified — resolved from the licence file or project documentation)_

**Model / data licence:** Indicators of compromise come from Amnesty and other publishers under their own terms.

**Restrictions:** §3.0 Consensual Use Restriction (verbatim): use is permitted provided 'the Data Owner must explicitly consent to the procedure, free from any form of coercion, and must be fully informed about the nature of the procedure, its privacy implications, and any data retention and disposal policy.' Non-consensual forensic acquisition is prohibited. The restriction flows downstream on redistribution, and MPL-style file-level copyleft also applies.

**Licence evidence:** https://github.com/mvt-project/mvt/blob/main/LICENSE

### 10. Costs

No fee. A forensic workstation and storage for backups (phone backups are tens of GB each). The real cost is skilled analyst time per examination plus the consent and support process around it. Estimate.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

Processing is local, which is essential since a phone backup is the most intimate dataset a journalist will ever hand you. The obligations are correspondingly serious: encrypted storage, a short retention period, documented disposal, and access limited to the examining analyst. The licence makes several of these contractual rather than optional.

### 12. Verdict

**Adopt**

### Material blockers

_Tracked separately from the score._

- MVT License 1.1 §3.0 consensual-use restriction — written informed consent and a disclosed retention policy are contractual requirements, and the licence is not OSI-approved

### 13. Alternatives

- [androidqf](docs/projects/SUR-B3-09.md) for Android acquisition before MVT analysis
- [iLEAPP](docs/projects/SUR-B3-15.md) and ALEAPP for broader artefact parsing beyond spyware indicators
- Referral to Amnesty Security Lab, Access Now's Digital Security Helpline or Citizen Lab where the stakes are high and in-house capacity is thin

### 14. Evidence

Verified **2026-11-17** · confidence **high** · assessment depth `repo-inspected`

- https://github.com/mvt-project/mvt/blob/main/LICENSE
- https://docs.mvt.re/

`SUR-B3-13` · B3 · Protecting journalists and sources · Cell-site simulator detection · **application** · bucket `verified-oss` · maintainer Electronic Frontier Foundation
[Project page](docs/projects/SUR-B3-13.md) · [repository](https://github.com/EFForg/rayhunter) · [docs](https://eff.org/rayhunter)

**Scores** — relevance 5/5 · capability 4/5 · maintenance 5/5 · privacy 5/5 · usability 3/5 · licence+cost 4/5 → **weighted 90/100** (pillar rank 12, segment rank 10)

### 1. Purpose

Rust application that runs on an inexpensive mobile hotspot to analyse the cellular control plane and detect behaviour characteristic of cell-site simulators (IMSI catchers), such as downgrade attacks and unusual identity requests.

### Journalism / investigative use case

Detecting whether a protest, a courthouse, a border crossing or a newsroom's surroundings are being surveilled with an IMSI catcher — a question journalists have had no practical way to answer, and one that is both a protective measure and, when a detection occurs, a story in itself.

### 2. Audience

specialist investigator, engineer

### 3. Project type

application · bucket `verified-oss`

### 4. Pros

- Addresses a surveillance technique that was effectively undetectable by journalists until now, and does so on hardware costing tens rather than thousands — a genuine capability change for the field
- Dual value: protective (know when your communications are being intercepted) and investigative (document that a specific location was surveilled at a specific time)
- GPL-3.0, very actively maintained (v0.13.0, 2026-09-16; pushed 2026-11-17) with 6,069 stars and EFF's institutional backing and legal literacy
- Runs on specific inexpensive hotspot hardware, so a newsroom can deploy several and build a picture over time

### 5. Cons

- Detections are heuristic signals about anomalous network behaviour, not proof that a cell-site simulator was present — and publishing 'an IMSI catcher was deployed' on a heuristic alone would be a serious overreach
- Requires specific supported hotspot hardware, and the supported-device list is a procurement constraint that varies by region and carrier bands
- Cellular-network behaviour varies legitimately by carrier and location, so baselining is necessary before anomalies mean anything — and that takes time and local knowledge
- GPL-3.0 and 6,069 stars indicate a young, rapidly developing project, so expect behaviour changes between versions and keep notes on which version produced which detection

### 6. Feedback (documented)

No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 6,069 stars with release v0.13.0 (2026-09-16) and a push on 2026-11-17, GPL-3.0, maintained by EFF. The rapid growth in stars for a hardware-dependent tool indicates substantial interest in the capability; EFF publishes guidance on interpreting results, which is the relevant support context.

### 7. Assessment

Adopt it — this is one of the most interesting items in the whole catalogue for your context, because it converts an invisible threat into something observable and reportable. Two disciplines are essential. First, baseline normal cellular behaviour in your locations before treating anomalies as detections, otherwise you will produce false alarms. Second, in published work describe what was observed (specific control-plane anomalies, at a time and place) rather than asserting the presence of a device, and get a cellular-security expert to review before publication. Deploy several units if protest or courthouse coverage is a regular beat.

### 8. Maintenance

**Actively maintained** — GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release v0.13.0 (2026-09-16), 6,069 stars, GPL-3.0. Same-day commits with frequent releases under EFF's institutional maintenance; a young project with strong momentum.

### 9. Licensing

**Licence:** GPL-3.0 _(SPDX verified)_

**Model / data licence:** n/a

**Restrictions:** GPL-3.0; immaterial for internal use. Note that operating cellular-monitoring equipment may engage local radio or wiretapping law — a legal question entirely separate from the licence, and one to check in each jurisdiction where you deploy.

**Licence evidence:** https://github.com/EFForg/rayhunter/blob/main/LICENSE

### 10. Costs

No software fee. Hardware: a supported mobile hotspot (low tens to low hundreds, estimate) per deployment plus a mobile data plan if you want it operating in the field. Among the best capability-per-cost items in the catalogue.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

Analysis is local on the device; nothing is transmitted to EFF. The data collected is about the network rather than about individuals, which keeps the privacy profile clean. Possession and operation of the device may itself attract attention in a hostile jurisdiction.

### 12. Verdict

**Adopt**

### Material blockers

_Tracked separately from the score._

- Requires specific supported hotspot hardware; operating cellular monitoring may engage local radio law

### 13. Alternatives

- Commercial IMSI-catcher detection products, which are expensive and opaque
- Crowdsourced cell-tower databases (OpenCellID) for corroborating anomalies against known infrastructure
- SnoopSnitch and similar Android apps, with narrower device support

**Scores** — relevance 5/5 · capability 3/5 · maintenance 5/5 · privacy 5/5 · usability 5/5 · licence+cost 4/5 → **weighted 90/100** (pillar rank 15, segment rank 8)

### 1. Purpose

Browser extension (and CLI) that saves a complete web page as a single self-contained HTML file with all assets inlined, preserving the page exactly as rendered.

### Journalism / investigative use case

One-click preservation of a page or social post exactly as rendered in your browser, including content behind a login you legitimately hold — the fastest capture available, and the one reporters will actually use because it takes one keystroke.

### 2. Audience

journalist, newsroom analyst, engineer

### 3. Project type

application · bucket `verified-oss`

### 4. Pros

- Lowest-friction capture in this catalogue: one click, one portable file that opens in any browser forever with no replay software
- Captures the rendered state including authenticated pages, so it reaches content crawlers cannot
- Extremely active (release v1.38.0 on 2026-11-17, same-day push) with a very large community (22,931 stars)
- A CLI exists, so the same engine can be scripted for bulk preservation of a URL list

### 5. Cons

- Not WARC: a single HTML snapshot lacks HTTP headers, request/response records and capture provenance, so it is materially weaker evidence than a WACZ and can be edited afterwards undetectably
- Inlining assets alters the document, so the file is a faithful rendering rather than a faithful record of what was transmitted
- AGPL-3.0 matters if you redistribute a modified version or embed the engine in a product
- 99 open issues reflecting the variety of pages users try to capture; very complex pages can produce large files

### 6. Feedback (documented)

No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 22,931 stars with 99 open issues, release v1.38.0 published 2026-11-17 with same-day push — one of the most actively maintained tools in this catalogue. Its evidentiary limitation relative to WARC is a general property of single-file snapshots, widely discussed in archiving practice.

### 7. Assessment

Deploy it to every reporter as the default 'save this now' action, and be explicit that it is a reading copy rather than evidence of record. The combination I would standardise for your profile: SingleFile for immediate, universal capture; ArchiveWeb.page or Scoop for the pages that will carry a story. The honest trade-off is that the weaker tool is the one people will actually use, so having both and knowing which is which matters more than mandating the stronger one.

### 8. Maintenance

**Actively maintained** — GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release v1.38.0 published the same day, 22,931 stars, 99 open issues. Same-day release and push with a very large user base — exceptional maintenance for a single-maintainer project.

### 9. Licensing

**Licence:** AGPL-3.0 _(SPDX verified)_

**Model / data licence:** n/a. Captured content belongs to the original publisher.

**Restrictions:** AGPL-3.0: redistributing a modified version or offering it as a network service obliges source publication. Ordinary use as an extension is unaffected.

**Licence evidence:** https://github.com/gildas-lormeau/SingleFile/blob/master/LICENSE

### 10. Costs

Free. No infrastructure. Disk for saved files.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

The saved file is written locally with no upload by default — a clean privacy position. As with any authenticated capture, a saved logged-in page may contain personal account context, so treat files accordingly.

### 12. Verdict

**Adopt**

### 13. Alternatives

- [ArchiveWeb.page](docs/projects/OSINT-C1-31.md) for WARC/WACZ capture of the same authenticated content
- [monolith](docs/projects/OSINT-C1-39.md) for a CLI-driven equivalent in bulk
- [Scoop](docs/projects/OSINT-C1-36.md) where provenance metadata is required

High-throughput LLM inference and serving engine using paged attention and continuous batching, with an OpenAI-compatible API and support for many model architectures and quantisation schemes.

Serving a local model to a whole newsroom or processing a large document corpus: continuous batching means dozens of concurrent requests or a million-document extraction job complete in a fraction of the time a single-stream engine would take.

engineer

framework · bucket `verified-oss`

Adopt it where you have GPUs and either concurrency or corpus scale — that is the specific case it wins, and it wins decisively. For your profile the clean architecture is vLLM on the GPU server for batch and shared use, Ollama or llama.cpp on laptops for individual work, and the same OpenAI-compatible interface everywhere so tools do not care which they are talking to. ### 1. Purpose

Production-oriented NLP library providing tokenisation, part-of-speech tagging, dependency parsing, named-entity recognition and rule-based matching, with trained pipelines for around 25 languages.

### Journalism / investigative use case

Baseline workhorse for pulling person, organisation, location and money mentions out of leaked documents and mailboxes. The EntityRuler is the feature that matters most in practice: reporters supply a gazetteer of target names and companies, and the pipeline flags every occurrence across a corpus before any statistical NER runs.

### 2. Audience

engineer, newsroom analyst

### 3. Project type

library · bucket `verified-oss`

### 4. Pros

- Fast, stable and predictable at corpus scale — the practical default when you need to process a million documents on CPU without GPU infrastructure

### 5. Cons

- Statistical NER degrades noticeably on OCR-noisy leak text, unusual transliterations and non-Latin scripts — exactly the material investigations contain

- Fixed label set unless you retrain, which makes investigation-specific types (vessel, shell company) impractical — GLiNER is the better answer there

No individual user reports verified. Documented: 34,061 stars, 276 open issues, pushed 2026-10-27 with release-v3.8.18 (2026-10-26) and a v4.0.0.dev10 tag in progress. spaCy is a dependency of Presidio and many newsroom pipelines, which is verifiable from those projects.

### 7. Assessment

Adopt as the baseline, but use it the right way round: gazetteer matching first (high precision, defensible), statistical NER second (recall, needs review). For your profile the honest limitation is non-Latin scripts and OCR noise, where Stanza or GLiNER will outperform it — keep all three available and choose per corpus rather than standardising on one.

No fee. CPU-efficient; large-scale NER over millions of documents is a compute-hours cost on commodity hardware. Explosion sells Prodigy (annotation tool) separately — a paid product, price not verified here, and not required.

`SUR-B3-20` · B3 · Protecting journalists and sources · Compartmentalised operating system · **application** · bucket `verified-oss` · maintainer Qubes OS Project
