**Scores** — relevance 5/5 · capability 5/5 · maintenance 4/5 · privacy 5/5 · usability 2/5 · licence+cost 4/5 → **weighted 89/100** (pillar rank 14, segment rank 11)

### 1. Purpose

Security-focused desktop operating system that runs applications in isolated Xen-based virtual machines organised by trust level, with disposable VMs, a separate networking VM and controlled inter-VM file transfer.

### Journalism / investigative use case

A daily-use environment where compromise is contained: open an untrusted attachment in a disposable VM that is destroyed afterwards, keep source communications in one compartment and ordinary browsing in another, so a malicious document or a phishing click cannot reach your notes or your keys.

### 2. Audience

engineer, specialist investigator, journalist

### 3. Project type

application · bucket `verified-oss`

### 4. Pros

- Compartmentalisation is the only architecture here that assumes compromise will happen and limits what it reaches — the right model for a journalist who must open attachments from strangers
- Disposable VMs make opening an untrusted document safe by construction, which is Dangerzone's protection generalised to everything
- Underpins SecureDrop Workstation, so adopting Qubes brings the recommended submission-handling workflow within reach
- Long-standing project with institutional respect in the security community and a documented release and security-advisory process

### 5. Cons

- Hardware compatibility is genuinely restrictive: Qubes needs specific virtualisation and IOMMU support, and the certified-hardware list is short — procurement is the first obstacle and in some regions a decisive one
- Steep learning curve and real daily friction: moving files between compartments is deliberate work, and users who find it tedious will subvert it
- The GitHub presence is an issue tracker (QubesOS/qubes-issues, no releases, no detected licence), so repository metadata tells you nothing about the OS's health — assessment must come from the project's own release and advisory channels
- Resource-hungry: comfortable use needs substantial RAM and a fast SSD, so older laptops are unusable

### 6. Feedback (documented)

No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: the GitHub repository QubesOS/qubes-issues is a tracker (624 stars, no releases, last push 2026-07-08, no detected licence) rather than the OS source, so maintenance was not assessed from it. Qubes's adoption in high-threat journalism and its use as the basis of SecureDrop Workstation are documented by FPF.

### 7. Assessment

Adopt for the people who most need it — reporters handling unsolicited material and anyone working on a high-risk investigation — provided you can procure certified hardware and support the learning curve. For your profile the realistic path is a small number of Qubes machines for specific roles rather than an organisation-wide rollout, paired with SecureDrop Workstation if you run a submission system. Where Qubes is impractical, Tails for sessions plus Dangerzone for documents covers much of the same risk at far lower cost.

### 8. Maintenance

**Actively maintained** — Assessed from the project's own release and security-advisory process rather than GitHub, since QubesOS/qubes-issues is only a tracker (no releases, pushed 2026-07-08, no detected licence). The project maintains a published advisory stream and a certified-hardware programme; this classification is therefore medium-confidence on evidence type, not on the conclusion.

### 9. Licensing

**Licence:** GPL-2.0 (project licensing; the distribution aggregates components under their own licences) _(SPDX not verified — resolved from the licence file or project documentation)_

**Model / data licence:** n/a

**Restrictions:** Aggregate free-software licensing; immaterial for use.

**Licence evidence:** https://www.qubes-os.org/doc/license/

### 10. Costs

No software fee. Certified hardware is the cost: a Qubes-capable laptop with substantial RAM and SSD (estimate: mid-to-upper four figures for a small team), plus training and support time. The hardware constraint is the real budget item.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

Compartmentalisation limits what a compromise reaches, and the networking VM isolates the network stack. It is not an anonymity system — Qubes protects against compromise, Tails protects against tracing, and they answer different questions. Whonix VMs inside Qubes combine both.

### 12. Verdict

**Pilot**

### Material blockers

_Tracked separately from the score._

- Restrictive certified-hardware requirement; substantial learning curve and resource needs

### 13. Alternatives

- [Tails](docs/projects/SUR-B3-19.md) for amnesic, Tor-routed sessions rather than daily compartmentalisation
- [Dangerzone](docs/projects/SUR-B3-03.md) plus a hardened conventional OS as a much cheaper partial mitigation
- A dedicated, network-isolated laptop for the highest-risk material

Run queries across dozens of engines from one self-hosted instance, compare result sets to see what each engine suppresses or elevates, and avoid personalised results during research — which matters because a logged-in Google session quietly shapes what an investigation finds.

journalist, newsroom analyst, engineer

platform · bucket `verified-oss`

No individual user reports verified in this survey. Adopt and self-host — this is the cheapest meaningful improvement to search-based research, and the de-personalisation property alone justifies it. - Depends on you operating a receiving server (or a Uwazi instance), so it is part of a system rather than a standalone tool

### 6. Feedback (documented)

No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: the repository is live and non-archived under Horizontal's maintenance. Tella's use in human-rights documentation is documented by the organisation; I verified no specific deployment.

### 7. Assessment

Adopt it where you work with field documenters or stringers in hostile environments — the combination of encrypted capture, camouflage and upload to your own infrastructure has no real alternative. For your profile two things must accompany deployment: an honest briefing that camouflage delays discovery rather than preventing it, and a receiving server you actually operate, because the app's value depends on evidence getting off the device and into a collection you control.

### 8. Maintenance

**Actively maintained** — Verified via the GitHub API 2026-11-17 as live and non-archived under Horizontal's institutional maintenance, with ongoing development on the Android client. Maintenance assessed on activity and institutional backing; release cadence was not separately itemised in this survey.

### 10. Costs

Free. You need a receiving server or Uwazi instance — the real cost, and one you may already have. Estimate.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

Encrypted local storage, camouflage, and upload only to infrastructure you specify — a strong posture designed for exactly this threat. Residual risks are physical: device search by a trained searcher, and the incriminating presence of the app itself.

## 49. Playwright — 89/100

`JAI-A1-08` · A1 · Discovery, scraping, ingestion, data journalism and newsroom workflow · Browser automation · **framework** · bucket `verified-oss` · maintainer Microsoft
[Project page](docs/projects/JAI-A1-08.md) · [repository](https://github.com/microsoft/playwright) · [docs](https://playwright.dev/)

**Scores** — relevance 4/5 · capability 5/5 · maintenance 5/5 · privacy 4/5 · usability 4/5 · licence+cost 5/5 → **weighted 89/100** (pillar rank 18, segment rank 4)

### 1. Purpose

Browser-automation framework driving Chromium, Firefox and WebKit with a unified API, auto-waiting, network interception, tracing and headless or headed operation.

### Journalism / investigative use case

Reaching the content that simple HTTP requests cannot: government portals behind JavaScript, dashboards that render client-side, document viewers that paginate via XHR, and forms that must be filled to produce a report. It is also the engine under browsertrix-crawler, shot-scraper and Crawlee.

### 2. Audience

engineer

### 3. Project type

framework · bucket `verified-oss`

### 4. Pros

- Network interception is the underused feature for investigative work: rather than scraping rendered HTML, you can capture the JSON API calls a dashboard makes and get structured data directly
- Cross-browser support matters more than it sounds — some government portals work only in specific engines, and WebKit coverage occasionally rescues an otherwise inaccessible source
- Apache-2.0 with exceptional maintenance (v1.65.1, 2026-11-13; pushed 2026-11-17) and only 71 open issues against 100,396 stars — outstanding triage at enormous scale
- Tracing and video capture make a scraping run auditable, which is useful when you need to show how data was obtained

### 5. Cons

- Resource-heavy relative to HTTP scraping: each browser instance costs hundreds of megabytes, so large crawls need orchestration and patience
- Browser automation is detectable, and portals increasingly block it — so you may win access and lose it again, which makes a brittle dependency for ongoing monitoring
- Browser binaries are large downloads tied to Playwright versions, which complicates air-gapped and reproducible deployments
- General-purpose: it is included here for the concrete journalism use case, but most of its documentation and community are about software testing

### 6. Feedback (documented)

No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 100,396 stars with 71 open issues, release v1.65.1 (2026-11-13), pushed 2026-11-17, Apache-2.0. Its role in journalism tooling is verifiable from dependency relationships: browsertrix-crawler, shot-scraper and Crawlee all build on it.

### 7. Assessment

Adopt it for the specific cases that defeat plain HTTP, and resist using it where requests would do — the resource and brittleness costs are real. For your profile the highest-leverage technique is network interception: find the underlying API call a portal makes, then call that directly without the browser, which is faster, more stable and often yields cleaner data than the rendered page. Use Playwright to discover the API, not necessarily to run the collection.

### 8. Maintenance

**Actively maintained** — GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release v1.65.1 (2026-11-13), 100,396 stars, 71 open issues. Same-day commits, near-weekly releases, corporate backing, and an exceptionally low backlog for the scale.

### 9. Licensing

**Licence:** Apache-2.0 _(SPDX verified)_

**Model / data licence:** n/a

**Restrictions:** None material. Note that automating access to a site may breach its terms of service — separate from the licence.

**Licence evidence:** https://github.com/microsoft/playwright/blob/main/LICENSE

### 10. Costs

No fee. Infrastructure: browser instances are memory-hungry (budget several hundred MB each) plus disk for browser binaries. For large crawls this is the dominant cost. Estimate.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

Requests originate from your host, so targets see your IP and an automatable browser fingerprint. Processing is local. Use a dedicated egress for sensitive targets.

### 12. Verdict

**Adopt**

### 13. Alternatives

- Direct HTTP requests to the underlying API once discovered — faster and more stable
- [Crawlee](docs/projects/OSINT-C1-17.md) for a crawling framework that wraps Playwright with queueing and anti-blocking
- Puppeteer for a Chromium-only alternative

### 14. Evidence

Verified **2026-11-17** · confidence **high** · assessment depth `metadata-verified`

## 50. IODA (Internet Outage Detection and Analysis) — 88/100

`SUR-B1-07` · B1 · Monitoring public information, narratives, disinformation, censorship and harassment · Outage detection · **platform** · bucket `source-available-restricted` · maintainer Georgia Tech InetIntel (previously CAIDA)
[Project page](docs/projects/SUR-B1-07.md) · [repository](https://github.com/InetIntel/ioda-ui) · [docs](https://ioda.inetintel.cc.gatech.edu/)

**Scores** — relevance 5/5 · capability 5/5 · maintenance 4/5 · privacy 4/5 · usability 5/5 · licence+cost 2/5 → **weighted 88/100** (pillar rank 15, segment rank 3)

### 1. Purpose

System that detects and visualises internet outages by combining three independent signals — BGP routing withdrawals, active ICMP probing of address space, and background radiation observed at a network telescope — at country, region and ASN granularity.

### Journalism / investigative use case

The standard first stop for confirming and timestamping a national or regional internet shutdown, because agreement across three unrelated signals is hard to explain away as a measurement artefact — which is exactly the standard a shutdown story needs to survive official denial.

### 2. Audience

journalist, specialist investigator, newsroom analyst

### 3. Project type

platform · bucket `source-available-restricted`

### 4. Pros

- Triangulation across three independent signal types is the methodological strength: a shutdown visible in BGP, active probing and telescope data simultaneously is very strong evidence
- Country and ASN granularity lets you say which operator went dark and when, which is the attribution-relevant detail
- Hosted dashboard requires no technical skill and no in-country action, so there is no risk to anyone
- Actively operated (pushed 2026-11-16) with institutional backing at Georgia Tech

### 5. Cons

- The LICENSE text read on both the CAIDA and InetIntel copies grants use for academic research and education without fee and directs other uses to contact the university — so despite public code this is NOT open source for a commercial newsroom
- Release objects are stale (v1.0.0 from 2024-02-21) and the repository has 59 open issues with only 3 stars — the hosted service is the real artefact and the code is hard to assess
- Measures reachability, not cause: it shows that address space became unreachable, not who ordered it or why — attribution remains reporting work
- Self-hosting is impractical: it requires BGP collector feeds, probeable address space and a darknet telescope, which no newsroom has

### 6. Feedback (documented)

No individual user reports verified. Documented: the academic-research-and-education licence text read on both the CAIDA and InetIntel copies (verified session 1, retained); 59 open issues; v1.0.0 release from February 2024. IODA is widely cited in shutdown reporting and advocacy, which is credible usage evidence for the hosted dashboard.

### 7. Assessment

Use the hosted dashboard freely for confirming and timestamping shutdowns — that is its purpose and it is excellent at it. Do not plan to self-host or to build a product on the code, because the licence directs non-academic use to the university. For your profile the practical combination on a shutdown story is IODA for the timestamp and the affected ASNs, PyBGPStream for independently reconstructing the route withdrawals, and OONI for what was blocked rather than merely unreachable.

### 8. Maintenance

**Actively maintained** — GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-16, latest release v1.0.0 (2024-02-21), SPDX NOASSERTION (actual: academic-use licence), 3 stars, 59 open issues. The hosted service is continuously operated and the UI repository receives current commits; institutional maintenance at Georgia Tech.

### 9. Licensing

**Licence:** NOT OSS — academic research and education use without fee; other uses directed to contact the university (LICENSE text read on both the CAIDA and InetIntel copies) _(SPDX not verified — resolved from the licence file or project documentation)_

**Model / data licence:** Published IODA data terms were not separately verified in this survey.

**Restrictions:** Commercial use of the code requires contacting the university. Using the public dashboard and citing it in reporting is ordinary use of a public service; redistributing the code or data commercially is not covered.

**Licence evidence:** https://github.com/InetIntel/ioda-ui

### 10. Costs

Free to use the dashboard. Self-hosting is impractical (BGP feeds, probeable address space, a network telescope). No realistic infrastructure estimate because the architecture is not reproducible by a newsroom.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

Aggregates network-level public measurement data to country, region and ASN granularity; it observes reachability of address space rather than individuals. Using the dashboard runs no measurement from your machine and exposes no one in-country.

### 12. Verdict

**Adopt**

### Material blockers

_Tracked separately from the score._

- Academic-use licence on the code — not usable as commercial newsroom infrastructure (the public dashboard is fine to use and cite)

### 13. Alternatives

- PyBGPStream to independently reconstruct BGP withdrawals from public archives
- [OONI Explorer](docs/projects/SUR-B1-03.md) for what was blocked rather than unreachable

`JAI-A2-60` · A2 · Documents and language: OCR, transcription, translation, entities, entity resolution · Transcription with alignment and diarisation · **cli** · bucket `verified-oss` · maintainer Max Bain (m-bain)
[Project page](docs/projects/JAI-A2-60.md) · [repository](https://github.com/m-bain/whisperX) · [docs](https://github.com/m-bain/whisperX#readme)

**Scores** — relevance 5/5 · capability 5/5 · maintenance 4/5 · privacy 4/5 · usability 3/5 · licence+cost 4/5 → **weighted 88/100** (pillar rank 19, segment rank 11)

### 1. Purpose

Pipeline combining faster-whisper transcription, wav2vec2 forced alignment for word-level timestamps, VAD-based batching and pyannote speaker diarisation.

### Journalism / investigative use case

Producing quote-accurate, speaker-attributed transcripts of multi-party interviews and hearings where you must jump to the exact second a phrase was spoken to verify it — the combination that turns a machine transcript into something an editor can check line by line.

### 2. Audience

engineer

### 3. Project type

cli · bucket `verified-oss`

### 4. Pros

- Word-level timestamps from forced alignment are materially more accurate than Whisper's native estimates, which is what makes quote verification practical at scale
- Bundles the three stages (transcribe, align, diarise) that every newsroom audio pipeline needs, saving substantial integration work
- BSD-2-Clause and actively released (v3.8.6, 2026-05-25) with 25,401 stars
- VAD-based batching gives a large throughput gain over sequential processing

### 5. Cons

- Heavy dependency stack (faster-whisper, pyannote.audio, torchaudio, ffmpeg) and ~10GB VRAM for large-v3 plus diarisation — the most demanding transcription option here
- Diarisation inherits pyannote's weaknesses: it degrades on overlapping speech and telephone-band audio, which describes much covertly recorded material
- Alignment-model coverage is uneven outside major languages, so word-level timing quality varies by language in a way that is easy to overlook
- Obtaining diarisation weights requires accepting pyannote's HuggingFace gate, which discloses your identity to the model authors

### 6. Feedback (documented)

No individual user reports verified. Documented: 25,401 stars, 219 open issues, last release v3.8.6 (2026-05-25) with commits through 2026-11-12. The HuggingFace gating requirement is documented on pyannote's model card and is the most commonly reported setup obstacle for this project.

### 7. Assessment

The right choice for an engineer-run interview and hearing pipeline, and the one I would build on for any investigation where quotes must be verifiable to the second. For your profile: pre-fetch the pyannote weights centrally, pin the whole stack in a container because the dependency graph is fragile, and check alignment quality explicitly for each non-major language before trusting the timestamps editorially.

### 8. Maintenance

**Actively maintained** — GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-12, latest release v3.8.6 (2026-05-25), 25,401 stars, 219 open issues. Current commits with a release about six months old; active but with a slower release cadence than its dependencies, so pinning matters.

### 9. Licensing

**Licence:** BSD-2-Clause _(SPDX verified)_

**Model / data licence:** Mixed: Whisper MIT; wav2vec2 aligners vary by language; pyannote diarisation weights MIT but gated on HuggingFace.

**Restrictions:** No field-of-use restrictions found. The practical constraint is the pyannote access gate; check individual wav2vec2 aligner licences for less common languages.

**Licence evidence:** https://github.com/m-bain/whisperX/blob/main/LICENSE

### 10. Costs

No fee. GPU with ~10GB VRAM recommended; CPU operation is impractical for the full pipeline. One GPU host serves a small newsroom's audio needs. Infrastructure estimate.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

Local inference end to end; audio does not leave the machine. One-time external touchpoint is the gated pyannote weights download, best performed centrally.

### 12. Verdict

**Adopt**

### Material blockers

_Tracked separately from the score._

- Gated pyannote diarisation weights — plan a central download for air-gapped deployments

### 13. Alternatives

## 52. Whisper — 88/100

`JAI-A2-58` · A2 · Documents and language: OCR, transcription, translation, entities, entity resolution · Transcription (reference model) · **model** · bucket `verified-oss` · maintainer OpenAI
[Project page](docs/projects/JAI-A2-58.md) · [repository](https://github.com/openai/whisper) · [docs](https://github.com/openai/whisper#readme)

**Scores** — relevance 5/5 · capability 4/5 · maintenance 3/5 · privacy 5/5 · usability 4/5 · licence+cost 5/5 → **weighted 88/100** (pillar rank 20, segment rank 12)

### 1. Purpose

Encoder-decoder speech model trained on 680,000 hours of multilingual audio, performing transcription, language identification and speech translation, released with MIT code and MIT weights.

### Journalism / investigative use case

Baseline transcription of interviews and leaked audio where model provenance matters, and the canonical implementation that nearly every newsroom transcription tool wraps — so its documented failure modes are the failure modes you will encounter whichever wrapper you deploy.

### 2. Audience

engineer

### 3. Project type

model · bucket `verified-oss`

### 4. Pros

- MIT weights as well as MIT code — a genuinely unrestricted model, which is rare and removes every commercial-publication concern
- Multilingual performance across many languages from a single model, so one deployment covers a cross-border newsroom
- Reference status means every wrapper, benchmark and bug report in the ecosystem is interpretable against it
- Still the baseline against which newer ASR is measured, so quality is well characterised rather than claimed

### 5. Cons

- Documented hallucination on silence and poor recordings is the critical journalism risk: Whisper can emit fluent, plausible, entirely invented sentences, which is far more dangerous than a garbled transcript
- No speaker diarisation and only approximate word timestamps, so quote verification needs WhisperX or forced alignment
- large-v3 needs roughly 10GB VRAM, and the reference implementation is much slower than faster-whisper or whisper.cpp for the same output
- Repository has slowed: pushed 2026-08-31 with the last release v20250625 (2025-06-26) — OpenAI's attention is elsewhere, and the ecosystem forks are where development happens

### 6. Feedback (documented)

No individual user reports verified in this survey, but Whisper's hallucination behaviour on silence and low-quality audio is a widely documented phenomenon discussed extensively in the project's issue tracker and in published evaluations — I am treating it as an established property of the model rather than an anecdote. 112,964 stars, 186 open issues.

### 7. Assessment

Use the weights, not this implementation: faster-whisper or whisper.cpp give the same output far more efficiently. The operationally important point for your work is procedural rather than technical — any Whisper-derived transcript used for quotation must be checked against the audio at the quoted passage, because the model's failure mode is fluent invention. VAD preprocessing (which faster-whisper includes) materially reduces but does not eliminate this.

### 8. Maintenance

**Stable with low activity** — GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-08-31, latest release v20250625 (2025-06-26), 112,964 stars, 186 open issues. Nearly 17 months without a release and ~2.5 months since last push. Classified stable-low rather than declining because the artefact that matters — the weights — is final and unchanging, and the ecosystem maintains the tooling; but do not expect fixes from this repository.

### 9. Licensing

**Licence:** MIT _(SPDX verified)_

**Model / data licence:** MIT (weights).

**Restrictions:** None — unusually clean for a model of this capability.

**Licence evidence:** https://github.com/openai/whisper/blob/main/LICENSE

### 10. Costs

No fee. GPU with ~10GB VRAM for large-v3, or slow CPU inference. Note the separate OpenAI hosted Whisper API is a paid service under OpenAI's terms — a different thing from these weights, and inappropriate for sensitive audio.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

Fully local inference after weight download; no audio leaves the machine. The confusion to guard against is between these local weights and OpenAI's hosted transcription API, which does transmit audio.

### 12. Verdict

**Adopt**

### 13. Alternatives

- [faster-whisper](docs/projects/JAI-A2-17.md) for the same weights with much better throughput
- [whisper.cpp](docs/projects/JAI-A2-59.md) for CPU and field hardware
- NVIDIA Parakeet (CC-BY-4.0) for higher English accuracy

### 14. Evidence

Self-hostable entity-matching API that indexes OpenSanctions (or your own FollowTheMoney) data in Elasticsearch/OpenSearch and exposes search, match and OpenRefine-compatible reconciliation endpoints.

### Journalism / investigative use case

Screen a leaked client or shareholder list against sanctions and PEP data in bulk on your own infrastructure, then reconcile the same spreadsheet from OpenRefine — without the names ever leaving your network. engineer, specialist investigator

application · bucket `verified-oss`

No individual user reports verified. Adopt it specifically to keep screening in-house — the privacy argument is decisive and this is the only tool here that delivers it. Then resolve the data licence separately and in writing: if your outlet is commercially operated, 'we are journalism so it is non-commercial' is not a defensible reading of CC-BY-NC, and you should price the OpenSanctions commercial licence before building a workflow on it. **Actively maintained** — GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release v5.5.1 (2026-10-30), 184 stars, 49 open issues. Frequent releases tracking the OpenSanctions data pipeline; maintained by a commercial entity that depends on it.

### 1. Purpose

iOS Logs, Events And Plist Parser: processes iOS backups and filesystem extractions into readable reports covering app usage, locations, connections, notifications, installed applications and hundreds of other artefact types.

Going beyond spyware indicators to understand what actually happened on a device: when a journalist believes their phone was accessed at a border crossing, iLEAPP's artefact timeline — unlocks, connections, app launches, file access — is how you establish what was done and when.

specialist investigator

cli · bucket `verified-oss`

Adopt for the specific case where you need to know what happened on a device rather than merely whether known spyware is present — border searches, suspected physical access, device handover after detention. ## 57. NetworkX — 88/100

`OSINT-C3-31` · C3 · Public records, corporate ownership, finance, infrastructure, link analysis, collaboration · Link analysis · **library** · bucket `verified-oss` · maintainer NetworkX developers (NumFOCUS)
[Project page](docs/projects/OSINT-C3-31.md) · [repository](https://github.com/networkx/networkx) · [docs](https://networkx.org/documentation/stable/)

**Scores** — relevance 4/5 · capability 4/5 · maintenance 5/5 · privacy 5/5 · usability 4/5 · licence+cost 5/5 → **weighted 88/100** (pillar rank 19, segment rank 4)

### 1. Purpose

Python library for creating, manipulating and analysing graphs and networks, with a comprehensive collection of algorithms for centrality, community detection, paths, flows and structural analysis.

### Journalism / investigative use case

The analytical layer for any relationship question: compute who sits at the centre of a corporate network, find the shortest ownership path between two entities, detect communities in a co-sharing network, or identify the broker whose removal disconnects a cluster — the findings that turn a graph picture into a reportable claim.

### 2. Audience

engineer, newsroom analyst

### 3. Project type

library · bucket `verified-oss`

### 4. Pros

- Algorithm breadth is the point: centrality, community detection and path analysis are what produce findings, and NetworkX implements essentially all of them with documented definitions you can cite
- Pure Python with a clear API, so a data journalist can compute a betweenness centrality without learning a graph database
- BSD-3-Clause under NumFOCUS governance with exceptional maintenance (release 3.6.1 2026-02-13 era line, pushed 2026-11-17) — stable, long-lived and institutionally supported
- Integrates with the whole Python data stack and exports to Gephi for visualisation, so analysis and presentation connect cleanly

### 5. Cons

- Pure Python means performance limits: graphs beyond a few hundred thousand edges become slow, where igraph or a graph database is appropriate
- Centrality metrics are easy to compute and easy to over-interpret — 'most central' is a mathematical property of your graph construction, not a finding about real-world importance, and that distinction is routinely lost in published network journalism
- Graph construction decisions (what counts as an edge, which entities are included) determine the results entirely, and the library cannot help you make them defensibly
- No visualisation worth publishing; Gephi or a web library is needed for the graphic

### 6. Feedback (documented)

No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented from the metadata sweep: the repository is live and non-archived under NumFOCUS-affiliated governance with same-day commits. NetworkX is the standard Python graph library, well established across scientific computing and data journalism.

### 7. Assessment

Adopt it as the standard link-analysis tool — the algorithms are what produce findings and the documentation lets you cite definitions precisely. For your profile the methodological discipline matters more than the code: state how edges were defined, publish the construction rules, and never present a centrality score as a claim about real-world power without corroboration. Move to igraph when performance binds.

### 8. Maintenance

**Actively maintained** — Verified via the GitHub API 2026-11-17 as live and non-archived with same-day commits, under NumFOCUS-affiliated community governance and a long, consistent release history. Among the most dependable maintenance profiles in this catalogue.

### 9. Licensing

**Model / data licence:** n/a

**Restrictions:** None.

**Licence evidence:** https://github.com/networkx/networkx/blob/main/LICENSE.txt

### 10. Costs

No fee. CPU and memory proportional to graph size; pure-Python performance is the limiting factor rather than cost. Estimate.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

Entirely local, no network calls.

### 12. Verdict

**Adopt**

Adopt it as the PST entry point for any mailbox leak, and plan the pipeline around it: libpff to extract, Tika or your own code to normalise, datasketch to deduplicate threads, and a search index for review. ## 59. OpenRefine — 87/100

`JAI-A2-36` · A2 · Documents and language: OCR, transcription, translation, entities, entity resolution · Data cleaning and reconciliation · **application** · bucket `verified-oss` · maintainer OpenRefine community (Code for Science & Society fiscal host)
[Project page](docs/projects/JAI-A2-36.md) · [repository](https://github.com/OpenRefine/OpenRefine) · [docs](https://openrefine.org/docs)

**Scores** — relevance 5/5 · capability 4/5 · maintenance 4/5 · privacy 3/5 · usability 5/5 · licence+cost 5/5 → **weighted 87/100** (pillar rank 23, segment rank 14)

### 1. Purpose

Desktop application for exploring, cleaning and transforming messy tabular data, with faceting, clustering algorithms, a transformation expression language (GREL), undo/redo history and a reconciliation framework for linking values to external identifier services.

### Journalism / investigative use case

The most accessible tool in this pillar: a reporter with no code can cluster 4,000 variant company names in a leaked spreadsheet down to 900 real entities, then reconcile them to Wikidata or a self-hosted yente instance for stable identifiers — and the operation history is an auditable record of every change made to the data.

### 2. Audience

journalist, newsroom analyst

### 3. Project type

application · bucket `verified-oss`

### 4. Pros

- Reporters genuinely use it unaided — the clustering UI is the rare case where a statistical operation is exposed in terms a non-engineer can judge
- The operation-history JSON is an underrated accountability feature: you can replay, review or publish exactly what was done to the data
- Reconciliation framework is extensible, and pointing it at your own yente instance keeps identifier lookups inside the perimeter
- Long-lived, institutionally stewarded and still actively developed (pushed 2026-11-17; release 3.10.1 2026-03-04)

### 5. Cons

- Reconciliation is the leak risk in an otherwise offline tool: it sends cell values to a web service, and the default suggestions are public endpoints — for a confidential list this is an exfiltration path hiding inside a cleaning workflow
- Clustering is heuristic and over-merges distinct entities with similar names; accepting clusters uncritically creates false identities in the data
- Large datasets strain the JVM heap, and the practical ceiling (hundreds of thousands of rows) is well below leak scale
- No probabilistic record linkage — it clusters within a column but does not link two datasets with match weights, so Splink is still needed

### 6. Feedback (documented)

No individual user reports verified. Documented signals: 12,109 stars, 738 open issues, continuous commits with a slower release cadence (3.10.1 in March 2026). OpenRefine's role in data journalism is long-established and reflected in its documentation and training materials; I verified no specific newsroom testimonial.

### 7. Assessment

Adopt it and train reporters on it — the capability-per-hour-of-training ratio is the best in the catalogue. Then write one rule: reconciliation is disabled or pointed only at an internal yente/Wikidata mirror for any dataset derived from source material. That single control turns the tool's one serious privacy flaw into a non-issue, and it is a configuration change, not a code change.

### 8. Maintenance

**Actively maintained** — GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release 3.10.1 (2026-03-04), 12,109 stars, 738 open issues. Daily commits with a slow, deliberate release cadence typical of a mature desktop application; the large backlog reflects a decade of accumulated requests rather than recent neglect.

### 9. Licensing

**Licence:** BSD-3-Clause _(SPDX verified)_

**Model / data licence:** n/a

**Restrictions:** None material. Reconciliation services you connect to have their own terms.

**Licence evidence:** https://github.com/OpenRefine/OpenRefine/blob/master/LICENSE.txt

### 10. Costs

Free. Runs on a reporter's laptop; JVM heap is the only tuning concern. No paid dependencies unless you use a commercial reconciliation service.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

Cleaning and clustering are entirely local. The material exception is reconciliation, which transmits the cell values being reconciled to a third-party web service — this must be treated as a policy-controlled action for sensitive data, not a routine step.

platform · bucket `verified-oss`

- 268 open issues against only 189 stars — a high ratio indicating a complex system with a small user base, so you will encounter unresolved problems

- Still bound to a SecureDrop deployment, so it adds to rather than replaces the institutional commitment

### 6. Feedback (documented)

No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 189 stars with 268 open issues, release 1.9.0 (2026-09-02), pushed 2026-11-16, AGPL-3.0. FPF documents it as the recommended journalist-side workflow for SecureDrop, which is the relevant institutional signal.

### 7. Assessment

Adopt it alongside SecureDrop rather than as an alternative — the usability gain over the air-gapped SVS is the difference between a protocol that is followed and one that is nominally in place. For your profile the gating factor is hardware: confirm certified Qubes machines are procurable where you operate before committing, because in some exile contexts importing specific laptop models is itself difficult. Budget training time; Qubes is not intuitive.

### 8. Maintenance

**Actively maintained** — GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-16, latest release 1.9.0 (2026-09-02), 189 stars, 268 open issues. Current commits and versioned releases under institutional maintenance; the backlog reflects system complexity and a small contributor pool.

No software fee. Qubes-certified laptop per journalist handling submissions (estimate: upper four figures for a small team), plus training and support time. Replaces the SVS hardware cost rather than adding to it.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

Compartmentalised handling keeps decryption, viewing and export isolated, so a malicious submission cannot reach the journalist's general environment. Residual risk is the journalist's own operational discipline and the physical security of the laptop.

## 62. SimpleX Chat — 87/100

`SUR-B3-25` · B3 · Protecting journalists and sources · Secure communications · **application** · bucket `verified-oss` · maintainer SimpleX Chat Ltd
[Project page](docs/projects/SUR-B3-25.md) · [repository](https://github.com/simplex-chat/simplex-chat) · [docs](https://simplex.chat/docs/)

**Scores** — relevance 5/5 · capability 4/5 · maintenance 4/5 · privacy 5/5 · usability 3/5 · licence+cost 4/5 → **weighted 87/100** (pillar rank 19, segment rank 14)

### 1. Purpose

Messaging network with no user identifiers of any kind: contacts connect via one-time invitation links through relay servers that hold no account records, with end-to-end encryption and optional self-hosted relays.

### Journalism / investigative use case

First contact with a source who must not reveal a phone number, email address or any persistent identifier — the gap Signal cannot fill. A reporter publishes a one-time invitation link, the source connects, and no account exists on either side to be subpoenaed or correlated.

### 2. Audience

journalist, specialist investigator, engineer

### 3. Project type

application · bucket `verified-oss`

### 4. Pros

- No user identifiers at all is a genuinely different architecture, not a privacy feature bolted on — there is no account, no phone number and no username to correlate or compel
- Self-hostable relays mean a newsroom can run its own infrastructure, so even relay metadata stays within your control
- AGPL-3.0 and very actively maintained (v7.1.4, 2026-11-14; pushed 2026-11-17) with a large community (19,711 stars)
- Fills the specific operational gap between anonymous submission systems and identified messaging, which nothing else here covers well

### 5. Cons

- 1,333 open issues — the largest backlog of any communications tool here — reflecting a young, fast-moving project; security-critical software with that profile warrants caution for the highest-risk use
- Far less independent cryptographic review than Signal, which is the decisive consideration when the threat is a state adversary — novel architecture means novel risk
- Usability is weaker than Signal: invitation-link exchange is unfamiliar, and because there are no accounts, losing the app or device can mean losing contacts irrecoverably
- A source must install an app nobody has heard of, which is itself a barrier and, in a hostile environment, a conspicuous artefact on their device

### 6. Feedback (documented)

No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 19,711 stars with 1,333 open issues, release v7.1.4 (2026-11-14), pushed 2026-11-17, AGPL-3.0. The identifier-free design is documented by the project; the volume of open issues relative to other messengers here is the notable signal and is visible in the API data.

### 7. Assessment

Pilot it for the identifier-free first-contact case, where it does something nothing else does — but do not displace Signal for ongoing source communication, because Signal's review record matters more than SimpleX's architectural elegance when the adversary is capable. For your profile the sensible posture is: publish a SimpleX invitation alongside your SecureDrop or Hush Line address as an alternative for sources who want live conversation without an identifier, self-host the relay, and keep Signal as the workhorse.

### 8. Maintenance

**Actively maintained** — GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release v7.1.4 (2026-11-14), 19,711 stars, 1,333 open issues. Same-day commits and a rapid release cadence; the large backlog indicates a project moving faster than it can close issues, which is a maturity caveat rather than a neglect signal.

### 9. Licensing

**Licence:** AGPL-3.0 _(SPDX verified)_

**Model / data licence:** n/a

**Restrictions:** AGPL-3.0: a modified self-hosted relay offered to users obliges source publication.

**Licence evidence:** https://github.com/simplex-chat/simplex-chat/blob/stable/LICENSE

### 10. Costs

Free to use. Self-hosting relays: a small VM each — low cost and worth it for metadata control. Estimate.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

Architecturally the strongest metadata position of any messenger here: no identifiers, no accounts, and relays that hold no user records; self-hosting removes even relay-operator visibility. The counterweight is maturity — less reviewed code in a source-protection path is itself a risk.

### 12. Verdict

**Pilot**

_Tracked separately from the score._

## 63. Apache Tika — 87/100

`JAI-A2-02` · A2 · Documents and language: OCR, transcription, translation, entities, entity resolution · Document ingestion and extraction · **framework** · bucket `verified-oss` · maintainer Apache Software Foundation
[Project page](docs/projects/JAI-A2-02.md) · [repository](https://github.com/apache/tika) · [docs](https://tika.apache.org/)

**Scores** — relevance 4/5 · capability 5/5 · maintenance 5/5 · privacy 4/5 · usability 3/5 · licence+cost 5/5 → **weighted 87/100** (pillar rank 24, segment rank 15)

### 1. Purpose

One API over roughly 1,400 file formats that detects type, extracts text and returns metadata, available as a Java library, a REST server (tika-server) and a CLI.

### Journalism / investigative use case

The format-coverage backbone of leak processing: a single call handles PDFs, legacy Office, RTF, Outlook PST/MSG, archives and images, and the metadata it returns (authors, creation timestamps, producing software, revision history) is frequently the story itself — as it was in document-provenance work on leaked memos.

### 2. Audience

engineer

### 3. Project type

framework · bucket `verified-oss`

### 4. Pros

- Format breadth no other single component matches, including the legacy and email formats that dominate real leaks and that modern Python-first parsers handle badly
- Returns metadata as a first-class output, not an afterthought — critical for provenance questions about who made a document and when
- Battle-tested as the extraction layer inside ICIJ extract, Datashare and the Aleph/OpenAleph ingest path, so your pipeline inherits a well-trodden route
- Stable, versioned ASF releases with a long compatibility record, so pinning a version is realistic

### 5. Cons

- Extraction only: no layout model, no table structure, no reading-order reconstruction — a two-column scanned report comes out interleaved and you need Surya/Docling-class tooling on top
- Parsing untrusted files in-process is a genuine security risk (parser CVEs are a recurring class); you must run tika-server sandboxed, which is extra architecture
- JVM footprint and startup cost make it awkward inside lightweight Python workers; most teams end up running it as a service
- No 'latest release' object exposed on GitHub (ASF distributes via dist.apache.org and git tags), so dependency tooling needs manual version tracking

### 6. Feedback (documented)

No direct user reports collected. Documented deployment evidence is strong and verifiable from source: ICIJ extract and Datashare both declare Tika as the extraction dependency, which is a credible production signal at terabyte scale.

### 7. Assessment

I would treat Tika as near-mandatory infrastructure rather than a choice, but always behind a sandbox. For your work the decisive property is that it is the only component that will not silently drop the ten-year-old .doc or the PST mailbox in a dump. Pair it with Dangerzone for anything from an unknown source, and do not expect it to solve layout — that is a separate stage.

### 8. Maintenance

**Actively maintained** — GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-16, 4,153 stars, 64 open issues (low for a project this size, indicating issues are processed). ASF release process with a 2.x/3.x line and a security reporting channel. The low open-issue count relative to breadth is the strongest maintenance signal here.

### 9. Licensing

**Licence:** Apache-2.0 _(SPDX verified)_

**Model / data licence:** n/a

**Restrictions:** None material; note that Tika bundles many third-party parsers whose own notices are aggregated in NOTICE.txt and must be reproduced if you redistribute.

**Licence evidence:** https://github.com/apache/tika/blob/main/LICENSE.txt

### 10. Costs

No software fee. Operating cost is a JVM service: 2-4GB RAM per tika-server instance plus CPU proportional to corpus size; OCR, if enabled through Tesseract, dominates compute. Infrastructure estimate only, assuming self-hosted containers.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

Fully local processing; no network calls in the extraction path. The material privacy caveat is the inverse of the usual one — Tika extracts metadata you may not want to republish, so pair it with mat2 or an explicit scrubbing step before any document goes out.

### 12. Verdict

**Adopt**

### 13. Alternatives

- [Unstructured](docs/projects/JAI-A1-10.md) (Python-native, narrower format coverage, licence caveats)
- [Docling](docs/projects/JAI-A2-12.md) for layout-aware parsing
- [libpff](docs/projects/JAI-A1-12.md) / libratom specifically for PST/email forensics

### 14. Evidence

Verified **2026-11-17** · confidence **high** · assessment depth `metadata-verified`

`JAI-A2-48` · A2 · Documents and language: OCR, transcription, translation, entities, entity resolution · Probabilistic record linkage · **library** · bucket `verified-oss` · maintainer UK Ministry of Justice Analytical Services
[Project page](docs/projects/JAI-A2-48.md) · [repository](https://github.com/moj-analytical-services/splink) · [docs](https://moj-analytical-services.github.io/splink/)

**Scores** — relevance 4/5 · capability 5/5 · maintenance 4/5 · privacy 5/5 · usability 3/5 · licence+cost 5/5 → **weighted 87/100** (pillar rank 26, segment rank 17)

### 1. Purpose

Probabilistic record-linkage library implementing the Fellegi-Sunter model with unsupervised parameter estimation (expectation maximisation), running on DuckDB, Spark, Athena or Postgres backends, with diagnostic visualisations.

### Journalism / investigative use case

Link people across two large datasets with no shared key — a sanctions list against a corporate registry, or a leak's client list against a property register — at a scale where dedupe would stall, and with auditable per-comparison match weights you can show an editor or a lawyer.

### 2. Audience

engineer, newsroom analyst

### 3. Project type

library · bucket `verified-oss`

### 4. Pros

- Produces an interpretable match weight per comparison rather than an opaque score, which is the difference between a defensible linkage and an assertion — the single most important property for published investigations
- Scales to tens of millions of records on a laptop via the DuckDB backend, which removes the infrastructure barrier that normally forces this work into a cluster
- Built and used by a government analytical service for operational data linkage, with published methodology — strong institutional provenance
- Excellent diagnostic charts (match weight waterfalls, parameter estimates) that make the model's behaviour inspectable rather than magical

### 5. Cons

- Requires genuine understanding of blocking rules and m/u probabilities; naive use produces confidently wrong links, and the library will not stop you
- Output is a probability, not a verdict — the adjudication threshold is an editorial decision that must be documented, and teams often skip that step
- v5 broke APIs relative to v3/v4, while most tutorials and blog posts still circulating describe the older versions — a real friction point (221 open issues)
- No built-in UI for human adjudication of borderline pairs, so you must build that review step yourself

### 6. Feedback (documented)

No individual user reports verified. Documented: MoJ Analytical Services is the maintainer and publishes its methodology, which is credible institutional production evidence; 2,588 stars, 221 open issues, v5.0.0 released 2026-09-18. Note that the v5 API break against widely circulating v3/v4 tutorials is verifiable from the project's own migration documentation.

### 7. Assessment

My recommended record-linkage tool for your work, replacing dedupe. The reason is specifically evidentiary: when a story asserts that two records are the same person, Splink lets you state the match weight and the comparison features that produced it. Budget time to learn the model properly — this is the one tool here where shallow use is actively dangerous — and build a small review interface for pairs above your threshold.

### 8. Maintenance

**Actively maintained** — GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-11, latest release v5.0.0 (2026-09-18), 2,588 stars, 221 open issues. A major release in 2026 with current commits and public-sector institutional backing.

### 9. Licensing

**Licence:** MIT _(SPDX verified)_

**Model / data licence:** n/a

**Restrictions:** None.

**Licence evidence:** https://github.com/moj-analytical-services/splink/blob/master/LICENSE

### 10. Costs

No fee. DuckDB backend runs locally with no infrastructure. Spark/Athena backends incur cloud costs and would move data to that infrastructure — avoid for sensitive linkage. Estimate.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

Local with the DuckDB backend, which is the recommended configuration for sensitive data. Choosing a cloud Spark or Athena backend relocates the data to that provider — a configuration decision with major privacy consequences.

### 12. Verdict

**Adopt**

### 1. Purpose

Converts PDFs, Office files and images to Markdown, JSON or HTML using the Surya model family for layout, reading order, table structure and OCR, with optional LLM-assisted accuracy enhancement.

### Journalism / investigative use case

Workhorse for turning a heterogeneous leak — mixed PDFs, Office files, scans — into clean Markdown that is searchable, diffable and quotable, with page-level traceability back to the original. In practice the best-quality local conversion available for messy real-world documents.

engineer

cli · bucket `source-available-weights`

Technically my first choice for conversion quality, but the weights licence makes it a conditional recommendation. ## 68. Exodus Privacy — 86/100

`SUR-B2-01` · B2 · Investigating surveillance companies, infrastructure, procurement and tracking tech · Tracker analysis (mobile) · **platform** · bucket `verified-oss` · maintainer Exodus Privacy (association)
[Project page](docs/projects/SUR-B2-01.md) · [repository](https://github.com/Exodus-Privacy/exodus) · [docs](https://exodus-privacy.eu.org/en/)

**Scores** — relevance 5/5 · capability 4/5 · maintenance 4/5 · privacy 4/5 · usability 4/5 · licence+cost 4/5 → **weighted 86/100** (pillar rank 21, segment rank 4)

### 1. Purpose

Platform that statically analyses Android applications to identify embedded trackers and requested permissions, publishing per-app reports and maintaining a public tracker database.

### Journalism / investigative use case

Establishing what an app actually does to its users: analyse a government service app, a state-promoted messaging app or a commercial app a story concerns, and show which tracking SDKs it embeds and what permissions it demands. For reporting on state apps that surveil citizens, this is the evidence base.

### 2. Audience

newsroom analyst, specialist investigator, engineer

### 3. Project type

platform · bucket `verified-oss`

### 4. Pros

- Produces citable per-app reports with a named tracker list, which converts a vague privacy concern into a specific, checkable finding a reader can verify
- The maintained tracker database is itself the asset: identifying an SDK as belonging to a particular data broker is the analytical step most reporters cannot do alone
- AGPL-3.0 and self-hostable, so you can analyse an app that the public instance has not covered or that you do not want to publicly request
- Actively maintained (v1.33.0, 2026-09-13; pushed the same day) by a focused association with 820 stars

### 5. Cons

- Static analysis identifies embedded SDKs, not actual behaviour: an app may include a tracker it never activates, or exfiltrate data through code the analysis does not flag — so a report is evidence of capability rather than of conduct
- Android only, so iOS apps (and therefore a large share of apps used in wealthier markets) are out of scope
- Requesting an analysis on the public instance is a public act, disclosing your interest in a specific app — self-host if that matters
- Tracker attribution depends on the database's completeness, so a novel or in-house tracking SDK will be missed or unnamed

### 6. Feedback (documented)

No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 820 stars with 52 open issues, release v1.33.0 (2026-09-13) with same-day push, AGPL-3.0. Exodus reports are widely cited in privacy journalism and advocacy, and the project publishes its methodology — note that session 1's URL for the tracker list (exodus-privacy.eu.org/en/page/trackers/) now 404s; the current entry point is the site root (verified 2026-11-17).

### 7. Assessment

Adopt it as the first step in any story about an app's data practices, and pair it with dynamic analysis (mitmproxy) before publishing a claim about what an app sends — static presence of an SDK and observed transmission are different claims, and the stronger story uses both. For your profile the self-hosting option matters: if the app you are examining belongs to a government you are investigating, a public analysis request is a tip-off.

### 8. Maintenance

**Actively maintained** — GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-09-13, latest release v1.33.0 published the same day, 820 stars, 52 open issues. Regular releases from an established association that also operates the public analysis service.

### 9. Licensing

**Licence:** AGPL-3.0 _(SPDX verified)_

**Model / data licence:** The tracker database is published by the project; check its terms before redistributing the database itself.

**Restrictions:** AGPL-3.0: a modified self-hosted instance offered to users obliges source publication.

**Licence evidence:** https://github.com/Exodus-Privacy/exodus/blob/v3/LICENSE

### 10. Costs

No fee. Public instance free. Self-hosting estimate: a Django application plus static-analysis workers — one modest VM. Assumptions: occasional analysis volume.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

Self-hosting keeps your analysis requests private. Using the public instance publishes the fact that an app was analysed, which discloses interest. The analysis itself involves no user data.

### 12. Verdict

**Adopt**

### 13. Alternatives

## 69. GlobaLeaks — 86/100

`SUR-B3-05` · B3 · Protecting journalists and sources · Secure submission · **platform** · bucket `verified-oss` · maintainer Hermes Center for Transparency and Digital Human Rights
[Project page](docs/projects/SUR-B3-05.md) · [repository](https://github.com/globaleaks/globaleaks-whistleblowing-software) · [docs](https://docs.globaleaks.org/)

**Scores** — relevance 5/5 · capability 4/5 · maintenance 5/5 · privacy 3/5 · usability 4/5 · licence+cost 4/5 → **weighted 86/100** (pillar rank 22, segment rank 15)

### 1. Purpose

Configurable whistleblowing platform supporting anonymous submissions over Tor or HTTPS, multi-tenant deployments, customisable questionnaires, case management and multilingual interfaces.

### Journalism / investigative use case

A whistleblowing channel you can shape to the reporting context: unlike SecureDrop's deliberately minimal model, GlobaLeaks lets you build structured intake (questionnaires, categories, recipient routing), which suits a newsroom running several tip lines or a consortium where submissions must route to different partners.

### 2. Audience

engineer, newsroom analyst

### 3. Project type

platform · bucket `verified-oss`

### 4. Pros

- Configurability and multi-tenancy are the distinguishing features: one deployment can serve multiple outlets or desks with separate recipients, which matters for consortium investigations
- Supports both Tor and HTTPS access, so a source who cannot use Tor still has a protected channel — broader reach than Tor-only systems, at a stated cost in anonymity
- AGPL-3.0, very actively maintained (v5.0.101, 2026-10-28; pushed 2026-11-17), with a long deployment history across NGOs, anti-corruption bodies and public institutions
- Repository renamed (globaleaks/globaleaks → globaleaks/globaleaks-whistleblowing-software, transfer verified by redirect), so the canonical path is current

### 5. Cons

- The HTTPS option is a genuine trade-off, not just convenience: a submission over HTTPS exposes the source's IP to the hosting path, so the default must be understood and the choice explained to sources
- 620 open issues — the largest backlog in this subcategory — reflecting a broad feature surface and configurability that can be misconfigured
- Decryption happens on the platform rather than on an air-gapped station, so a compromised server is a more consequential event than with SecureDrop's model
- Configuration flexibility means security depends on your choices; a badly configured GlobaLeaks can retain far more than it should

### 6. Feedback (documented)

No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 1,529 stars with 620 open issues, release v5.0.101 (2026-10-28), pushed 2026-11-17, AGPL-3.0; repository transfer confirmed by API redirect on 2026-11-17. GlobaLeaks' use by anti-corruption authorities and NGOs is documented by the project, which is relevant institutional adoption evidence.

### 7. Assessment

The right choice when you need structured intake or multi-recipient routing and can accept a weaker threat model than SecureDrop's; the wrong choice if your sources face state-level adversaries and you want minimal retained data. For your profile the decisive question is who you are protecting sources from: GlobaLeaks protects against opportunistic exposure and gives you workflow, while SecureDrop is built for the case where the newsroom itself may be compelled. Document which model you are offering, publicly and accurately.

### 8. Maintenance

**Actively maintained** — GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release v5.0.101 (2026-10-28), 1,529 stars, 620 open issues. Same-day commits and a very frequent release cadence under an established non-profit maintainer.

### 9. Licensing

**Licence:** AGPL-3.0 _(SPDX verified)_

**Model / data licence:** n/a

**Restrictions:** AGPL-3.0: a modified instance offered over a network obliges source publication. Relevant if you customise the platform for partners, which is a common GlobaLeaks use.

**Licence evidence:** https://github.com/globaleaks/globaleaks-whistleblowing-software/blob/main/LICENSE

### 10. Costs

No software fee. Infrastructure estimate: a hardened VM or dedicated server with Tor and HTTPS endpoints, plus encrypted storage — modest hardware, but security-critical hosting and permanent administrator attention. Assumptions: single-tenant newsroom deployment.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

Tor submissions give no IP to the newsroom; HTTPS submissions do expose source IPs to the network path, which must be communicated to sources rather than left implicit. Server-side decryption means a seized or compromised server is a serious event — plan key handling and retention accordingly.

### 12. Verdict

**Pilot**

### Material blockers

_Tracked separately from the score._

- HTTPS submission path exposes source IPs; server-side decryption weakens the seizure threat model relative to SecureDrop

### 13. Alternatives

- [SecureDrop](docs/projects/SUR-B3-01.md) where the threat model requires air-gapped decryption and minimal retained data
- [Hush Line](docs/projects/SUR-B3-06.md) for a lightweight encrypted tip line
- [OnionShare](docs/projects/SUR-B3-04.md) receive mode for ad-hoc intake with no platform at all

## 70. Outline — 86/100

`SUR-B3-31` · B3 · Protecting journalists and sources · Censorship circumvention · **application** · bucket `verified-oss` · maintainer Outline Foundation (transferred from Jigsaw-Code)
[Project page](docs/projects/SUR-B3-31.md) · [repository](https://github.com/OutlineFoundation/outline-apps) · [docs](https://getoutline.org/)

**Scores** — relevance 5/5 · capability 4/5 · maintenance 4/5 · privacy 4/5 · usability 4/5 · licence+cost 4/5 → **weighted 86/100** (pillar rank 23, segment rank 16)

### 1. Purpose

VPN system built on Shadowsocks that lets an organisation run its own servers and distribute access keys, with a manager application for creating servers and clients for all major platforms.

### Journalism / investigative use case

Giving reporters and sources in censored countries a circumvention channel the newsroom controls: you run the server, distribute keys to specific people, and revoke them individually — rather than relying on a commercial VPN whose infrastructure, logging and blocking status are outside your control.

### 2. Audience

engineer, journalist

### 3. Project type

application · bucket `verified-oss`

### 4. Pros

- You control the infrastructure, which is the decisive difference from a commercial VPN: no third-party logs, no shared IP reputation, and keys you can revoke per person
- Shadowsocks-based transport is designed to resist protocol-based blocking, so it survives in networks where standard VPN protocols are detected and dropped
- Apache-2.0 with very active development (pushed 2026-11-17) and clients for all major platforms, so a mixed-device team is covered
- Repository transfer Jigsaw-Code/outline-apps → OutlineFoundation/outline-apps verified by redirect — governance moved from Google's Jigsaw to an independent foundation, which is arguably an improvement for this use case

### 5. Cons

- Release metadata is badly stale (v1.10.1 from 2023-03-20 against a windows-v1.9.1 tag) despite current commits, so determining what version users should run takes effort — a real problem for security software
- 595 open issues across a multi-platform client suite
- Running your own circumvention server makes you responsible for its operational security, and a server compromised by the adversary becomes a surveillance point on your most at-risk users
- Circumvention is an arms race: your server's IP can be blocked, and maintaining access means rotating infrastructure, which is ongoing work rather than a one-time deployment

### 6. Feedback (documented)

No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 9,282 stars with 595 open issues, release v1.10.1 (2023-03-20) against current commits (pushed 2026-11-17), Apache-2.0; transfer from Jigsaw-Code to OutlineFoundation confirmed by API redirect on 2026-11-17. Outline's design for organisational circumvention is documented by the project.

### 7. Assessment

Adopt it if you support people in censored networks — controlling your own circumvention infrastructure is materially better than recommending a commercial VPN. For your profile the realities to plan for: budget for IP rotation because servers get blocked, distribute keys through a channel that is itself protected, and treat the server as a high-value target since it sits in the path of your most exposed users' traffic. The stale release metadata is an irritant: pin and document the client versions you deploy.

### 8. Maintenance

**Actively maintained** — GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release object v1.10.1 (2023-03-20), tag windows-v1.9.1, 9,282 stars, 595 open issues. Same-day commits with abandoned release tagging; activity is unambiguous but release hygiene is poor, which matters for a security tool.

### 9. Licensing

**Licence:** Apache-2.0 _(SPDX verified)_

**Model / data licence:** n/a

**Restrictions:** None material.

**Licence evidence:** https://github.com/OutlineFoundation/outline-apps/blob/master/LICENSE

### 10. Costs

No software fee. Infrastructure: a VPS per server (low single-digit monthly cost each, estimate) plus bandwidth, and — the real cost — periodic replacement of blocked servers. Budget for several servers and rotation rather than one.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

You hold the infrastructure, so there is no third-party logging. The counterpart responsibility is that your server sees users' traffic destinations, making its security and your logging policy a source-protection question in their own right. Set logging to minimal deliberately.

### 12. Verdict

**Adopt**

### 13. Alternatives

- Tor with bridges where anonymity rather than access is the goal
- Commercial VPNs for convenience, accepting third-party trust and shared blocking
- Self-hosted WireGuard where protocol-based blocking is not the problem

### 1. Purpose

Official US federal spending portal with searchable and bulk-downloadable award data covering contracts, grants and subawards, including recipient, agency, amount, date and product/service codes.

### Journalism / investigative use case

Establishing which US federal agencies bought surveillance and forensic technology, from whom and for how much — including the Cellebrite, Magnet Forensics and biometric-system contracts that recur in surveillance reporting. The custom download lets you extract an entire category of spending for analysis rather than clicking through records.

### 2. Audience

newsroom analyst, specialist investigator, engineer

dataset · bucket `proprietary-service`

- Authoritative primary data with recipient names, amounts and dates, downloadable in bulk — the strongest openly available procurement dataset of any jurisdiction

### 7. Assessment

Adopt it as the primary source for US surveillance procurement and plan for entity resolution as a first-class step — the names are messy enough that aggregate totals are wrong without it. For your profile the high-value technique is combining prime and subaward data: a vendor absent from prime contracts often appears as a subcontractor, and that linkage is where the story usually is. Note that absence of a contract is not evidence of no purchase, given classified procurement.

### 8. Maintenance

### 10. Costs

Free. Cost is storage and compute for bulk analysis, plus entity-resolution effort. Estimate.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

Public records about agencies and corporate recipients. Your queries are visible to the portal.

**Adopt**

Translator library and command-line suite for raster and vector geospatial formats, with reprojection, warping, mosaicking, clipping and format conversion across several hundred drivers.

### Journalism / investigative use case

The plumbing under every spatial pipeline: convert a government shapefile to GeoJSON for the web, reproject a leaked dataset into a measurable coordinate system, clip a 40GB satellite scene to the area of interest, or mosaic tiles into a single image for before-and-after comparison.

engineer

library · bucket `verified-oss`

Adopt — you will use it whether you choose to or not, since it sits beneath everything else. Fastest route to rasterising pages for OCR at corpus scale, and — critically — to applying genuine redactions that delete the underlying text rather than drawing a black rectangle over it. ### 2. Audience

engineer

### 3. Project type

library · bucket `verified-oss`

Use it for internal batch processing and redaction, where AGPL is harmless; think carefully before putting it inside a public-facing service. `SUR-B2-05` · B2 · Investigating surveillance companies, infrastructure, procurement and tracking tech · Mobile app reverse engineering · **cli** · bucket `verified-oss` · maintainer Connor Tumbleson (iBotPeaches) and contributors
[Project page](docs/projects/SUR-B2-05.md) · [repository](https://github.com/iBotPeaches/Apktool) · [docs](https://apktool.org/)

**Scores** — relevance 4/5 · capability 4/5 · maintenance 5/5 · privacy 5/5 · usability 3/5 · licence+cost 5/5 → **weighted 86/100** (pillar rank 25, segment rank 6)

### 1. Purpose

Tool for reverse engineering Android APK files: decodes resources to near-original form, disassembles bytecode to smali, and can rebuild a modified APK.

### Journalism / investigative use case

Reading what an app actually contains: extract the hardcoded endpoints, API keys, strings and configuration from a surveillance or state app to show which servers it talks to and which third parties it embeds — often the most quotable evidence in an app investigation, because strings in a binary are hard to deny.

### 2. Audience

engineer, specialist investigator

### 3. Project type

cli · bucket `verified-oss`

### 4. Pros

- Resource and string extraction gives concrete, quotable artefacts (endpoint URLs, provider names, hidden configuration) that make an app story specific
- The foundational tool in this space — MobSF and most analysis pipelines depend on it — so understanding it underpins everything else
- Apache-2.0 with excellent maintenance: release v3.0.3 (2026-07-20), pushed 2026-11-16, 78 open issues against 27,258 stars
- Mature and stable, so results are reproducible across versions — important when an analysis will be challenged

### 5. Cons

- Produces smali rather than readable source, so understanding logic (as opposed to extracting strings) requires real reverse-engineering skill
- Obfuscated and packed apps resist analysis, and commercial spyware is typically heavily obfuscated — which is exactly the case you most want to analyse
- Reverse engineering may breach terms of service and local law; the rebuild capability in particular can stray into territory you do not want to be in during an investigation
- Narrow scope by design: it decodes, and everything analytical is yours to do

### 6. Feedback (documented)

No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 27,258 stars with 78 open issues, release v3.0.3 (2026-07-20), pushed 2026-11-16, Apache-2.0. Its position as the standard APK decoder is evidenced by MobSF and the wider Android-analysis ecosystem depending on it.

### 7. Assessment

Adopt as the low-level complement to MobSF — when you need to pull specific strings or configuration out of an APK, this is the tool, and the output is often the most publishable evidence in the story. For your profile the realistic expectation is that it works well on ordinary apps and poorly on deliberately obfuscated spyware; for the latter, the realistic route is a specialist partner (Amnesty Security Lab, Citizen Lab) rather than in-house analysis.

### 8. Maintenance

**Actively maintained** — GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-16, latest release v3.0.3 (2026-07-20), 27,258 stars, 78 open issues. Long-running project with a consistent release history and a low backlog relative to scale.

### 9. Licensing

**Licence:** Apache-2.0 _(SPDX verified)_

**Model / data licence:** n/a

**Restrictions:** None material for the tool. The legal constraints are external: reverse-engineering prohibitions in app terms and, in some jurisdictions, in law.

**Licence evidence:** https://github.com/iBotPeaches/Apktool/blob/master/LICENSE.md

### 10. Costs

No fee. Java runtime; negligible resources.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

Entirely local decoding; the APK and your interest in it stay on your machine.

### 12. Verdict

**Adopt**

### Material blockers

_Tracked separately from the score._

- Reverse engineering may breach app terms and local law

### 1. Purpose

Pythonic interface to GDAL's raster capabilities, reading and writing geospatial raster datasets as NumPy arrays with windowed reads, reprojection and masking.

### Journalism / investigative use case

The analysis layer for satellite work: compute a vegetation or burn index to show deforestation or fire damage over time, difference two scenes to detect new construction at a military or industrial site, or extract pixel values at incident coordinates to corroborate a claim about ground conditions.

### 2. Audience

engineer

### 3. Project type

library · bucket `verified-oss`

### 4. Pros

- Windowed reads let you work with a small area of a very large scene without loading it all, which is what makes satellite analysis practical on an ordinary machine
- NumPy array interface means band arithmetic (NDVI, NBR, change detection) is a few lines, so the analytical techniques used in environmental and conflict reporting are directly accessible

- Depends on GDAL, so installation inherits that complexity — wheels have improved this but environment conflicts remain the common complaint

### 7. Assessment

Adopt for satellite analysis, with a methodological caution that matters more than the tooling: before publishing a change-detection finding, verify that the apparent change is not an artefact of cloud cover, seasonal variation, sensor differences or scaling. For your profile the strongest pattern is to pair rasterio analysis with manual visual confirmation in QGIS on the same scenes — the index tells you where to look, the human confirms what is there.

### 8. Maintenance

**Actively maintained** — GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-03, latest release 1.5.2 (2026-09-30), 2,595 stars, 158 open issues. Regular releases with a broad contributor base; two weeks since last push is normal cadence for a mature library.

**Model / data licence:** n/a. Satellite imagery carries the provider's licence — this is where restrictions actually apply.

**Restrictions:** Code permissive. The material restrictions are on imagery: Sentinel and Landsat are openly licensed, but commercial providers (Planet, Maxar) restrict redistribution of imagery and sometimes of derived products — check before publishing a processed image.

**Licence evidence:** https://github.com/rasterio/rasterio/blob/main/LICENSE.txt

No fee. CPU and disk proportional to scene size; satellite scenes are large (hundreds of MB to GB each). The real cost is imagery acquisition where commercial data is needed. Estimate.

Local processing. If reading remotely (S3, HTTP), the host sees your range requests and therefore your area of interest — relevant when the area itself is sensitive.
