My preferred lightweight monitoring approach for an engineer-led team, because the evidence artefact (a git history) is simultaneously the audit trail and the alerting substrate. ## 123. VeraCrypt — 83/100

`SUR-B3-22` · B3 · Protecting journalists and sources · Disk and volume encryption · **application** · bucket `verified-oss` · maintainer IDRIX / Mounir Idrassi
[Project page](docs/projects/SUR-B3-22.md) · [repository](https://github.com/veracrypt/VeraCrypt) · [docs](https://veracrypt.io/en/Documentation.html)

**Scores** — relevance 4/5 · capability 4/5 · maintenance 4/5 · privacy 5/5 · usability 4/5 · licence+cost 4/5 → **weighted 83/100** (pillar rank 34, segment rank 21)

### 1. Purpose

Disk-encryption software creating encrypted containers and full-disk encryption on Windows, macOS and Linux, with hidden volumes and plausible-deniability features, derived from TrueCrypt.

### Journalism / investigative use case

Encrypting the archive of source material that must travel or be stored outside a controlled environment — an external drive carried across a border, a backup held off-site, or a container holding a leak on a shared workstation. The hidden-volume feature is sometimes used in high-risk travel, with serious caveats.

### 2. Audience

journalist, engineer, specialist investigator

### 3. Project type

application · bucket `verified-oss`

### 4. Pros

- Cross-platform encrypted containers are the practical answer for material that must move between operating systems, where platform-native encryption (BitLocker, FileVault, LUKS) does not interoperate
- Full-disk and container modes cover both the laptop and the external drive cases with one tool and one mental model
- Actively maintained (VeraCrypt_1.26.31, 2026-11-02; pushed 2026-11-16) with a large user base (12,148 stars) and a TrueCrypt lineage that has been independently audited over the years
- Open source, so the encryption implementation can be examined rather than trusted on vendor assurance

### 5. Cons

- Hidden volumes provide plausible deniability only in theory: under coercive questioning at a border, the existence of VeraCrypt plus a refusal to produce a second password can itself be the problem, and several jurisdictions can compel disclosure — do not present this feature to journalists as safety
- GitHub reports SPDX NOASSERTION; the project is licensed under the Apache-2.0 plus TrueCrypt Licence 3.0 combination, which is unusual and needs reading before redistribution
- 515 open issues and a complex codebase with a single principal maintainer — a notable bus factor for security-critical software
- Full-disk encryption on a machine that is seized while running or suspended offers much less protection than users assume

### 6. Feedback (documented)

No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 12,148 stars with 515 open issues, release VeraCrypt_1.26.31 (2026-11-02), pushed 2026-11-16, SPDX NOASSERTION (the project's licensing combines Apache-2.0 with the TrueCrypt Licence 3.0 for inherited code). VeraCrypt and its TrueCrypt ancestor have been the subject of published independent audits, which is the strongest assurance signal available for encryption software here.

### 7. Assessment

Adopt for cross-platform encrypted containers, and be careful about how you present it. Two messages for the people you support: encryption protects data at rest on a powered-off device and little else, so shut down rather than suspend when crossing a border; and hidden volumes are not a safe answer to coercion, because the threat at a border is a person, not a cryptanalyst. Where the platform permits, native full-disk encryption (LUKS, FileVault) is simpler and better integrated — use VeraCrypt specifically for portable, cross-platform containers.

### 8. Maintenance

**Actively maintained** — GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-16, latest release VeraCrypt_1.26.31 (2026-11-02), 12,148 stars, 515 open issues. Regular releases over many years; the large backlog and single-principal-maintainer structure are the notable risks, not activity.

### 9. Licensing

**Licence:** Apache-2.0 plus TrueCrypt Licence 3.0 for inherited code (GitHub reports NOASSERTION) _(SPDX not verified — resolved from the licence file or project documentation)_

**Model / data licence:** n/a

**Restrictions:** The TrueCrypt Licence 3.0 component is not an OSI-approved licence and has known redistribution ambiguities — relevant if you bundle VeraCrypt into a distributed product or image, immaterial for ordinary use.

**Licence evidence:** https://github.com/veracrypt/VeraCrypt/blob/master/License.txt

### 10. Costs

No fee. No infrastructure. Cost is user training and the discipline of key management — a forgotten passphrase on an encrypted archive is a permanent data loss.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

Strong at-rest protection when used correctly on a powered-off device. Residual risks are the ones that actually occur: suspended machines, keys in memory, coerced disclosure, and passphrases written down or reused.

### 12. Verdict

**Adopt**

### Material blockers

_Tracked separately from the score._

- Hidden-volume plausible deniability should not be relied on against coercive questioning

### 13. Alternatives

- LUKS (Linux), FileVault (macOS) or BitLocker (Windows) for native full-disk encryption where cross-platform portability is not needed
- age or GPG for encrypting individual files for transfer
- [Tails](docs/projects/SUR-B3-19.md) with an encrypted persistent volume for a portable working environment

### 14. Evidence

Verified **2026-11-17** · confidence **high** · assessment depth `metadata-verified`

- https://github.com/veracrypt/VeraCrypt
- https://veracrypt.io/en/Documentation.html

- Breadth and accessibility: a reporter with no technical background can run keyframe extraction plus multi-engine reverse search in under a minute, which is why it dominates practical newsroom verification
- Actively maintained with a current release (v0.94, 2026-11-03) and pushed 2026-11-17, backed by AFP and an EU research consortium rather than a volunteer
- Extension code is MIT, so the client side is auditable
- Consolidates workflows (keyframes, reverse search, EXIF, archiving) that would otherwise require four separate tools and manual file shuffling

### 5. Cons

- NOT local-only, and this is the critical caveat: media submitted for keyframes, forensics, deepfake detection, translation or archiving is uploaded to AFP/vera.ai backend services, and reverse search sends it to Google, Baidu and Yandex. Submitting unpublished source material is a disclosure
- Forensic and deepfake panel outputs are probabilistic signals and investigative leads, NOT conclusive proof of manipulation or synthesis — false positives and negatives occur, and platform recompression degrades every forensic signal
- Matomo analytics is present in the extension, so usage telemetry exists
- Backend model weights are not distributed and their licences were not verified, so you cannot reproduce or audit the detector outputs

### 6. Feedback (documented)

No individual user reports verified in this survey, but the plugin's standing among verification practitioners is well documented by the InVID/WeVerify/vera.ai projects and by its adoption in verification training curricula. The upload-to-backend behaviour and the Matomo analytics are documented in the project's own privacy information — treat these as project-disclosed facts, not inferences.

### 7. Assessment

Adopt it for public, already-circulating media — that is the case it is built for and it is excellent there. Write an explicit rule against using it on unpublished source material, because the convenient buttons are the ones that upload. For media-in-exile work, note additionally that reverse-image search through Yandex or Baidu discloses the image to jurisdictions you may be investigating. Treat every forensic panel as a lead that must be corroborated by non-forensic reporting.

### 8. Maintenance

**Actively maintained** — GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release v0.94 (2026-11-03), 53 stars, 28 open issues. Same-day push with a current release; funded consortium backing (AFP Medialab, vera.ai). Star count understates adoption because users install from browser stores, not GitHub.

### 9. Licensing

**Licence:** MIT (extension code) _(SPDX verified)_

**Model / data licence:** n/a for the extension; deepfake and forensics models run on AFP/vera.ai backend services, weights not distributed and model licences not verified.

**Restrictions:** Extension code unrestricted. The backend services operate under the consortium's terms, not an open licence, so the analytical capability is not self-hostable.

**Licence evidence:** https://github.com/AFP-Medialab/verification-plugin/blob/master/LICENSE

### 10. Costs

Free to use. No infrastructure. The cost is non-monetary: dependency on third-party backends you do not control and cannot audit.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

The weakest privacy profile among widely recommended verification tools, and it must be understood plainly: media sent to the forensics, deepfake, keyframe, translation or archiving panels is uploaded to AFP/vera.ai; reverse-image search sends the image to Google, Baidu and Yandex; Matomo analytics records usage. Appropriate for public media, inappropriate for unpublished source material.

### 12. Verdict

**Adopt**

### Material blockers

_Tracked separately from the score._

- Uploads media to third-party backends — unsuitable for unpublished or source-sensitive material

### 13. Alternatives

- [Sherloq](docs/projects/OSINT-C2-12.md) for a fully local image-forensics workbench
- [PySceneDetect](docs/projects/OSINT-C2-10.md) plus ExifTool plus ImageHash for a local equivalent of the keyframe and metadata workflow
- Hosted verification services only where the media is already public

### 14. Evidence

Verified **2026-11-17** · confidence **high** · assessment depth `metadata-verified`

- https://weverify.eu/verification-plugin/

## 127. BERTopic — 82/100

`JAI-A2-04` · A2 · Documents and language: OCR, transcription, translation, entities, entity resolution · Topic modelling and corpus triage · **library** · bucket `verified-oss` · maintainer Maarten Grootendorst
[Project page](docs/projects/JAI-A2-04.md) · [repository](https://github.com/MaartenGr/BERTopic) · [docs](https://maartengr.github.io/BERTopic/)

**Scores** — relevance 4/5 · capability 4/5 · maintenance 4/5 · privacy 4/5 · usability 4/5 · licence+cost 5/5 → **weighted 82/100** (pillar rank 54, segment rank 31)

### 1. Purpose

Topic modelling pipeline that embeds documents, reduces dimensionality with UMAP, clusters with HDBSCAN and derives human-readable topic labels via class-based TF-IDF.

### Journalism / investigative use case

The strongest current answer to 'what is actually in this dump': cluster 200,000 leaked emails into a few hundred labelled themes, see which clusters are unexpected, and drill into those first instead of reading chronologically.

### 2. Audience

engineer, newsroom analyst

### 3. Project type

library · bucket `verified-oss`

### 4. Pros

- Produces topic labels a reporter can read, which is what makes it usable in a newsroom where raw LDA output is not
- Modular by design — you can swap in a local embedding model, so the whole pipeline stays offline
- Strong documentation with worked examples for dynamic (over-time) and hierarchical topic modelling, both directly useful for narrative-change stories
- Active release cadence and a 1.0 beta line, with the maintainer visibly responsive in the repo

### 5. Cons

- UMAP/HDBSCAN memory grows sharply past a few hundred thousand documents; at leak scale you need sampling, incremental fitting or a different approach, and this is the most common practical failure
- Topic labels are statistical artefacts and over-merge or split in ways that mislead if taken at face value — every cluster needs human interpretation before it informs reporting
- 480 open issues suggests support load exceeds maintainer capacity, so expect to debug integration problems yourself
- Results are sensitive to embedding model and UMAP random state; two runs can tell slightly different stories, which is awkward if you need a reproducible methodology note

### 6. Feedback (documented)

No individual deployment reports verified. The 480 open issues against 7,963 stars is itself documented evidence of a single-maintainer project with heavy user demand. I did not verify any specific newsroom deployment, so treat journalism adoption as plausible rather than evidenced.

### 7. Assessment

Genuinely useful for the triage problem, and I would pilot it on a real corpus before committing, specifically to measure the memory ceiling on your hardware. For your profile the key design decision is to fix the embedding model locally (e.g. multilingual-e5 via sentence-transformers) so no document text leaves the perimeter, and to record the random seed and model version in the methodology note so the clustering is reproducible if challenged.

### 8. Maintenance

**Actively maintained** — GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-14, latest release v0.17.4 (2025-12-03) with a v1.0.0b1 tag since, 7,963 stars, 480 open issues. Active commits and a 1.0 beta in flight; the large open-issue backlog indicates responsiveness limits rather than abandonment.

### 9. Licensing

**Licence:** MIT _(SPDX verified)_

**Model / data licence:** Depends entirely on the embedding model you choose; not fixed by BERTopic and not verified here.

**Restrictions:** None from BERTopic itself. The licence risk is imported with the embedding model — a CC-BY-NC checkpoint would contaminate commercial use.

**Licence evidence:** https://github.com/MaartenGr/BERTopic/blob/master/LICENSE

### 10. Costs

No fee. Embedding is the cost driver: a GPU shortens a 200k-document embedding run from many hours to tens of minutes. Expect a GPU VM for hours, or a long CPU run, per corpus. Estimate only; assumptions are a mid-size sentence-transformer and a single pass.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

Local if and only if the embedding backend is local. Selecting an API-based embedding provider sends every document to a third party — a catastrophic default for leak material, and the one configuration choice that must be reviewed.

### 12. Verdict

**Pilot**

### 13. Alternatives

- [txtai](docs/projects/JAI-A2-55.md) for a lighter all-in-one semantic search plus clustering
- [Carrot2](docs/projects/JAI-A2-07.md) for labelling result sets rather than whole corpora
- [datasketch](docs/projects/JAI-A2-10.md) first, to collapse near-duplicates before topic modelling

Regularly regenerated dataset describing the most common third-party domains on the web: who owns them, what they do, their prevalence, fingerprinting behaviour and cookie usage.

### Journalism / investigative use case

The reference layer that turns a tracker domain into a named company: Blacklight tells you a site contacted a particular third-party domain, and Tracker Radar tells you which corporate entity owns it and what it does — which is the step that makes a story nameable rather than technical.

### 2. Audience

newsroom analyst, engineer, specialist investigator

dataset · bucket `source-available-restricted`

### 7. Assessment

Use it as reference while reporting, and do not build it into a product or publish a derived dataset if your outlet is commercially operated — the NonCommercial and ShareAlike terms both bite, and 'we are journalism' does not satisfy NonCommercial. Practically: look up the ownership, verify it against corporate registries, and cite the registry in print. That keeps the finding defensible and sidesteps the licence entirely.

ShareAlike: derivative datasets must carry CC-BY-NC-SA-4.0, which can contaminate a combined dataset you intend to publish. DuckDuckGo logos and marks are excluded from the licence.

### 1. Purpose

Data framework for retrieval-augmented generation: loaders for many sources, index structures, retrievers, rerankers, query engines and agent abstractions over document collections.

### Journalism / investigative use case

Building a question-answering interface over a document archive: a reporter asks 'what did the ministry say about the contract in 2019' and the system retrieves relevant passages and drafts an answer with citations back to specific documents. The citation requirement is what makes it usable in journalism at all.

### 2. Audience

engineer

### 3. Project type

framework · bucket `verified-oss`

### 4. Pros

- Easy to build something impressive and unreliable: the framework makes a demo trivial and a trustworthy system hard, and the gap is mostly evaluation work it does not do for you

### 7. Assessment

Use it, with an evaluation discipline attached: build a set of questions with known correct answers from your own corpus and measure retrieval and answer quality before anyone relies on the system. For your profile the architecture to insist on is fully local (local embeddings, local vector store, local model via vLLM) and citation-mandatory — an answer without a document reference should be suppressed rather than shown. Pin the version; this framework breaks across upgrades more than most.

### 8. Maintenance

**Actively maintained** — GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-14, latest release v0.14.26 (2026-11-13), 52,926 stars, MIT licence. Very frequent releases under commercial maintenance; the churn that follows is the practical cost.

**Scores** — relevance 3/5 · capability 4/5 · maintenance 5/5 · privacy 5/5 · usability 4/5 · licence+cost 5/5 → **weighted 82/100** (pillar rank 56, segment rank 9)

### 1. Purpose

Vector similarity search engine and database written in Rust, with payload filtering, quantisation, snapshots, distributed deployment and a REST and gRPC API.

### Journalism / investigative use case

The storage layer for semantic search over a document archive: millions of passage embeddings with metadata filters, so a reporter can search semantically within a date range or a specific document set rather than across everything.

### 2. Audience

engineer

### 3. Project type

platform · bucket `verified-oss`

### 4. Pros

- Payload filtering combined with vector search is the feature that matters for investigative use: 'semantically similar passages, but only in documents from this ministry in 2019' is a normal journalistic query and a hard technical one
- Rust implementation with quantisation support keeps memory requirements manageable at millions of vectors, which decides whether a corpus fits on your hardware
- Apache-2.0 with very active maintenance (v1.20.2, 2026-11-16; pushed 2026-11-17) and strong adoption (35,603 stars)
- Snapshots make the index backup-able and portable, which matters when the index represents substantial embedding compute

### 5. Cons

- Another stateful service to operate alongside whatever search engine you already run — and for many newsroom corpora, a vector extension in OpenSearch or pgvector avoids that
- Commercial company with a managed cloud offering, the usual open-core direction consideration
- Embedding storage is only as good as the embedding model, and switching models means re-embedding the entire corpus — a cost that is easy to underestimate when choosing a model
- At small corpus sizes (tens of thousands of documents) a dedicated vector database is unnecessary overhead compared with FAISS or an in-memory index

### 6. Feedback (documented)

No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 35,603 stars with release v1.20.2 (2026-11-16) and a push on 2026-11-17, Apache-2.0. Strong adoption in the RAG ecosystem is evident from the metrics.

### 7. Assessment

Adopt it when your corpus genuinely needs a vector database — millions of passages with filtered search — and use pgvector or FAISS below that threshold. For your profile the decision that costs most is the embedding model, not the database: choose it once with care (multilingual-e5-large is a reasonable default with a clear licence), because re-embedding a leak-scale corpus is days of GPU time. Keep the index on infrastructure you control.

### 8. Maintenance

**Actively maintained** — GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release v1.20.2 (2026-11-16), 35,603 stars, Apache-2.0. Same-day commits and frequent releases under well-funded commercial maintenance.

### 9. Licensing

**Licence:** Apache-2.0 _(SPDX verified)_

**Model / data licence:** n/a. Embeddings are derived from your documents using a model whose licence applies to that use.

**Restrictions:** None material for the database. The managed cloud service is a separate commercial product.

**Licence evidence:** https://github.com/qdrant/qdrant/blob/master/LICENSE

### 10. Costs

No fee for self-hosting. Infrastructure: RAM-proportional to vector count (quantisation reduces this substantially) plus disk — one VM for several million vectors. Managed cloud priced separately (not verified). Estimate.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

Self-hosted, local, no external calls. The index itself is disclosive about your corpus, so it needs the same protection as the documents.

**Integrate**

- pgvector if you already run PostgreSQL — usually the right answer below millions of vectors

## 136. c2pa-rs / c2patool — 81/100

`OSINT-C2-13` · C2 · Image/video verification, geolocation, satellite, aviation and maritime · Content provenance · **library** · bucket `verified-oss` · maintainer Content Authenticity Initiative (contentauth)
[Project page](docs/projects/OSINT-C2-13.md) · [repository](https://github.com/contentauth/c2pa-rs) · [docs](https://opensource.contentauthenticity.org/)

**Scores** — relevance 4/5 · capability 4/5 · maintenance 5/5 · privacy 4/5 · usability 3/5 · licence+cost 4/5 → **weighted 81/100** (pillar rank 43, segment rank 19)

### 1. Purpose

Rust implementation of the C2PA content-provenance specification, with a CLI (c2patool) for inspecting, validating and signing Content Credentials manifests embedded in media files.

### Journalism / investigative use case

Validate Content Credentials on images from C2PA-enabled cameras and tools to confirm a signed capture-and-edit chain, and sign the newsroom's own published assets so downstream users can verify they came from you unaltered — the only approach here that works by establishing provenance rather than guessing at manipulation.

### 2. Audience

engineer, newsroom analyst

### 3. Project type

library · bucket `verified-oss`

### 4. Pros

- Provenance-based verification is structurally more reliable than detection: a valid signature chain is checkable evidence, whereas a detector score is a guess — and the detection field's in-the-wild failure rates make this the better bet
- Signing your own published assets is a genuine newsroom capability: it lets partners and readers confirm an image came from you unmodified, which matters when your work is misappropriated
- Very actively maintained (c2pa-c-ffi-v0.92.2 released 2026-11-16, pushed 2026-11-17) with dual Apache-2.0 OR MIT licensing
- Industry-backed specification with camera and tool vendors implementing it, so coverage will grow rather than shrink

### 5. Cons

- Only informative for files that carry credentials, and absence of a manifest is extremely common and means nothing — most media you encounter will have no credentials at all, which limits present-day utility
- A valid signature proves who signed and the declared edit history, not that the depicted events occurred — a distinction that will be misunderstood as C2PA becomes more visible
- Signing requires certificates and a trust list, so there is real PKI work and key management before you can sign your own assets
- 310 open issues against 449 stars and a confusing release scheme (per-crate tags), so integration takes orientation; GitHub reports SPDX NOASSERTION for the dual licence

### 6. Feedback (documented)

No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 449 stars with 310 open issues, release c2pa-c-ffi-v0.92.2 (2026-11-16), pushed 2026-11-17, dual Apache-2.0 OR MIT with SPDX NOASSERTION. The specification's industry backing is evidenced by the Content Authenticity Initiative's membership, though actual camera-side coverage in the wild was not measured in this survey.

### 7. Assessment

Worth integrating now on the signing side and monitoring on the validation side. Concretely for your profile: start signing published images, because that capability compounds in value and costs only PKI setup; treat validation as a bonus that occasionally helps rather than a workflow you can rely on, since most material carries no manifest. The strategic point is that provenance is the only verification approach whose reliability improves over time, while detection's degrades as generators improve.

### 8. Maintenance

**Actively maintained** — GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release c2pa-c-ffi-v0.92.2 (2026-11-16), 449 stars, 310 open issues. Same-day commits and near-daily releases across crates; industry-funded maintenance. The large backlog reflects an evolving specification rather than neglect.

### 9. Licensing

**Licence:** Apache-2.0 OR MIT (dual; GitHub reports NOASSERTION) _(SPDX not verified — resolved from the licence file or project documentation)_

**Model / data licence:** n/a. Trust lists and certificates are governed by the issuing authorities' terms.

**Restrictions:** Dual permissive licensing — choose either and record the choice. The practical constraints are PKI-related: obtaining a certificate recognised by the relevant trust list is a governance question, not a licence one.

**Licence evidence:** https://github.com/contentauth/c2pa-rs/blob/main/LICENSE-MIT

### 10. Costs

No software fee. Signing requires a certificate: costs depend on the issuing authority and were NOT verified in this survey. Rust toolchain for building; negligible runtime cost. No GPU.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

Local validation of embedded manifests, with an optional network fetch for trust-list checks — so validation can be done offline if you pre-stage the trust list. Note that signing embeds assertions about your newsroom's tools and workflow into published files, so review what the manifest discloses before signing.

### 12. Verdict

**Pilot**

### 13. Alternatives

- Signing with standard detached signatures plus published hashes, if C2PA's complexity is unjustified
- [Community Forensics](docs/projects/JAI-A4-21.md) or CAT-Net for detection-based approaches, with their much weaker reliability
- [ExifTool](docs/projects/OSINT-C2-01.md) plus MediaInfo for the pre-C2PA provenance signals that remain useful

### 14. Evidence

Verified **2026-11-17** · confidence **medium** · assessment depth `metadata-verified`

- https://github.com/contentauth/c2pa-rs
- https://opensource.contentauthenticity.org/

`OSINT-C2-47` · C2 · Image/video verification, geolocation, satellite, aviation and maritime · Aviation tracking (ADS-B receiver) · **cli** · bucket `verified-oss` · maintainer FlightAware
[Project page](docs/projects/OSINT-C2-47.md) · [repository](https://github.com/flightaware/dump1090) · [docs](https://github.com/flightaware/dump1090#readme)

**Scores** — relevance 4/5 · capability 4/5 · maintenance 4/5 · privacy 5/5 · usability 3/5 · licence+cost 4/5 → **weighted 81/100** (pillar rank 44, segment rank 20)

### 1. Purpose

Mode S and ADS-B decoder for RTL-SDR software-defined radio receivers, decoding aircraft transponder broadcasts into position, altitude, speed and identity data with a local web map.

### Journalism / investigative use case

Independent aircraft tracking from your own receiver: record every aircraft overhead with timestamps, including flights that commercial tracking sites filter, block or do not cover. For reporting on surveillance aircraft, rendition flights or military movements, your own receiver is evidence nobody can retract.

### 2. Audience

engineer, specialist investigator

### 3. Project type

cli · bucket `verified-oss`

### 4. Pros

- Your own receiver produces your own data, which cannot be blocked, filtered or withdrawn — the decisive advantage over commercial tracking sites that honour blocking requests from aircraft owners
- Hardware cost is trivial (an RTL-SDR dongle and an antenna), making this one of the cheapest independent evidence-collection capabilities available to a newsroom
- GPL-2.0-or-later (licence resolved in this session; GitHub reports NOASSERTION) with active maintenance (pushed 2026-11-03, tag v11.1) and a maintainer who explicitly invites contact for GPL-incompatible uses
- The FlightAware fork is the practically maintained line in a family of forks, so it is the right starting point

### 5. Cons

- Coverage is line-of-sight from your antenna — typically 100-400km in good conditions — so a single receiver sees only its own region, and building wider coverage means recruiting receivers
- Aircraft can disable or spoof ADS-B transmission, and military aircraft frequently do, so absence of a track means nothing and presence can be falsified
- Requires hardware, an antenna with a reasonable sky view, and some radio literacy — a real setup effort rather than a software install
- GitHub reports NOASSERTION so automated licence scanning does not resolve it, and the fork landscape (antirez, MalcolmRobb, FlightAware) confuses newcomers about which to use

### 6. Feedback (documented)

No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 1,153 stars with 86 open issues, latest tag v11.1, pushed 2026-11-03, licence resolved by reading the blob to GPL-2.0-or-later with the maintainer inviting contact for GPL-incompatible use. The fork lineage (antirez original, MalcolmRobb last pushed 2024-08-14, FlightAware current) was verified via the API.

### 7. Assessment

Adopt if aviation is a live beat — the cost is negligible and the independence is the point. For your profile the strongest pattern is a small network: two or three receivers at reporters' homes or offices covering an airport or a flight corridor, feeding a shared store, which gives you coverage a single site cannot. Pair with bellingcat/adsb-history for querying accumulated data, and never treat absence of a track as evidence an aircraft did not fly.

### 8. Maintenance

**Actively maintained** — GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-03, no release objects, latest tag v11.1, SPDX NOASSERTION (GPL-2.0-or-later per the licence blob), 1,153 stars, 86 open issues. Corporate-maintained fork with current commits; by comparison antirez/dump1090 last pushed 2026-02-15 and MalcolmRobb/dump1090 2024-08-14.

### 9. Licensing

**Licence:** GPL-2.0-or-later (licence blob read 2026-11-17 — 'licensed under the GPL, v2 or later', with the maintainer inviting contact for GPL-incompatible uses; GitHub reports NOASSERTION) _(SPDX not verified — resolved from the licence file or project documentation)_

**Model / data licence:** n/a. The ADS-B data you receive is broadcast in the clear; your recordings are your own.

**Restrictions:** GPL-2.0-or-later on the software. Note that receiving and recording broadcast ADS-B is lawful in most jurisdictions but not all — check local radio law before deploying, as this is a legal rather than licence question.

No software fee. Hardware: an RTL-SDR dongle and antenna (tens of dollars/euros each, prices not verified here) plus a small always-on computer such as a Raspberry Pi. Storage grows with traffic volume — modest. Among the best capability-per-cost ratios in this catalogue.

Entirely local reception and decoding: nothing is transmitted unless you choose to feed an aggregator. Feeding FlightAware or similar networks shares your data and your receiver's location with them — a deliberate choice, and one to decline if your receiver's location should stay private.

**Adopt**

## 139. GLiNER — 81/100

`JAI-A2-19` · A2 · Documents and language: OCR, transcription, translation, entities, entity resolution · Zero-shot entity extraction · **model** · bucket `verified-oss` · maintainer Urchade Zaratiana and contributors
[Project page](docs/projects/JAI-A2-19.md) · [repository](https://github.com/urchade/GLiNER) · [docs](https://github.com/urchade/GLiNER#readme)

**Scores** — relevance 4/5 · capability 4/5 · maintenance 4/5 · privacy 5/5 · usability 3/5 · licence+cost 4/5 → **weighted 81/100** (pillar rank 57, segment rank 32)

### 1. Purpose

Compact bidirectional-transformer NER model that extracts arbitrary user-specified entity types at inference time without retraining, running on CPU or a small GPU.

### Journalism / investigative use case

Define bespoke labels for one investigation — 'shell company', 'vessel', 'bank account', 'politically exposed person' — and sweep a leak for them without annotating training data and without sending documents to an API. That flexibility is what spaCy's fixed label set cannot give you.

### 2. Audience

engineer

### 3. Project type

model · bucket `verified-oss`

### 4. Pros

- Zero-shot custom labels change the economics of entity extraction for investigations, where the interesting entity type is always project-specific
- Small enough to run on CPU, so it is deployable on an isolated evidence machine rather than requiring GPU infrastructure
- Apache-2.0 code with Apache-2.0 v2.1 checkpoints available — a genuinely open path exists
- Active development (v0.2.30, 2026-11-02) with a multilingual checkpoint line

### 5. Cons

- Licence trap, verified and material: the older but still widely cited v0/v1 checkpoints (gliner_base, gliner_multi, gliner_small/medium/large-v1) are CC-BY-NC-4.0 and unusable by a commercial newsroom; only the v2.1 line (gliner_small-v2.1, gliner_multi-v2.1) is Apache-2.0
- Recall is prompt-sensitive: label wording materially changes what you find, which makes systematic coverage hard to evidence in a methodology note
- Long documents must be chunked, and entities spanning chunk boundaries are missed
- Extracts but does not link or deduplicate — 'Rosneft Trading' and 'OOO Rosneft-Trading' remain separate strings until you add rigour/nomenklatura

### 6. Feedback (documented)

No individual user reports verified. The documented, checkable finding is the split model licensing recorded in session 1 and retained here: HuggingFace cards for the v0/v1 checkpoints state cc-by-nc-4.0 while the v2.1 cards state apache-2.0. 4,270 stars, 54 open issues.

### 7. Assessment

High-value and I would use it, but with a hard rule: pin a v2.1 Apache-2.0 checkpoint and record the exact model ID in the pipeline, because the NC checkpoints are the ones most tutorials link to. Treat its output as a candidate list for human review rather than a finding — prompt sensitivity means absence of a hit is not evidence of absence. Pair with rigour for normalisation before any matching.

### 8. Maintenance

**Actively maintained** — GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-11, latest release v0.2.30 (2026-11-02), 4,270 stars, 54 open issues. Frequent releases on a 0.2.x line with current commits; research-origin project that has sustained a release cadence.

### 9. Licensing

**Licence:** Apache-2.0 (code) _(SPDX verified)_

**Model / data licence:** SPLIT AND MATERIAL: v2.1 checkpoints (urchade/gliner_small-v2.1, urchade/gliner_multi-v2.1) are Apache-2.0; older v0/v1 checkpoints (urchade/gliner_base, gliner_multi, gliner_small/medium/large-v1) are CC-BY-NC-4.0, research only.

**Restrictions:** Using a v0/v1 checkpoint in commercially published journalism breaches CC-BY-NC-4.0. The code licence does not cure this. Verify the checkpoint, not the repository.

**Licence evidence:** https://github.com/urchade/GLiNER/blob/main/LICENSE

### 10. Costs

No fee for the Apache-2.0 path. CPU inference is viable; a small GPU speeds bulk sweeps. No paid dependencies. Estimate only.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

Local inference after checkpoint download; no text leaves the machine. Weights can be pre-staged for air-gapped use.

### 12. Verdict

**Adopt**

### Material blockers

_Tracked separately from the score._

- CC-BY-NC-4.0 on the v0/v1 checkpoints — a commercial-use blocker if the wrong model ID is pinned

JVM command-line tool that walks a file tree or archive, extracts text and metadata via Apache Tika with parallel workers and Redis-backed queueing, OCRs images, and writes results to Solr or Elasticsearch.

### Journalism / investigative use case

Purpose-built for this domain: the lineage ICIJ used to process multi-terabyte leaks, designed to chew through millions of mixed files, OCR the scanned ones at scale, and feed a search index — the unglamorous stage where most home-grown leak pipelines fall over.

engineer

### 1. Purpose

Cross-platform protocol library and tools for communicating with iOS devices without jailbreaking — creating backups, reading device information, mounting filesystems and accessing diagnostic services.

The acquisition layer for iOS device checks on Linux: create the encrypted backup that MVT analyses, read device identifiers and diagnostics, and do it from a forensic workstation rather than requiring macOS and iTunes.

### 2. Audience

engineer, specialist investigator

library · bucket `verified-oss`

- Enables iOS forensic acquisition on Linux, which is what makes a dedicated forensic workstation (rather than a journalist's Mac) practical — a meaningful operational-security improvement

No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 8,352 stars with 850 open issues, release 1.4.0 (2025-10-10), pushed 2026-11-17, LGPL-2.1. The large backlog alongside daily commits is characteristic of a reverse-engineering project chasing a moving proprietary target.

### 7. Assessment

Adopt as infrastructure for iOS device checks, and plan around the iOS-version lag: keep a note of which library version successfully acquired from which iOS version, and expect to build from source after a major iOS release. For your profile the broader point is that iOS acquisition capability is a dependency on a volunteer reverse-engineering effort — worth supporting, and worth having a fallback (a macOS machine for backups) when a check cannot wait for the library to catch up.

### 8. Maintenance

**Actively maintained** — GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release 1.4.0 (2025-10-10), 8,352 stars, 850 open issues. Same-day commits with infrequent releases; the backlog is intrinsic to chasing Apple's undocumented protocols rather than evidence of neglect.

**Model / data licence:** n/a

### 10. Costs

No fee. A Linux forensic workstation and storage for backups (tens of GB per device). Build-from-source effort is the hidden cost.

**Scores** — relevance 4/5 · capability 4/5 · maintenance 5/5 · privacy 4/5 · usability 4/5 · licence+cost 3/5 → **weighted 81/100** (pillar rank 45, segment rank 10)

### 1. Purpose

Graph database with the Cypher query language, ACID transactions, indexing and a browser interface, available as a GPL-3-licensed Community Edition and commercial Enterprise editions.

### Journalism / investigative use case

A persistent, queryable investigation graph that several people share: load entities and relationships from leaks, registries and sanctions data, then answer questions in Cypher — 'find paths of length three between this politician and this company' — interactively rather than by rerunning a script.

### 2. Audience

engineer, specialist investigator

### 3. Project type

platform · bucket `verified-oss`

### 4. Pros

- Cypher makes relationship queries expressible and readable, which matters when an analyst rather than an engineer needs to ask the next question — path queries in particular are awkward in SQL and natural here
- Persistent and multi-user, so an investigation graph becomes shared infrastructure rather than one person's notebook state
- Browser interface lets a non-engineer explore and visualise query results directly, lowering the barrier to using the graph
- Community Edition is GPL-3 licensed and free to download (verified on the vendor pricing page), so the capability is genuinely available without a licence purchase

### 5. Cons

- Community Edition is deliberately limited — single database, no clustering, no role-based access control — and the Enterprise features that a multi-user newsroom might want are quote-only with no public price (verified on the vendor pricing page 2026-11-16)
- GPL-3 on the Community Edition constrains embedding it in a distributed product, and the licensing split is a deliberate commercial funnel
- Operating a JVM graph database with adequate memory is real infrastructure, and a badly tuned Neo4j performs poorly in ways that look like a data problem
- AuraDB, the managed option, is priced per GB-hour (from $0.09/GB/hour Professional, from $0.20/GB/hour Business Critical, verified 2026-11-16) and places your investigation graph in a vendor's cloud

### 6. Feedback (documented)

No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented pricing, verified on the vendor page 2026-11-16 and recorded in sources/recovered/cat/pricing.tsv: Community Edition GPL-3 and free to download; Enterprise and Infinigraph editions contact-sales (quote required); AuraDB Free $0, Professional from $0.09/GB/hour (minimum 1GB), Business Critical from $0.20/GB/hour (minimum 2GB), with hourly metering including storage, compute, IO, network and backups.

### 7. Assessment

Adopt the Community Edition for a shared investigation graph where Cypher's expressiveness earns its operational cost — which is mainly when several people need to ask relationship questions over months. For your profile avoid AuraDB for investigation data: per-GB-hour billing on a graph you will keep for years is both expensive and a custody decision. If Community Edition's single-database and access-control limits bind, consider whether DuckDB or a FollowTheMoney-based store would serve, since Enterprise pricing is quote-only.

### 8. Maintenance

**Actively maintained** — Verified via the GitHub API 2026-11-17 as live and non-archived with continuous development under commercial maintenance. Vendor pricing page verified 2026-11-16 confirming Community Edition availability under GPL-3.

### 9. Licensing

**Licence:** GPL-3.0 (Community Edition); Enterprise and Infinigraph editions are commercially licensed _(SPDX not verified — resolved from the licence file or project documentation)_

**Model / data licence:** n/a

**Restrictions:** GPL-3.0 on Community Edition: embedding in a distributed product triggers copyleft, which is the deliberate commercial boundary. Enterprise features (clustering, role-based access control, multi-database) require a paid licence at a price not publicly listed.

**Licence evidence:** https://neo4j.com/pricing/

### 10. Costs

Community Edition: no licence fee, free download (verified 2026-11-16). Enterprise/Infinigraph: quote required, no public price. AuraDB: Free $0; Professional from $0.09/GB/hour (min 1GB); Business Critical from $0.20/GB/hour (min 2GB); Virtual Dedicated Cloud contact sales — hourly metering includes storage, compute, IO, network and backups (all verified 2026-11-16, USD). Self-hosting infrastructure: a JVM host with substantial RAM. Estimate for self-hosting.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

Self-hosted Community Edition keeps the graph entirely on your infrastructure. AuraDB places it with the vendor, which for an investigation graph containing leak-derived entities is a significant custody decision.

### 12. Verdict

**Integrate**

Entity-resolution and deduplication toolkit for FollowTheMoney data: candidate generation, scoring algorithms, an interactive adjudication loop, and a resolver file recording every merge decision.

The deduplication engine behind OpenSanctions: merge the same oligarch or company across sanctions lists, leaks and corporate registries while keeping an auditable record of every merge a human approved — so a later challenge to 'how do you know these are the same person' has a documented answer.

engineer, specialist investigator

### 1. Purpose

Neural speaker-diarisation toolkit providing pretrained pipelines for voice activity detection, speaker segmentation, embedding and clustering, answering 'who spoke when' in an audio recording.

### Journalism / investigative use case

The de facto open diarisation layer for newsroom pipelines: separating speakers in interviews, conference calls and intercepted audio before transcription, so a transcript attributes each statement to a person rather than producing an undifferentiated wall of text.

### 2. Audience

engineer

### 3. Project type

library · bucket `verified-oss`

### 4. Pros

- The reference open diarisation implementation — WhisperX, noScribe and most newsroom transcription stacks depend on it, so it is the de facto standard
- Very actively developed with a 4.x line (4.1.0 released 2026-11-17) and an exceptionally clean tracker (35 open issues against 10,806 stars)

- Accuracy drops materially on overlapping speech, telephone-band audio and recordings with many speakers — exactly the conditions of covertly recorded material
- Increasingly coupled to a commercial offering (pyannote.ai) whose Precision models are better than the open ones, creating a structural incentive toward the paid tier
- Engineer-facing: no UI, and tuning clustering parameters for a specific recording type takes experimentation

No individual user reports verified. Documented and checkable: the HuggingFace model card for pyannote/speaker-diarization-3.1 states the information-sharing requirement and also states the pipeline will remain open source. ### 7. Assessment

Necessary rather than optional if you need speaker attribution, and the gating is a manageable but real nuisance: download the weights once on a non-sensitive machine with an organisational HuggingFace account, then distribute internally so individual journalists never authenticate. For media-in-exile work that one-time disclosure matters and should be a deliberate decision. Where diarisation accuracy on bad audio is critical, benchmark against NeMo Sortformer — but note Sortformer's CC-BY-NC licence blocks commercial publication.

**Actively maintained** — GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release 4.1.0 published the same day, 10,806 stars, 35 open issues. **Licence:** MIT _(SPDX verified)_

**Model / data licence:** MIT but GATED — the speaker-diarization-3.1 card requires agreeing to share your HuggingFace information to access the model. The card also states the pipeline will remain open-source.

**Restrictions:** No field-of-use restriction, but access is conditioned on identity disclosure to HuggingFace and the model authors. That is an access barrier with privacy consequences rather than a licence limitation.

### 1. Purpose

Python web-archiving toolkit providing high-fidelity replay of WARC and WACZ collections, a recording proxy mode, collection management and a Wayback-style interface.

### Journalism / investigative use case

Stand up a private Wayback Machine over your own captures so editors and lawyers can click through dated versions of a government page side by side without relying on a public archive staying online — the piece that turns a WARC collection from a pile of files into usable evidence.

engineer, newsroom analyst

framework · bucket `verified-oss`

Adopt it as the replay layer for any serious capture programme — without replay, WARCs are write-only. For your profile the deployment decision that matters is access control: a pywb instance over an investigation's captures is a high-value target and must not be publicly reachable. Pair with OutbackCDX if the collection grows large enough that URL/timestamp lookup becomes slow.

**Model / data licence:** n/a. Replayed content belongs to the original publishers.

**Restrictions:** GPL-3.0: distributing a modified pywb-based product triggers source-release obligations. Internal deployment is unaffected.

**Licence evidence:** https://github.com/webrecorder/pywb/blob/main/LICENSE

### 10. Costs

No fee. Infrastructure estimate: a small Python service plus storage for your WARC/WACZ collection — storage dominates and scales with capture volume. Operating effort is modest once configured.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

Serves local archive files; what it exposes to the network depends entirely on your deployment. A misconfigured public instance would publish your entire capture collection, including anything sensitive you captured — bind it internally and authenticate.

### 1. Purpose

Browser extension that learns to block third-party trackers by observing cross-site tracking behaviour rather than relying solely on blocklists, and removes outgoing link tracking and some fingerprinting vectors.

### Journalism / investigative use case

Reducing the trail a journalist leaves while researching: visiting a target's website, a procurement portal or an extremist forum would otherwise notify a dozen analytics and ad-tech companies, building a profile that associates your newsroom with the subjects you are investigating.

### 2. Audience

journalist, newsroom analyst

### 3. Project type

application · bucket `verified-oss`

### 4. Pros

- Behavioural learning catches trackers that blocklists miss, which matters on the obscure regional and niche sites investigations actually visit — exactly where curated lists have gaps
- Addresses a genuine and under-appreciated operational-security problem: research browsing builds a commercially held profile linking your organisation to your subjects
- Maintained by EFF with a current release (release-2026.9.15, 2026-09-15; pushed 2026-11-12) and a clear institutional mission

- Breaks some sites, and a journalist on deadline will disable it rather than diagnose it — so deployment needs a quick 'disable for this site' habit taught alongside it

- GitHub reports SPDX NOASSERTION (EFF's licensing is GPL-family) so the licence needs reading for records
- Behavioural learning means protection improves over time per profile, so a fresh browser profile starts weaker — relevant if reporters use disposable profiles for research

### 6. Feedback (documented)

No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 3,889 stars with 102 open issues, release release-2026.9.15 (2026-09-15), pushed 2026-11-12, SPDX NOASSERTION. EFF's maintenance and the behavioural-learning approach are documented by the project.

### 7. Assessment

Adopt it newsroom-wide — it is free, requires nothing of users, and reduces a real exposure. For your profile the important framing is that it addresses third-party tracking, not visibility to the site itself: a reporter researching a surveillance vendor should use a separate browser profile and a non-newsroom egress as well, because the vendor's own server logs are the more consequential record. Teach the per-site disable so people do not switch it off globally.

### 8. Maintenance

**Actively maintained** — GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-12, latest release release-2026.9.15 (2026-09-15), 3,889 stars, 102 open issues, SPDX NOASSERTION. Regular dated releases under EFF's institutional maintenance.

**Model / data licence:** n/a

**Restrictions:** Unverified exactly in this survey; immaterial for use as a browser extension.

**Licence evidence:** https://github.com/EFForg/privacybadger

### 10. Costs

Free. No infrastructure.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

Blocks third-party tracking locally in the browser with no data sent to EFF. It does not conceal you from the visited site, which is the limitation to communicate clearly.

### 1. Purpose

Python library for downloading panoramas and metadata from several street-level imagery services, including Google Street View, Apple Look Around, Yandex Panorama and Mapillary, via their internal or public interfaces.

### Journalism / investigative use case

The practical workhorse of photograph geolocation: pull panoramas for a candidate location and compare building façades, signage and street furniture against the image you are trying to place — and pull the capture dates, which tell you whether a feature visible in your photo existed when the panorama was taken.

### 2. Audience

specialist investigator, engineer

### 3. Project type

library · bucket `verified-oss`

### 4. Pros

- Multi-provider coverage including Apple Look Around and Yandex Panorama is the key advantage: Yandex coverage of Russia, Central Asia and parts of the Middle East is far better than Google's, which matters enormously for reporting on those regions
- Programmatic panorama download enables systematic comparison across many candidate locations, which manual Street View browsing cannot
- Capture-date metadata is exposed, which is essential for temporal reasoning about what a photograph shows

### 7. Assessment

Genuinely valuable for geolocation in regions where Google coverage is absent, and the Yandex access in particular has no real substitute. For your profile three cautions apply together: route requests through an egress not identifiable as your newsroom, be aware that querying Yandex discloses your interest to a Russian service, and treat panorama images as third-party copyrighted material requiring a rights decision before publication. Expect breakage and keep manual browsing as a fallback.

### 8. Maintenance

**Actively maintained** — GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-12, latest release v0.13.0 published the same day, 249 stars, 5 open issues. **Licence:** MIT _(SPDX verified)_

**Model / data licence:** n/a for the library. Downloaded panoramas remain the imagery providers' copyrighted content.

**Restrictions:** Code permissive. The substantive constraints are external: providers' terms of service may prohibit programmatic access, and panorama imagery is copyrighted, so republication in a story needs a rights assessment or fair-dealing judgement.

**Licence evidence:** https://github.com/sk-zk/streetlevel/blob/main/LICENSE

### 10. Costs

No fee and no API keys for the internal interfaces — which is precisely why terms-of-service risk substitutes for monetary cost. Negligible compute; storage for panoramas.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

Desktop application for interactive network visualisation and exploration, with force-directed layouts, filtering, community detection, statistics and publication-quality export.

Exploring and presenting a network: load a co-sharing graph or a corporate-ownership network, apply a layout, colour by community, filter to the dense core, and export a figure for publication — the step that turns an edge list into something a reader can understand.

Adopt it for exploration and figure production, with an explicit rule about what the figure claims. ### 1. Purpose

Hardened fork of Signal for Android that adds database encryption at rest with a separate passphrase, automatic locking, memory wiping, and a build free of proprietary Google dependencies.

### Journalism / investigative use case

Signal for a journalist whose device may be seized: Molly encrypts the local message database behind a passphrase and locks automatically, so a seized or borrowed phone does not immediately surrender the message history that standard Signal keeps accessible once the device is unlocked.

### 2. Audience

journalist, specialist investigator

### 3. Project type

application · bucket `verified-oss`

### 4. Pros

- Addresses the specific gap that matters most in device seizure: standard Signal's local database is protected only by device encryption, so an unlocked phone exposes the history, while Molly requires a separate passphrase
- A Google-free build (Molly-FOSS) matters for de-Googled and GrapheneOS devices, which is the configuration many high-risk journalists use
- AGPL-3.0, actively maintained (pushed 2026-11-16) with a substantial community (3,838 stars) and builds tracking upstream Signal releases
- Keeps Signal protocol compatibility, so contacts need not change anything

### 5. Cons

- A third-party fork of a security-critical application: you are trusting the Molly maintainers' build and patches in addition to Signal's, which is a genuine supply-chain consideration for the most sensitive use
- Running a modified client against Signal's servers is contrary to the service's terms, so there is a (small, historically untested) risk of access disruption
- Release cadence trails upstream Signal (v8.19.2-4 from 2026-07-31 against Signal's November release), meaning a period without upstream security fixes after each Signal update
- Android only; iOS users have no equivalent, so a mixed-device team cannot standardise on it

### 6. Feedback (documented)

No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 3,838 stars, release v8.19.2-4 (2026-07-31), pushed 2026-11-16, AGPL-3.0. The release-version gap against upstream Signal (8.19 versus 8.35) is visible in the API data and is the key operational caveat.

### 7. Assessment

Recommend it selectively — for journalists at genuine risk of device seizure, on Android, who will manage a second passphrase. The at-rest protection is a real improvement over standard Signal for that threat. But the trailing release cadence is a serious counter-consideration: a fork that is sixteen minor versions behind upstream may lack recent security fixes, so check the current gap before deploying and re-check periodically. For most users, standard Signal plus disappearing messages plus strong device encryption is the better trade.

### 8. Maintenance

**Actively maintained** — GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-16, latest release v8.19.2-4 (2026-07-31), 3,838 stars, AGPL-3.0. Commits are current but the published release trails upstream Signal (v8.35.2) by a substantial margin — activity is clear, release timeliness is the concern.

**Licence:** AGPL-3.0 _(SPDX verified)_

**Model / data licence:** n/a

**Restrictions:** AGPL-3.0. Separately, Signal's terms of service address use of modified clients against its servers — a service-terms rather than licence question.

**Licence evidence:** https://github.com/mollyim/mollyim-android/blob/main/LICENSE

### 10. Costs

Free. No infrastructure. Cost is the user managing an additional passphrase and the administrator tracking the upstream version gap.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

Improves on Signal specifically at rest (encrypted local database, auto-lock, memory wiping). In transit it is Signal, with the same phone-number disclosure. The Google-free build removes a dependency on proprietary services.

### 12. Verdict

**Pilot**

_Tracked separately from the score._

## 152. Presidio — 80/100

`JAI-A2-40` · A2 · Documents and language: OCR, transcription, translation, entities, entity resolution · PII detection and redaction · **framework** · bucket `verified-oss` · maintainer data-privacy-stack (transferred from microsoft/presidio)
[Project page](docs/projects/JAI-A2-40.md) · [repository](https://github.com/data-privacy-stack/presidio) · [docs](https://microsoft.github.io/presidio/)

**Scores** — relevance 4/5 · capability 4/5 · maintenance 4/5 · privacy 4/5 · usability 3/5 · licence+cost 5/5 → **weighted 80/100** (pillar rank 62, segment rank 36)

### 1. Purpose

Framework for detecting and anonymising personally identifiable information in text and images, combining NER models, regex recognisers, checksum validators and context words, with pluggable anonymisation operators.

### Journalism / investigative use case

Works in both directions, which is why it matters here: find names, national IDs, IBANs and phone numbers inside a leak to map what sensitive data it contains, and redact them before publishing documents or sharing a corpus with a partner outlet — the step that prevents a collaboration from becoming a data breach.

### 2. Audience

engineer, newsroom analyst

### 3. Project type

framework · bucket `verified-oss`

### 4. Pros

- Bidirectional utility (discovery and redaction) fits the real newsroom need: you must understand a leak's PII before you can decide what to publish
- Pluggable recognisers mean you can add country-specific identifier formats (tax numbers, passport patterns) that matter for a specific investigation
- Image redaction support covers scanned documents, not just text — a common gap in PII tooling
- Active and frequently released (2.2.366, 2026-10-27) with a large user base (11,917 stars)

### 5. Cons

- Recall on unusual name forms and non-English entities depends entirely on the chosen NER backend; out of the box it will miss transliterated names that an investigation hinges on
- Governance recently changed hands — microsoft/presidio now redirects to data-privacy-stack/presidio (verified this session) — so pin versions and watch the new stewardship before depending on it long-term
- Redaction is best-effort and must never be treated as a guarantee; published redactions need human review, and the tool's confidence scores can create false assurance
- 290 open issues; integration problems are common because the quality ceiling is set by components you supply

### 6. Feedback (documented)

No individual user reports verified. Documented and checkable: the repository transfer from Microsoft to data-privacy-stack, confirmed by API redirect on 2026-11-17 — a governance change that was not announced in the catalogue's prior data and is material for dependency planning. 11,917 stars, 290 open issues, release 2026-10-27.

### 7. Assessment

Use it as an assistive scanner, never as a redaction authority. For your profile the right pattern is: Presidio to produce a candidate list of PII locations, a human to adjudicate each one, and PyMuPDF to apply true redactions that remove underlying text. The governance transfer is worth monitoring for a release or two — the code is MIT and the community is large, so the risk is drift rather than disappearance.

### 8. Maintenance

**Actively maintained** — GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-14, latest release 2.2.366 (2026-10-27), 11,917 stars, 290 open issues. Note the transfer: microsoft/presidio redirects to data-privacy-stack/presidio. Activity is current; the stewardship change is the item to watch rather than a decline signal.

### 9. Licensing

**Licence:** MIT _(SPDX verified)_

**Model / data licence:** n/a for the framework; the NER backends you plug in carry their own model licences (spaCy, Stanza, transformers checkpoints).

**Restrictions:** Code unrestricted. Imported licence risk from the chosen NER model — a CC-BY-NC checkpoint would contaminate commercial use.

**Licence evidence:** https://github.com/data-privacy-stack/presidio/blob/main/LICENSE

### 10. Costs

No fee. CPU-viable; GPU helps for transformer backends at volume. Optional Tesseract for image redaction. No paid dependencies unless you configure a hosted LLM recogniser. Estimate.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

Local by default and appropriate for sensitive corpora. One configuration risk: optional LLM-based recognisers would send text to a third party if enabled — review before use. Note the inherent irony that a PII tool mishandled becomes a PII exposure.

### 12. Verdict

**Integrate**

### 13. Alternatives

[Project page](docs/projects/OSINT-C2-12.md) · [repository](https://github.com/GuidoBartoli/sherloq) · [docs](https://github.com/GuidoBartoli/sherloq#readme)

**Scores** — relevance 4/5 · capability 4/5 · maintenance 3/5 · privacy 5/5 · usability 4/5 · licence+cost 4/5 → **weighted 80/100** (pillar rank 50, segment rank 22)

### 1. Purpose

Desktop GUI aggregating a wide set of image-forensics techniques — metadata inspection, error-level analysis, noise and JPEG-ghost maps, clone/copy-move detection, PCA and frequency analysis — in one local workbench.

### Journalism / investigative use case

A single local workbench to triage a suspicious photo: pull metadata, look for ELA, noise and JPEG-ghost anomalies, test for copy-move or splicing, and build a documented list of anomalies to take to further reporting — all without uploading the image anywhere.

### 2. Audience

newsroom analyst, specialist investigator

### 3. Project type

application · bucket `verified-oss`

### 4. Pros

- Breadth of techniques in one local GUI is the practical advantage: an analyst can run eight different tests in ten minutes rather than installing eight research repos
- Fully local with no third-party service or API key documented, which matters enormously for unpublished or source-supplied imagery — the direct contrast with the InVID plugin's uploads
- Largest community of any dedicated image-forensics GUI here (3,264 stars) with a modest backlog (25 open issues)
- GPL-3.0 and inspectable, so the methods are auditable rather than black-box

### 5. Cons

- The author frames it as an educational and research toolkit rather than a definitive forgery detector — every panel output is a probabilistic signal requiring expert interpretation, NOT conclusive proof
- ELA in particular is notoriously over-interpreted: it is the classic example of a forensic visualisation that looks compelling and proves little, and an analyst without training will produce false findings
- Last push 2026-07-16 with no releases at all, so there is no version to pin and the project runs on a maintainer's spare attention
- PySide2 and OpenCV dependencies of a certain vintage make installation fiddly on current systems

### 6. Feedback (documented)

No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 3,264 stars with 25 open issues, no releases, last push 2026-07-16; the author's own framing as an educational/research toolkit is stated in the repository. The over-interpretation risk of ELA is a well-established point in image-forensics literature, not a criticism specific to Sherloq.

### 7. Assessment

Adopt it as the local alternative to uploading images to a forensics service, with a firm internal rule: outputs are leads for an analyst, never findings for a story, and no ELA image is ever published as evidence. For your profile its real value is privacy plus breadth — it lets you examine source-supplied imagery without disclosure. Pair with CAT-Net for a commercially usable model-based second opinion, and be realistic that interpreting these panels well requires training you may need to arrange.

### 8. Maintenance

**Stable with low activity** — GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-07-16, no releases or tags, 3,264 stars, 25 open issues. Four months since last push on a single-maintainer GUI; low backlog suggests attention, absence of releases suggests informal maintenance. Not declining, but the bus factor is one.

### 9. Licensing

**Licence:** GPL-3.0 _(SPDX verified)_

**Model / data licence:** n/a — classical signal-processing techniques, no trained models.

**Restrictions:** GPL-3.0; immaterial for desktop use by analysts.

**Licence evidence:** https://github.com/GuidoBartoli/sherloq/blob/master/LICENSE

### 10. Costs

No fee. Runs on an analyst workstation; ExifTool binary and OpenCV required. Real cost is analyst training to interpret the outputs responsibly.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

No third-party service or API key documented for the core tools; analysis runs locally, which is the decisive advantage for unpublished or source-sensitive imagery.

**Adopt**

### 1. Purpose

Python astronomy library computing high-precision positions of the Sun, Moon, planets, stars and Earth-orbiting satellites for any time and observer location, using JPL ephemerides and TLE data.

### Journalism / investigative use case

Programmatic verification at scale: check Moon phase and altitude for a hundred claimed timestamps in one pass, or compute whether a specific reconnaissance satellite was overhead at the moment an incident was recorded — a question that recurs in conflict reporting and that cannot be answered by eye.

### 2. Audience

engineer, specialist investigator

library · bucket `verified-oss`

- Satellite-pass computation from TLE data is a distinctive investigative capability: establishing which imaging satellites could have seen an event tells you what imagery might exist and who holds it

### 7. Assessment

Adopt where astronomical checks need to be systematic rather than one-off — and specifically for the satellite-pass question, which is genuinely useful for knowing what imagery to request or FOIA. For your profile the practical caution is TLE freshness: fetch elements close in time to the event you are analysing, and record which element set you used, because a published claim about satellite coverage computed from stale TLEs is indefensible.

**Stable with low activity** — GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-09-29, no release objects, latest tag 1.55, 1,809 stars, 114 open issues. Six weeks since last push on a mature single-maintainer library with steady long-term development; stable rather than declining.

### 10. Costs

No fee. Ephemeris files are a one-off download of tens to hundreds of MB. Negligible compute.

Use it on Linux and, more importantly, make signature verification a trained habit for everyone regardless of platform — that is the transferable lesson. ## 158. FAISS — 80/100

`JAI-A3-08` · A3 · RAG, research agents, knowledge graphs, provenance and AI evaluation · Vector search library · **library** · bucket `verified-oss` · maintainer Meta AI Research
[Project page](docs/projects/JAI-A3-08.md) · [repository](https://github.com/facebookresearch/faiss) · [docs](https://faiss.ai/)

**Scores** — relevance 3/5 · capability 4/5 · maintenance 5/5 · privacy 5/5 · usability 3/5 · licence+cost 5/5 → **weighted 80/100** (pillar rank 63, segment rank 10)

### 1. Purpose

Library for efficient similarity search and clustering of dense vectors, with many index types trading memory against accuracy and speed, and GPU acceleration.

### Journalism / investigative use case

In-process vector search with no service to run: embed a corpus, build a FAISS index, and query it from the same Python process — the right level of infrastructure for a single investigation's document set, and what sentence-transformers examples assume.

### 2. Audience

engineer

### 3. Project type

library · bucket `verified-oss`

### 4. Pros

- No service to operate: an index is a file and a process, which suits per-investigation corpora and air-gapped machines where running a database is impractical
- Wide range of index types lets you trade memory for accuracy explicitly, which matters when a corpus must fit on available hardware
- MIT licensed with very active maintenance (v1.16.0, 2026-11-10; pushed 2026-11-17) and long institutional backing (41,767 stars)
- The reference implementation in this space, so its behaviour is well understood and widely documented

### 5. Cons

- No metadata filtering: FAISS searches vectors, so 'similar passages from 2019 only' requires filtering outside the index, which is awkward and slow at scale — Qdrant's main advantage
- No persistence model beyond saving index files, so updates, deletions and incremental additions need application-level handling
- Library-level: there is no API, no auth and no multi-user access, so sharing search with reporters means building something around it
- Index-type selection and training parameters materially affect recall, and a badly configured index silently misses results — which in investigative search is the dangerous failure

### 6. Feedback (documented)

No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 41,767 stars with release v1.16.0 (2026-11-10) and a push on 2026-11-17, MIT licence. Its status as the standard vector-search library is evident from its use across the ecosystem including txtai and sentence-transformers examples.

### 7. Assessment

Adopt it for per-investigation corpora and scripted analysis, and move to Qdrant or pgvector when you need filtering, persistence or multi-user access. For your profile the practical warning is recall: an approximate index can silently omit relevant passages, so for completeness-sensitive work either use an exact index (feasible for modest corpora) or pair semantic search with keyword search and tell reporters that neither alone is exhaustive.

### 8. Maintenance

**Actively maintained** — GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release v1.16.0 (2026-11-10), 41,767 stars, MIT licence. Same-day commits with regular releases under long-term corporate research maintenance.

### 9. Licensing

**Licence:** MIT _(SPDX verified)_

**Model / data licence:** n/a

**Restrictions:** None.

**Licence evidence:** https://github.com/facebookresearch/faiss/blob/main/LICENSE

### 10. Costs

No fee. RAM proportional to vectors and index type; GPU optional. No service infrastructure. Estimate.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

In-process and local; index files stay with you. Suitable for air-gapped work.

### 12. Verdict

**Adopt**

### 13. Alternatives

- [Qdrant](docs/projects/JAI-A3-07.md) where metadata filtering and persistence matter
- pgvector to keep vectors beside relational data
- HNSWlib for a lighter approximate-nearest-neighbour library

### 14. Evidence

Verified **2026-11-17** · confidence **high** · assessment depth `metadata-verified`

- https://github.com/facebookresearch/faiss
- https://faiss.ai/
- https://github.com/facebookresearch/faiss/blob/main/LICENSE

### 1. Purpose

Python library providing a unified interface to open weather and climate data from many national and international providers, including DWD, NOAA, ECCC, IMGW and others, with station metadata and interpolation.

### Journalism / investigative use case

Authoritative weather verification from the originating national service rather than an aggregator — which matters when a published claim will be challenged, because citing the national meteorological agency's own record is far stronger than citing a third-party API.

### 2. Audience

engineer

### 3. Project type

library · bucket `verified-oss`

### 4. Pros

- Goes to the national services directly, so your citation is the authoritative record — the decisive advantage for a contested published claim
- Unified interface across many providers removes the need to learn each agency's idiosyncratic portal and format, which is otherwise days of work per country

- 63 open issues and a small community (457 stars), so you will read source for unusual providers
- Each provider's data model differs underneath the unified interface, so results are not always directly comparable across countries

### 6. Feedback (documented)

### 7. Assessment

The right choice when the weather claim matters enough to need the national service's own record — which, for a contested verification, it usually does. For your profile I would use meteostat for quick triage and wetterdienst for anything heading to publication, pinning the version because the release cadence is brisk. Report the station identifier, distance and interval in the story so the reader can verify independently.

### 8. Maintenance

**Actively maintained** — GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release v0.191.0 published the same day, 457 stars, 63 open issues. Same-day release and push with a very high release count; unambiguously active, with API churn as the trade-off.

**Licence:** MIT _(SPDX verified)_

**Model / data licence:** Each national service's data carries its own terms; DWD and NOAA data are generally open with attribution, others vary.

**Restrictions:** Code permissive. Per-provider data terms apply to republication — check the specific agency before publishing a derived dataset.

**Licence evidence:** https://github.com/earthobservations/wetterdienst/blob/main/LICENSE

### 10. Costs

No fee. Negligible compute; some providers' bulk downloads are large. No paid dependencies.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

Requests go to the national services, which see your station and date queries — a weak indication of your area of interest and generally unproblematic.

The right answer when monitoring becomes a programme rather than a few watches — and for an outlet tracking state rewriting of official records, that threshold arrives quickly. ### 10. Costs

No software fee.
