## 293. warcprox — 64/100

`OSINT-C1-42` · C1 · Web and social research, archives and evidence capture · Recording proxy · **cli** · bucket `verified-oss` · maintainer Internet Archive
[Project page](docs/projects/OSINT-C1-42.md) · [repository](https://github.com/internetarchive/warcprox) · [docs](https://github.com/internetarchive/warcprox#readme)

**Scores** — relevance 3/5 · capability 4/5 · maintenance 3/5 · privacy 3/5 · usability 2/5 · licence+cost 4/5 → **weighted 64/100** (pillar rank 110, segment rank 34)

### 1. Purpose

HTTP/HTTPS man-in-the-middle proxy that writes every request and response passing through it into WARC files, used as the recording layer for browser-driven crawls.

### Journalism / investigative use case

Record every request made during a browsing or scraping session into WARC, so collection and evidence capture happen in one pass — you browse or scrape normally and come away with an evidentiary record of everything the server actually sent.

### 2. Audience

engineer

### 3. Project type

cli · bucket `verified-oss`

### 4. Pros

- Capture-by-proxy means any tool or browser you point at it produces WARC output, including tools that have no archiving support of their own — a genuinely elegant architecture
- Records the actual HTTP exchanges including headers, which is what gives WARC its evidentiary value over rendered snapshots
- Apache-adjacent open licensing, actively released (v2.13.1, 2026-05-11) under Internet Archive maintenance, and the recording layer beneath brozzler
- Pairs with any scraping workflow, so an existing Scrapy or Playwright collection can become evidentiary with no code changes

### 5. Cons

- All proxied traffic, including credentials and session tokens, is written into your WARCs — a serious handling consideration that is easy to overlook and makes the output highly sensitive
- Requires installing a local CA certificate in the browser to intercept TLS, which is a security-posture change on the capture machine that must be reversed afterwards
- The licence is declared only in packaging metadata rather than a LICENSE file (GitHub reports no SPDX), so the GPL-2.0-or-later position needs confirmation for compliance records
- Operator-level tool with 27 open issues and six months since the last push (2026-06-17); not something a reporter would run

### 6. Feedback (documented)

No individual user reports verified. Documented: 469 stars with 27 open issues, release v2.13.1 (2026-05-11), last push 2026-06-17, SPDX none with GPL-2.0-or-later declared in packaging metadata (verified session 1, retained). Production use at the Internet Archive via brozzler.

### 7. Assessment

Powerful and genuinely useful for turning any collection into evidence, with two cautions I would treat as mandatory for your context. First, WARCs produced by proxying a logged-in session contain your credentials and tokens — encrypt them and restrict access, or scrub before sharing. Second, the local CA certificate weakens the capture machine's TLS trust model while installed, so use a dedicated capture VM rather than a reporter's daily laptop.

### 8. Maintenance

**Stable with low activity** — GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-06-17, latest release v2.13.1 (2026-05-11), SPDX none, 469 stars, 27 open issues. Five months since last push on a mature component under institutional maintenance; stable rather than declining, since brozzler's continued releases depend on it.

### 9. Licensing

**Licence:** GPL-2.0-or-later (declared in packaging metadata; no LICENSE file and GitHub reports no SPDX) _(SPDX not verified — resolved from the licence file or project documentation)_

**Model / data licence:** n/a

**Restrictions:** GPL-2.0-or-later per packaging metadata. The absence of a LICENSE file is a compliance-record weakness — cite the packaging metadata explicitly if your legal team requires it.

**Licence evidence:** https://github.com/internetarchive/warcprox

### 10. Costs

No fee. A small Python service plus WARC storage. Negligible infrastructure; non-trivial setup time for the CA certificate arrangement.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

All proxied traffic, including credentials and session tokens, is written into your WARCs — treat output as highly sensitive. The local CA certificate installation changes the trust posture of the capture machine for as long as it is present.

### 12. Verdict

**Integrate**

### Material blockers

_Tracked separately from the score._

### 13. Alternatives

Useful as a ranking aid on top of PySceneDetect's shot segmentation, not as a replacement for it — and never as a filter that decides which frames a human sees. - Produces specific, verifiable technical findings: 'this government portal accepts a deprecated protocol' is a factual claim a reader can re-test, which is unusually solid ground for a technology story
- Certificate-chain detail supports infrastructure attribution: shared intermediate certificates or unusual issuance patterns link hosts that otherwise look unrelated
- Python API and JSON output make it scriptable across a list of targets, so a survey of a sector's TLS posture is feasible
- Well-established with a long maintenance history and a focused scope

### 5. Cons

- Active scanning: each check connects to the target, so the target can see it — and scanning a government portal's TLS, while unremarkable, is still a visible act
- Interpreting results requires TLS literacy: a 'weak' cipher may be present but unused, and publishing a misread finding would be embarrassing and correctable by the target
- Narrow scope by design — it tells you about TLS configuration and nothing else
- Findings age quickly as configurations change, so a published claim needs a date and ideally a saved JSON record

### 6. Feedback (documented)

No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented from the metadata sweep: the repository is live and non-archived with a long release history. SSLyze is a standard TLS assessment tool, well established in the security community.

### 7. Assessment

Integrate it for the specific story type where it produces hard findings — the security posture of organisations holding sensitive data — and for certificate-based infrastructure linking. For your profile the publication discipline is to save the raw JSON with a timestamp, have someone TLS-literate review the interpretation, and give the organisation an opportunity to respond, since configurations can be fixed between your scan and publication and you want the record of what you found.

### 8. Maintenance

**Stable with low activity** — Verified via the GitHub API 2026-11-17 as live and non-archived with a long release history and steady maintenance. Classified stable-low: a mature, focused tool where the pace reflects completeness.

### 9. Licensing

**Licence:** AGPL-3.0 (project licensing — confirm from the repository licence file) _(SPDX not verified — resolved from the licence file or project documentation)_

**Model / data licence:** n/a

**Restrictions:** Copyleft would apply to a modified network service built on it; immaterial for command-line use. Note that AGPL on a scanning tool is unusual and worth confirming if you embed it.

**Licence evidence:** https://github.com/nabla-c0d3/sslyze

### 10. Costs

No fee. Negligible compute.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

Active connections to the target, which are visible in its logs. Unremarkable for TLS assessment but still a disclosure of interest.

### 12. Verdict

**Integrate**

### 13. Alternatives

- testssl.sh as a shell-based alternative with similar coverage
- Qualys SSL Labs for a hosted assessment, which discloses the target to a third party and produces a citable public report
- Certificate transparency data for issuance patterns without connecting to the host

## 298. WhatWeb — 64/100

**Scores** — relevance 3/5 · capability 3/5 · maintenance 3/5 · privacy 3/5 · usability 4/5 · licence+cost 4/5 → **weighted 64/100** (pillar rank 72, segment rank 18)

### 1. Purpose

Web technology fingerprinting scanner with over a thousand plugins that identifies content management systems, frameworks, analytics, server software and embedded devices, with configurable aggression levels.

### Journalism / investigative use case

Fingerprinting a target's web infrastructure in one command: identify the CMS and server stack of a surveillance vendor's site, or sweep a list of suspected front organisations to find which share an unusual platform. The device-detection plugins also identify exposed appliances, which matters when mapping surveillance infrastructure.

### 2. Audience

engineer, specialist investigator

### 3. Project type

cli · bucket `verified-oss`

### 4. Pros

- Self-contained CLI with its own plugin database, so unlike webappanalyzer you get results immediately with no engine to build
- Aggression levels let you choose between passive identification and active probing, which is both an accuracy and an operational-security control
- Identifies embedded devices and appliances as well as web stacks, useful when the subject is physical surveillance infrastructure exposed to the internet

### 5. Cons

- Fingerprints are inferences and produce false positives, so an attribution based on a single match is weak

No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented from the metadata sweep: the repository is live and non-archived with a substantial history; maintenance is steady rather than frequent. WhatWeb's standing as a fingerprinting tool is established by its inclusion in standard security distributions.

### 7. Assessment

Keep it for quick reconnaissance, with the aggression level set low when the target would object to being probed. For your profile the practical pairing is WhatWeb for a first pass and certificate-transparency plus registry data for attribution, because fingerprint matches alone will not survive a challenge. Treat scanning a surveillance vendor's infrastructure as a visible act and route it through an egress that is not your newsroom.

### 8. Maintenance

**Stable with low activity** — Verified via the GitHub API 2026-11-17 as live and non-archived. A mature Ruby tool with a long release history and steady rather than frequent updates; the plugin database is the component that matters and it ages gradually against modern sites.

**Model / data licence:** n/a

**Restrictions:** GPL-family copyleft on the tool; immaterial for internal use. Active scanning may engage computer-misuse law depending on jurisdiction and target — a legal rather than licence question.

**Licence evidence:** https://github.com/urbanadventurer/WhatWeb

### 10. Costs

No fee. Ruby runtime; negligible resources.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

Scanning is visible to the target. Passive modes reduce but do not eliminate the footprint; use a dedicated egress for sensitive targets.

**Integrate**

## 299. OpenCellID — 63/100

`SUR-B2-19` · B2 · Investigating surveillance companies, infrastructure, procurement and tracking tech · Cellular infrastructure dataset · **dataset** · bucket `proprietary-service` · maintainer OpenCellID / Unwired Labs
[Project page](docs/projects/SUR-B2-19.md) · [docs](https://docs.opencellid.org/)

**Scores** — relevance 4/5 · capability 3/5 · maintenance 2/5 · privacy 3/5 · usability 4/5 · licence+cost 2/5 → **weighted 63/100** (pillar rank 73, segment rank 19)

> **Provisional assessment** — the evidence does not support a firm score; see Evidence below.

### 1. Purpose

Crowdsourced database of cell-tower locations and identifiers (MCC, MNC, LAC, cell ID) worldwide, with an API and bulk downloads for looking up or reverse-looking-up cell identifiers.

### Journalism / investigative use case

Two uses in surveillance work: corroborating Rayhunter or SnoopSnitch anomalies against known tower infrastructure to distinguish a legitimate cell from a suspected simulator, and resolving cell identifiers found in device records or leaked location data into physical locations.

### 2. Audience

specialist investigator, engineer

### 3. Project type

dataset · bucket `proprietary-service`

### 4. Pros

- Provides the reference layer that makes cell-site anomaly detection interpretable: an unknown cell ID at a location where no tower is recorded is a meaningful signal, and without a reference database it is just noise
- Bulk downloads allow offline lookup, which matters both for privacy and for field use without connectivity
- Global crowdsourced coverage means it reaches places commercial datasets neglect
- Documentation is clear and the API is straightforward to integrate

### 5. Cons

- Crowdsourced coverage is uneven and ages: a genuine new tower may be absent, producing a false 'unknown cell' signal — so absence from OpenCellID is weak evidence of a simulator and must not be reported as detection
- Operated by a commercial company (Unwired Labs), and access terms including any free-tier limits were NOT verified in this survey — treat as unknown pending a check
- Position estimates are derived from crowdsourced observations, so tower locations carry error that matters when you are reasoning about coverage areas
- Queries disclose which cell identifiers and areas you are investigating to the operator

### 6. Feedback (documented)

No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: docs.opencellid.org verified live on 2026-11-17 (200). The database's crowdsourced nature and the resulting coverage variability are documented characteristics rather than criticisms.

### 7. Assessment

Integrate it as the reference layer behind any cellular-surveillance work, with the limitation stated explicitly in anything you publish: an unrecorded cell is not evidence of an IMSI catcher, because the database is incomplete. For your profile the practical approach is to download bulk data for your regions of interest so lookups are offline and private, and to treat OpenCellID agreement as corroboration while treating disagreement as a question rather than a finding. Verify the access terms before building a dependency.

### 8. Maintenance

**Uncertain** — Documentation site verified live on 2026-11-17 (200), but this survey did not verify current access terms, free-tier limits or data-update cadence. The database is crowdsourced and commercially operated; classified Uncertain because continuity and terms for a commercially operated community dataset cannot be assessed from a documentation fetch alone.

### 9. Licensing

**Licence:** Not verified in this survey — OpenCellID has historically offered data under a Creative Commons licence with API access tiers operated by Unwired Labs; confirm current terms before use _(SPDX not verified — resolved from the licence file or project documentation)_

**Model / data licence:** Same.

**Restrictions:** Unverified and material: a CC-BY-SA-style licence would impose share-alike obligations on a derived dataset, and commercial API terms may restrict redistribution. Confirm before publishing derived data.

**Licence evidence:** https://docs.opencellid.org/

### 10. Costs

Not verified in this survey. Historically a free tier with API keys and paid tiers above it; confirm current pricing before planning. No software cost.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

API queries disclose the cell identifiers and areas you are investigating to the operator. Bulk download and offline lookup avoids this entirely and is the configuration to prefer for sensitive work.

### 12. Verdict

**Integrate**

### Material blockers

_Tracked separately from the score._

- Licence and access terms unverified; crowdsourced coverage gaps mean an unknown cell is not evidence of a simulator

### 13. Alternatives

- National regulator tower registries where published, which are authoritative rather than crowdsourced
- Mozilla Location Service-style datasets where still available
- Rayhunter's own anomaly analysis without external corroboration, accepting weaker conclusions

### 14. Evidence

## 300. Alaveteli — 63/100

`JAI-A1-28` · A1 · Discovery, scraping, ingestion, data journalism and newsroom workflow · Freedom of information · **platform** · bucket `verified-oss` · maintainer mySociety
[Project page](docs/projects/JAI-A1-28.md) · [repository](https://github.com/mysociety/alaveteli) · [docs](https://alaveteli.org/docs/)

**Scores** — relevance 3/5 · capability 4/5 · maintenance 3/5 · privacy 2/5 · usability 3/5 · licence+cost 4/5 → **weighted 63/100** (pillar rank 113, segment rank 28)

### 1. Purpose

Platform for running a public freedom-of-information request site: users submit requests to public bodies, correspondence is published automatically, and the resulting archive of requests and responses becomes a public resource.

### Journalism / investigative use case

Two uses: running a national FOI platform (as WhatDoTheyKnow and its many deployments do), and mining an existing deployment's archive — because every request and response is public, an Alaveteli instance is a searchable corpus of what public bodies have disclosed and refused.

### 2. Audience

engineer, newsroom analyst, journalist

### 3. Project type

platform · bucket `verified-oss`

### 4. Pros

- Publishing requests and responses by default creates a public accountability record, which is a genuinely different model from private FOI correspondence and produces a reusable archive
- Deployed nationally in many countries, so the model is proven and the codebase handles real administrative complexity (public-body registers, refusal handling, appeals)
- AGPL-3.0-or-later (licence verified in session 1 by reading the text) with mySociety's long institutional record in civic technology
- The archive of an existing instance is immediately useful to a journalist without running anything: searching prior requests shows what a body has already disclosed

### 5. Cons

- Running an instance is a substantial undertaking: a Rails application plus mail handling, a public-body register to maintain, and moderation of user-submitted content including the legal exposure that brings
- Publishing everything by default is the wrong model for a journalist's own sensitive requests, since it tells the target and competitors what you are asking
- Maintenance is steady rather than brisk, and the deployment documentation assumes operational competence with Rails and mail infrastructure
- Jurisdiction-specific configuration (bodies, laws, timescales) is significant work for a new country deployment

### 6. Feedback (documented)

No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: session 1's a1disc/notes.md independently recorded 'alaveteli AGPL-3.0-or-later' after reading the licence text, resolving a NOASSERTION. The platform's national deployments are documented by mySociety and constitute strong evidence that the model works at scale.

### 7. Assessment

For your profile the realistic value is as a source rather than software: mine existing Alaveteli instances for what bodies have already disclosed before filing your own requests, which saves time and reveals the body's refusal patterns. Running an instance makes sense only as a civic-infrastructure project, not as newsroom tooling, and the publish-by-default model is actively wrong for a sensitive investigation — file those directly and privately.

### 8. Maintenance

**Stable with low activity** — Verified via the GitHub API 2026-11-17 as live and non-archived, with mySociety's continued institutional maintenance. Release cadence is modest; the platform is mature and deployments are long-lived. Session 1 verified the licence by reading the text.

### 9. Licensing

**Licence:** AGPL-3.0-or-later (verified in session 1 by reading the licence text, resolving a GitHub NOASSERTION) _(SPDX not verified — resolved from the licence file or project documentation)_

**Model / data licence:** Request and response content published on an instance is public; the underlying disclosed documents remain subject to the releasing body's terms.

**Restrictions:** AGPL-3.0-or-later: a modified public instance obliges source publication — which, for a platform whose purpose is public deployment, is a real obligation rather than a theoretical one.

**Licence evidence:** https://github.com/mysociety/alaveteli/blob/develop/LICENSE.txt

### 10. Costs

No software fee. Running an instance: a Rails host, a database, reliable mail infrastructure and moderation staff time — the staff cost dominates and is ongoing. Not a small commitment. Estimate.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

Deliberately public: requests and responses are published, and requester names are typically visible. This is the point of the platform and the reason not to use it for a sensitive journalistic request.

### 12. Verdict

**Reference only**

### Material blockers

_Tracked separately from the score._

- Publish-by-default model is unsuitable for sensitive journalistic requests

## 301. SpiderFoot — 63/100

[Project page](docs/projects/OSINT-C3-29.md) · [repository](https://github.com/smicallef/spiderfoot) · [docs](https://www.spiderfoot.net/documentation/)

**Scores** — relevance 3/5 · capability 4/5 · maintenance 3/5 · privacy 2/5 · usability 4/5 · licence+cost 3/5 → **weighted 63/100** (pillar rank 115, segment rank 36)

### 1. Purpose

OSINT automation platform with 200-plus modules that take a seed (domain, IP, email, name) and query many data sources automatically, correlating results into an entity graph with a web interface.

### Journalism / investigative use case

Automated first-pass reconnaissance on an entity: give it a company domain and it queries dozens of sources — DNS, certificates, breach data, social platforms, scan databases — assembling a correlated picture that would take a day by hand.

### 2. Audience

engineer, specialist investigator

### 3. Project type

platform · bucket `verified-oss`

### 4. Pros

- Module breadth means a single scan covers ground that would otherwise require a dozen tools, which is genuinely time-saving on a new target
- Correlation into an entity graph surfaces relationships between findings rather than leaving you with a dozen separate outputs
- Web interface makes it usable by an investigator who is not comfortable in a terminal, which widens who can run reconnaissance
- Open source and self-hosted, so scan results stay with you

Pilot it with modules deliberately selected rather than running everything — the default breadth makes a single scan a broad disclosure of your target to dozens of third parties, which for a surveillance-industry investigation is the wrong trade. For your profile the better pattern is usually a small set of chosen tools (subfinder, httpx, asn, certstream) whose disclosure you understand, with SpiderFoot reserved for low-sensitivity targets where speed matters more than discretion.

### 8. Maintenance

### 10. Costs

No fee for the open edition. Many modules require paid API keys (not priced here), so realistic capability has a recurring cost. SpiderFoot HX is a separate commercial product. Estimate.

### 1. Purpose

Multilingual and multimodal similarity service exposing text, image, audio and video similarity search over a vector index, used as the matching engine behind Meedan Check.

### Journalism / investigative use case

Powers tipline and fact-check deduplication at scale: when a reader submits an image or claim, Alegre finds whether a near-identical item has already been received and checked, so the desk answers from existing work instead of re-verifying. At high tipline volume this is the difference between a functioning service and a backlog.

### 2. Audience

engineer

### 3. Project type

platform · bucket `verified-oss`

### 4. Pros

- Self-hostable, so media and hashes stay on infrastructure you control; important because tipline media is often sensitive

- Solves a specific, measurable problem (duplicate workload) rather than promising verification

### 5. Cons

No individual user reports verified. Production evidence is structural: Alegre is the matching layer of Meedan Check, which is deployed by fact-checking partners. The unverified bundled-model licences are an explicit gap carried into this entry rather than resolved.

### 7. Assessment

Worth running only as part of a Check deployment or where you specifically need multimodal near-duplicate matching at volume. For your profile a lighter alternative — ImageHash plus a sentence-transformers index — gives you most of the capability with components you control and whose licences you can verify. Alegre's advantage is that it is already integrated and battle-tested; its disadvantage is opacity about the models inside it.

### 8. Maintenance

**Actively maintained** — GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-09-28, latest tag v0.187.2, no GitHub release objects, 15 stars, 22 open issues. Continuous versioned tagging driven by Check's needs; maintenance is institutional rather than community-driven.

**Model / data licence:** Varies — bundles third-party sentence-transformer/BERT checkpoints whose own licences were NOT verified in this survey.

**Restrictions:** Code unrestricted; unresolved uncertainty at the bundled-model layer. Verify the specific checkpoints before commercial redistribution.

**Licence evidence:** https://github.com/meedan/alegre/blob/master/LICENSE

### 10. Costs

No fee. Infrastructure: Elasticsearch/OpenSearch plus PostgreSQL plus model-serving containers; GPU helpful for embedding throughput. Optional Google Translate API charges if enabled (not priced here). Estimate.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

Self-hostable so media and hashes remain yours. Optional translation and LLM integrations send text to third parties if configured — review before enabling, since tipline text can identify a submitter.

**Monitor**

## 303. CAT-Net — 63/100

`JAI-A4-19` · A4 · Fact-checking support and media verification · Image splicing detection · **model** · bucket `verified-oss` · maintainer Myung-Joon Kwon (mjkwon2021)
[Project page](docs/projects/JAI-A4-19.md) · [repository](https://github.com/mjkwon2021/CAT-Net) · [docs](https://github.com/mjkwon2021/CAT-Net#readme)

**Scores** — relevance 3/5 · capability 3/5 · maintenance 3/5 · privacy 4/5 · usability 2/5 · licence+cost 4/5 → **weighted 63/100** (pillar rank 115, segment rank 8)

### 1. Purpose

Neural network that detects and localises spliced regions in JPEG images by tracing compression-artefact inconsistencies, using both RGB and DCT-domain streams.

### Journalism / investigative use case

Spotting spliced-in regions in JPEGs that still retain their original compression history — for example a photo circulated as a camera original rather than a platform re-encode, where a pasted element carries a different compression signature from its surroundings.

### 2. Audience

specialist investigator, engineer

### 3. Project type

model · bucket `verified-oss`

### 4. Pros

- CC-BY-4.0 pretrained weights and Apache-2.0 code per the README licence section — a commercially usable combination, which is rare among forensic models and is the main reason to prefer it over TruFor
- Compression-artefact tracing is a physically grounded signal rather than a learned style cue, so a positive finding is more explainable to an editor
- Still receiving commits (pushed 2026-10-15) years after publication

### 5. Cons

- Depends on JPEG compression artefacts, so its signal is weak or absent for PNGs, screenshots and heavily re-encoded images — which is the state most social-media images arrive in, sharply limiting real-world applicability
- v1 handles splicing only, not other manipulation classes, so a negative result says very little
- Pretrained and trained weights are hosted on Google Drive and Baiduyun — an availability and supply-chain risk, and awkward for automated deployment

No individual user reports verified. Documented: the README licence section stating Apache-2.0 code and CC-BY-4.0 weights and datasets (read in session 1, retained); weights hosted on Google Drive and Baiduyun; 317 stars with 44 open issues.

### 7. Assessment

The commercially usable forensic localisation model in this catalogue, which makes it the default choice for a commercial newsroom despite TruFor's technical edge. Its real limitation is scope: it answers a narrow question about JPEG splicing, and the images you most want to check have usually been recompressed past the point where it helps. Use it when you have what purports to be a camera original, mirror the weights locally rather than depending on Google Drive, and treat output as a lead.

### 8. Maintenance

**Stable with low activity** — GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-10-15, no releases or tags, SPDX none, 317 stars, 44 open issues. Commits within the last month but no release engineering and a sizeable backlog; a research artefact receiving occasional attention.

**Licence:** Apache-2.0 (code), per the README licence section; GitHub API reports no detected licence _(SPDX not verified — resolved from the licence file or project documentation)_

**Model / data licence:** CC-BY-4.0 for pretrained weights and released datasets, per the README licence section.

**Restrictions:** CC-BY-4.0 requires attribution — cite the model in any methodology note. No non-commercial restriction, which is the key advantage. Because GitHub detects no licence file, confirm the README statement against the repository before commercial reliance.

**Licence evidence:** https://github.com/mjkwon2021/CAT-Net

No fee. GPU for inference. Weights from third-party file hosts (mirror them). Estimate.

**Pilot**

## 304. Conifer — 63/100

`OSINT-C1-35` · C1 · Web and social research, archives and evidence capture · Hosted capture platform · **platform** · bucket `verified-oss` · maintainer Rhizome (transferred from webrecorder/conifer)
[Project page](docs/projects/OSINT-C1-35.md) · [repository](https://github.com/Rhizome-Conifer/conifer) · [docs](https://conifer.rhizome.org/)

**Scores** — relevance 3/5 · capability 3/5 · maintenance 2/5 · privacy 3/5 · usability 4/5 · licence+cost 5/5 → **weighted 63/100** (pillar rank 116, segment rank 36)

### 1. Purpose

Web-archiving platform providing remote-browser capture sessions and organised, replayable collections, available as a hosted service or self-hosted Docker stack.

### Journalism / investigative use case

Capture a dynamic page or social feed through a remote browser session and keep it in an organised, replayable collection — the remote-browser aspect means the capture originates from Conifer's infrastructure rather than your own address, which can be useful when you do not want your newsroom IP visiting a target.

### 2. Audience

newsroom analyst, journalist

### 3. Project type

platform · bucket `verified-oss`

### 4. Pros

- Remote-browser capture provides a degree of separation between your network and the target, which is a genuine (if partial) operational-security benefit
- Collection organisation and replay in one place, usable by non-engineers without any infrastructure
- Apache-2.0 with a self-hostable Docker stack if you want the same model under your own control
- Substantial community (1,549 stars) and an institutional home at Rhizome, with the repository transfer from webrecorder confirmed by redirect

### 5. Cons

- Slower cadence than Webrecorder's newer tools: last push 2026-07-22 (four months before this survey) with no release objects at all, and 128 open issues
- Hosted quotas are small, so sustained use pushes you toward self-hosting or another tool
- Captures are held by the hosted instance unless you self-host, which is a third-party custody decision
- Superseded in practice by Browsertrix and ArchiveWeb.page for most use cases, so adopting it now means choosing the less-developed option

### 6. Feedback (documented)

No individual user reports verified. Documented: repository transfer webrecorder/conifer → Rhizome-Conifer/conifer confirmed by API redirect on 2026-11-17; 1,549 stars with 128 open issues; last push 2026-07-22; no release objects. The transfer plus slowing cadence is the significant pattern.

### 7. Assessment

Hard to recommend for new work when ArchiveWeb.page covers manual capture and Browsertrix covers team-scale, both under faster maintenance. The one feature that still distinguishes Conifer is remote-browser capture, which has a real use when you want capture traffic not to originate from your network — though a dedicated VPS running browsertrix-crawler achieves the same with more control. Treat as a monitoring item, and note the transfer when updating any old links.

### 8. Maintenance

**Maintenance appears to be declining** — GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false (repository transferred to Rhizome-Conifer), pushed_at 2026-07-22, no release objects, 1,549 stars, 128 open issues. Four months without commits, no release engineering, and functional overlap with faster-moving tools from the original maintainer. Declining rather than dormant.

### 9. Licensing

**Licence:** Apache-2.0 _(SPDX verified)_

**Model / data licence:** n/a

**Restrictions:** None material.

**Licence evidence:** https://github.com/Rhizome-Conifer/conifer/blob/develop/LICENSE

### 10. Costs

Self-hosting: no fee, a Docker stack plus storage. Hosted conifer.rhizome.org has storage quotas; any paid tiers were not verified in this survey. Estimate for self-hosting: one moderate VM plus capture storage.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

Captures are held by the hosted instance unless you self-host. The remote-browser model means the target sees Conifer's address rather than yours — a partial benefit, since the hosted operator then sees what you captured.

### 12. Verdict

**Monitor**

### 13. Alternatives

- [ArchiveWeb.page](docs/projects/OSINT-C1-31.md) for manual capture under your own control
- [Browsertrix](docs/projects/OSINT-C1-30.md) for a maintained team platform
- [browsertrix-crawler](docs/projects/OSINT-C1-29.md) on a dedicated VPS to get network separation with full control

### 14. Evidence

Verified **2026-11-17** · confidence **high** · assessment depth `metadata-verified`

## 307. juditha — 63/100

`OSINT-C3-09` · C3 · Public records, corporate ownership, finance, infrastructure, link analysis, collaboration · Entity lookup service · **library** · bucket `verified-oss` · maintainer Data and Research Center (DARC)
[Project page](docs/projects/OSINT-C3-09.md) · [repository](https://github.com/dataresearchcenter/juditha) · [docs](https://github.com/dataresearchcenter/juditha#readme)

**Scores** — relevance 3/5 · capability 3/5 · maintenance 2/5 · privacy 5/5 · usability 2/5 · licence+cost 4/5 → **weighted 63/100** (pillar rank 119, segment rank 39)

> **Provisional assessment** — the evidence does not support a firm score; see Evidence below.

### 1. Purpose

Fast lookup service for canonical entity names, built to check whether a string matches a known entity in a reference dataset such as OpenSanctions or a FollowTheMoney collection.

### Journalism / investigative use case

High-speed name checking inside an ingest pipeline: as documents are processed, test every extracted name against a reference set of sanctioned entities and known companies, so flagged documents surface immediately rather than after a separate screening pass.

### 2. Audience

engineer

### 3. Project type

library · bucket `verified-oss`

### 4. Pros

- Designed for the pipeline position where screening actually belongs — at ingest, not as a later batch — which shortens the time between receiving documents and knowing which matter
- Built by DARC, the same organisation maintaining OpenAleph, so it fits coherently with the FollowTheMoney and OpenSanctions stack
- Narrow scope done well: fast canonical-name lookup rather than a general matching framework, which makes it comprehensible and replaceable
- Self-hosted, so the names you check are not disclosed to anyone

### 5. Cons

- Very small project with minimal community, so documentation is thin and you are reliant on the maintainer's context — a real adoption cost
- Name lookup is not entity resolution: a match is a string correspondence requiring adjudication, and treating it as identification would produce false allegations
- Tightly coupled to the FollowTheMoney and OpenSanctions ecosystem, so its value depends on having adopted that stack
- Maintenance follows one organisation's needs, so continuity depends on DARC's priorities

### 6. Feedback (documented)

No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: the repository is live and non-archived under DARC's maintenance, in the same organisation that maintains OpenAleph. No independent deployment verified.

### 7. Assessment

Integrate it if you have adopted the OpenAleph and OpenSanctions stack and want screening at ingest — the pipeline position is the right one and the component is small enough to understand. For your profile the caution is interpretive rather than technical: a name match at ingest is a flag for human attention, and the pipeline should route flagged documents to a reviewer rather than labelling them. Outside that ecosystem, rigour plus RapidFuzz over your own reference list does the same job.

### 8. Maintenance

**Uncertain** — Verified via the GitHub API 2026-11-17 as live and non-archived under DARC's maintenance. The project is small with limited release history, and its continuity depends on one organisation's internal needs — classified Uncertain rather than inferring health from the parent organisation's activity on other repositories.

**Restrictions:** Code permissive as published. The data licence is the operative restriction if you load OpenSanctions.

**Licence evidence:** https://github.com/dataresearchcenter/juditha

### 10. Costs

No fee. A small service plus the reference dataset. Negligible infrastructure. Estimate.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

Self-hosted lookups disclose nothing externally — the key property for screening names from a confidential document set.

**Monitor**

### 1. Purpose

Hosted tracker documenting US federal datasets that have been terminated, altered or had variables removed, plus pending changes to statistical collections, with an email newsletter.

### Journalism / investigative use case

Check whether a federal dataset you are about to rely on has been terminated, altered or had variables removed — and pick up story leads from documented removals and pending collection changes. ### 2. Audience

journalist, newsroom analyst

### 3. Project type

platform · bucket `proprietary-service`

- Addresses a real and under-covered problem: datasets disappear or change definition quietly, and a story built on last year's variable can be silently wrong
- Curated by a credible policy organisation with subject expertise, so entries carry context rather than just diffs
- Zero effort to use — a reporter reads the site or subscribes to the newsletter
- Documented removals are themselves story leads, not just defensive checks

### 7. Assessment

Worth adding to your routine as a pre-flight check whenever a story leans on US federal statistics, and worth subscribing to for leads. But treat it as a secondary source: when a removal matters to a story, corroborate against the agency's own site, the Federal Register notice, and an archived capture (Wayback or your own), and cite those. Free to read; newsletter free. No infrastructure. Not self-hostable in practice.

journalist, newsroom analyst

For your profile the right habit is to find the figure on Pulse, then trace it back to OONI or IODA and cite the primary measurement with a permalink — that way the claim survives both official denial and the dashboard changing. Reserve direct Pulse citation for context and precedent rather than for the central factual claim of a story.

The dashboard is live but its code is not public, so repository-based maintenance assessment is not possible. Classified Uncertain deliberately rather than assuming continuity from the organisation's reputation.

**Model / data licence:** Upstream measurement providers' terms apply to the underlying data; Pulse's own presentation terms were not verified in this survey.

**Restrictions:** Unverified. Do not assume figures may be redistributed as a dataset; cite and link rather than republish.

### 10. Costs

## 312. mapillary_tools — 62/100

`OSINT-C2-31` · C2 · Image/video verification, geolocation, satellite, aviation and maritime · Street-level imagery · **cli** · bucket `verified-oss` · maintainer Mapillary (Meta)
[Project page](docs/projects/OSINT-C2-31.md) · [repository](https://github.com/mapillary/mapillary_tools) · [docs](https://github.com/mapillary/mapillary_tools#readme)

**Scores** — relevance 3/5 · capability 3/5 · maintenance 4/5 · privacy 2/5 · usability 3/5 · licence+cost 4/5 → **weighted 62/100** (pillar rank 122, segment rank 45)

### 1. Purpose

Command-line tools for processing and uploading street-level imagery to Mapillary, including geotagging from GPS tracks, sequence organisation and metadata handling.

### Journalism / investigative use case

Two uses: processing your own ground-truth imagery (a reporter driving a route with a dashcam) into a geotagged sequence for later reference, and understanding the metadata structure of Mapillary imagery you use for geolocation verification against a photograph.

### 2. Audience

engineer, specialist investigator

### 3. Project type

cli · bucket `verified-oss`

### 4. Pros

- Mapillary's crowd-sourced street-level imagery is often the only street-view coverage available in countries Google does not photograph — which is precisely where much conflict and corruption reporting happens
- Geotagging from GPS tracks lets a reporter turn a drive-through into a reusable, dated visual record of a location, useful when you cannot return
- BSD-2-Clause and actively maintained (v0.15.0, 2026-11-04; pushed 2026-11-16) with a clean tracker
- Processing happens locally, so you control what is uploaded and when

### 5. Cons

- Uploading contributes your imagery to a Meta-operated platform under its terms — a deliberate disclosure that also reveals where your reporter has been, with timestamps
- The tool is for contributing imagery, not for downloading it, so for geolocation verification you need the Mapillary API or streetlevel instead — a distinction that wastes people's time
- Narrow scope and engineer-facing; a reporter will not use it directly
- Coverage of the platform itself is uneven and contributor-dependent, so the imagery you want may simply not exist

### 6. Feedback (documented)

No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 320 stars with 33 open issues, release v0.15.0 (2026-11-04), pushed 2026-11-16, BSD-2-Clause. Mapillary's role as a street-level imagery source in regions without commercial coverage is well established in open-source investigation practice.

### 7. Assessment

Relevant mainly if your team does field work and wants to build a reusable visual record — in which case it is the right tool, with one serious caveat: uploading a geotagged sequence publishes where your reporter drove and when, which can endanger them or their sources in a hostile environment. Process locally, review carefully, and treat the upload decision as an editorial and security judgement rather than a technical step. For consuming imagery for geolocation, use streetlevel or the Mapillary API instead.

### 8. Maintenance

**Actively maintained** — GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-16, latest release v0.15.0 (2026-11-04), 320 stars, 33 open issues. Regular releases under corporate maintenance.

### 9. Licensing

**Licence:** BSD-2-Clause _(SPDX verified)_

**Model / data licence:** Imagery uploaded to Mapillary is licensed under the platform's terms (historically CC-BY-SA for the imagery database); imagery you consume from Mapillary carries those terms.

**Restrictions:** Code permissive. The imagery licensing is the substantive point: check Mapillary's current terms before republishing imagery from the platform in a story, and understand what rights you grant when uploading.

**Licence evidence:** https://github.com/mapillary/mapillary_tools/blob/main/LICENSE

### 10. Costs

No fee. Negligible compute; bandwidth for uploads. A Mapillary account is required to upload.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

Processing is local; uploading publishes geotagged imagery to a Meta-operated platform, disclosing locations and timestamps of your field movements. This is the dominant consideration for hostile-environment work.

### 12. Verdict

**Monitor**

### Material blockers

_Tracked separately from the score._

- Uploading discloses reporter movements with timestamps to a third-party platform

### 13. Alternatives

- [streetlevel](docs/projects/OSINT-C2-32.md) for downloading panoramas and metadata from Street View, Look Around and Mapillary for verification
- The Mapillary API directly for programmatic imagery access
- Keeping field imagery entirely internal with your own geotagging scripts (ExifTool can write GPS tags)

`SUR-B2-12` · B2 · Investigating surveillance companies, infrastructure, procurement and tracking tech · Police accountability records · **platform** · bucket `verified-oss` · maintainer Lucy Parsons Labs
[Project page](docs/projects/SUR-B2-12.md) · [repository](https://github.com/lucyparsons/OpenOversight) · [docs](https://github.com/lucyparsons/OpenOversight#readme)

**Scores** — relevance 3/5 · capability 3/5 · maintenance 3/5 · privacy 3/5 · usability 3/5 · licence+cost 4/5 → **weighted 62/100** (pillar rank 76, segment rank 20)

### 1. Purpose

Public, crowdsourced database and web application for identifying police officers from photographs and badge numbers, linking officers to departments, assignments and complaint records.

### Journalism / investigative use case

Identifying officers in protest footage or complaint records — the specific accountability problem where a journalist has an image and a badge number but no name, and where departments decline to assist. It is also a model for building an identifiable-public-official database in other jurisdictions.

### 2. Audience

newsroom analyst, specialist investigator

### 3. Project type

platform · bucket `verified-oss`

### 4. Pros

- Addresses a concrete accountability gap that journalists hit repeatedly, and does so with a crowdsourcing model that scales beyond what one newsroom could compile
- Self-hostable, so the approach is transferable to other jurisdictions and other categories of public official where records exist but are not searchable
- Built by a civil-liberties organisation with an explicit accountability purpose, so the data model and ethics are oriented to public-interest use
- Open source, so the methodology for assembling such a database is inspectable and reusable

### 5. Cons

- Jurisdiction-specific in practice: the deployed instances cover particular US departments, so outside those it is a template rather than a resource
- Building and operating such a database raises serious legal and ethical questions — data protection, accuracy obligations, the consequences of a wrong identification — that are entirely on the operator and are heavier outside the US
- A crowdsourced identification is a lead, not a fact: publishing a name from a photographic match without independent confirmation would be indefensible
- Small project with a specialist focus, so maintenance capacity is limited and a self-hosted deployment means owning the code

### 6. Feedback (documented)

No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented from the metadata sweep: the repository is live and non-archived. Lucy Parsons Labs operates public instances and the project's accountability purpose is documented, which is the relevant context; I verified no specific newsroom use.

### 7. Assessment

Relevant mainly as a model unless you work in a covered US jurisdiction. For your profile the transferable idea is strong — a searchable database of identifiable public officials, built from public records, is a durable accountability asset — but the legal exposure differs sharply by jurisdiction, and in Europe a comparable database of named officials with photographs would need a serious data-protection assessment before a line of code was written. Treat identifications as leads requiring independent confirmation.

### 8. Maintenance

**Stable with low activity** — Verified via the GitHub API 2026-11-17 as live and non-archived, maintained by a small civil-liberties organisation at modest velocity. Operating instances exist, which is the stronger signal for a database project than commit frequency.

### 9. Licensing

**Licence:** GPL-3.0 (project licensing — confirm from the repository licence file) _(SPDX not verified — resolved from the licence file or project documentation)_

**Model / data licence:** The database contents are compiled from public records and crowdsourced contributions; terms vary by instance and jurisdiction.

**Restrictions:** Copyleft on the application. The substantive constraints are data-protection law and accuracy obligations, which differ by jurisdiction and are far more restrictive than the software licence.

**Licence evidence:** https://github.com/lucyparsons/OpenOversight

### 10. Costs

No software fee. Self-hosting is a web application plus image storage — modest. The real costs are legal review and the editorial labour of verifying records. Estimate.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

The project's purpose is to make public officials identifiable, so its privacy posture is deliberately asymmetric: it protects contributors and exposes officials acting in a public capacity. Operating an instance makes you a data controller with the obligations that follow, which in some jurisdictions is a substantial undertaking.

### 12. Verdict

**Reference only**

### Material blockers

_Tracked separately from the score._

- Jurisdiction-specific coverage; operating a comparable database raises significant data-protection obligations outside the US

### 13. Alternatives

- A purpose-built internal database (Datasette over curated records) scoped to one investigation
- Collaboration with a local civil-liberties organisation that already holds the records

## 314. uroman — 62/100

`JAI-A2-56` · A2 · Documents and language: OCR, transcription, translation, entities, entity resolution · Transliteration · **cli** · bucket `verified-oss` · maintainer USC Information Sciences Institute (isi-nlp)
[Project page](docs/projects/JAI-A2-56.md) · [repository](https://github.com/isi-nlp/uroman) · [docs](https://github.com/isi-nlp/uroman#readme)

**Scores** — relevance 3/5 · capability 3/5 · maintenance 1/5 · privacy 5/5 · usability 3/5 · licence+cost 4/5 → **weighted 62/100** (pillar rank 116, segment rank 61)

### 1. Purpose

Universal romaniser that converts text in virtually any script to the Latin alphabet using rule tables, with no trained model and no language specification required.

### Journalism / investigative use case

Makes non-Latin-script corpora searchable and joinable: romanise Arabic, Cyrillic, Devanagari, Thai or Chinese names so a sanctions list, a corporate registry and a leaked ledger can be fuzzy-matched in one Latin-script index — the step that makes cross-script name matching possible at all.

### 2. Audience

engineer

### 3. Project type

cli · bucket `verified-oss`

### 4. Pros

- Script-agnostic with no language detection required, so it handles a mixed-script corpus without routing logic — a genuine simplification
- Rule-based and deterministic: the same input always romanises identically, which is what a reproducible matching pipeline needs
- No models, no dependencies of consequence, entirely offline — trivially deployable on an evidence machine
- Covers an unusually wide range of scripts for a single tool, including ones with little other tooling

### 5. Cons

- Romanisation is lossy and irreversible: distinct names can collide, which creates false matches that must be adjudicated
- Output follows no single standard scheme (not ALA-LC, not BGN/PCGN), so it is a matching aid rather than a citable rendering — never use uroman output as a published name spelling
- Licence carries a non-standard condition: the LICENSE.txt grants MIT-equivalent rights but states that 'Any publication of projects using uroman shall acknowledge its use', so it is not a clean SPDX identifier (GitHub reports NOASSERTION)
- Dormant: last push 2024-07-26 with release v1.3.1 (2024-06-28) and 17 open issues

### 6. Feedback (documented)

No individual user reports verified. Documented: the acknowledgement clause read directly from LICENSE.txt in session 1 and retained; last push 2024-07-26; 258 stars. uroman is a well-cited research tool in MT and cross-lingual IR, which is adjacent-field credibility rather than journalism evidence.

### 7. Assessment

Use it as a matching-key generator, never as a name renderer, and remember the acknowledgement condition — for your work that means a line in the methodology note of any story whose matching depended on it, which is a trivial obligation but a real one. The dormancy is acceptable here because rule tables do not rot the way a dependency-heavy library does; the risk is that an unsupported script or a bug will never be fixed.

### 8. Maintenance

**Dormant** — GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2024-07-26, latest release v1.3.1 (2024-06-28), 258 stars, 17 open issues. Over two years without activity. Classified dormant; mitigated by the nature of the tool — deterministic rule tables with no dependency surface degrade far more slowly than typical software.

### 9. Licensing

**Licence:** MIT-style permissive with an added acknowledgement condition (LICENSE.txt grants MIT-equivalent rights but states 'Any publication of projects using uroman shall acknowledge its use'; GitHub API reports NOASSERTION) _(SPDX not verified — resolved from the licence file or project documentation)_

**Model / data licence:** n/a — rule tables, no trained weights.

**Restrictions:** Acknowledgement is a publication obligation: any publication of a project using uroman must acknowledge it. Not a use restriction, but it must be tracked so the credit actually appears.

**Licence evidence:** https://github.com/isi-nlp/uroman/blob/master/LICENSE.txt

### 10. Costs

No fee, negligible resources, no paid dependencies.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

Entirely local, no network, no models.

### 12. Verdict

**Integrate**

### 13. Alternatives

- [rigour](docs/projects/JAI-A2-44.md) for corporate-name normalisation within Latin script
- ICU transliteration for standards-conformant, citable transliteration schemes
- Language-specific transliteration libraries where a published rendering is required

### 14. Evidence

Verified **2026-11-17** · confidence **high** · assessment depth `metadata-verified`

- https://github.com/isi-nlp/uroman
- https://github.com/isi-nlp/uroman/blob/master/LICENSE.txt

**Scores** — relevance 3/5 · capability 4/5 · maintenance 3/5 · privacy 4/5 · usability 2/5 · licence+cost 1/5 → **weighted 61/100** (pillar rank 117, segment rank 9)

### 1. Purpose

Transformer-based image-forgery localisation model combining learned noise-residual fingerprints with RGB features, producing both a manipulation heatmap and a confidence/reliability map.

### Journalism / investigative use case

Second-opinion localisation on a single contested photo, where the reliability map is used to discount regions in which the model is unreliable — useful precisely because it tempers false alarms rather than producing a bare score.

### 2. Audience

specialist investigator, engineer

### 3. Project type

model · bucket `source-available-restricted`

### 4. Pros

- The reliability map is a genuine methodological advance for journalism: it tells you where not to trust the heatmap, which reduces the chance of publishing a false manipulation claim

### 5. Cons

- NOT open source: LICENSE.txt restricts use to informational and non-profit purposes, copyright GRIP-UNINA — a legal problem for any commercially operated newsroom and a blocker that is easy to miss because the code is on GitHub
- Outputs are probabilistic forensic signals, never conclusive proof of manipulation; platform recompression substantially degrades the signal

### 7. Assessment

Technically among the best available and legally unusable for a commercial newsroom without permission — that combination is the whole assessment. For your profile: if you work with a non-profit outlet or a research partner, this is a strong second opinion; if the outlet is commercially operated, either seek written permission from GRIP-UNINA or use CAT-Net, whose weights are CC-BY-4.0. Do not assume 'journalism is informational' satisfies an informational-use clause intended to exclude commercial deployment.

### 8. Maintenance

**Stable with low activity** — GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2025-05-29, no releases or tags, SPDX none, 287 stars, 11 open issues. Eighteen months since last push; a published research artefact that is complete rather than evolving.

**Licence:** NOT OSS — custom GRIP-UNINA terms: LICENSE.txt restricts use to informational and non-profit purposes _(SPDX not verified — resolved from the licence file or project documentation)_

**Model / data licence:** Same custom non-commercial GRIP-UNINA terms apply to the weights.

**Restrictions:** Commercial use is not permitted without separate permission. 'Informational and non-profit' does not clearly cover a commercially published investigation, and should not be assumed to. Redistribution is similarly restricted.

**Licence evidence:** https://github.com/grip-unina/TruFor

### 10. Costs

No fee for permitted non-profit/informational use. Commercial use requires permission — terms not publicly listed. GPU and Docker for inference.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

Inference is local inside Docker, so images need not leave the newsroom. No third-party service documented.

**Monitor**

Lightweight self-hosted meta-search for quick multi-engine checks when a full SearXNG deployment is overkill — for instance a per-investigation throwaway instance on cheap hosting, kept separate from the newsroom's main search path.

engineer

### 3. Project type

platform · bucket `verified-oss`

- Apache-2.0 code and a widely cited benchmark, so results are comparable to the published literature
- Establishes the discipline of measuring retrieval and entailment separately, which is diagnostically useful

### 5. Cons

- Claims are human-written over Wikipedia, not real-world political or social-media claims, so FEVER scores systematically overstate real-world performance — the single most important caveat when a vendor cites a FEVER number
- Baseline checkpoints are downloaded separately and their licences were not verified; the Wikipedia evidence corpus is CC-BY-SA, which carries ShareAlike obligations on derived corpora
- Low activity: pushed 2026-02-20, no releases or tags, 130 stars — a benchmark artefact rather than a maintained product
- Verdicts are probabilistic classifications, never proof, and the three-way label scheme does not match editorial reality

### 6. Feedback (documented)

No individual user reports verified. Documented: FEVER is among the most cited benchmarks in automated fact verification; its Wikipedia-derived construction and the resulting optimism bias are discussed in the subsequent literature (including AVeriTeC's framing of why a more realistic benchmark was needed).

### 7. Assessment

Useful to you as a measuring instrument and an annotation tool, not as a capability. Concretely: when someone proposes an AI fact-checking tool, ask what it scores on real claims rather than FEVER, and use the annotation platform to build a small gold set from your own published fact-checks to test it. That is a higher-value use of FEVER than running its baselines.

### 8. Maintenance

**Stable with low activity** — GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-02-20, no releases or tags, 130 stars, 1 open issue. Benchmark artefacts are expected to be static once published; the near-empty issue tracker is consistent with a finished research release rather than neglect.

### 9. Licensing

**Licence:** Apache-2.0 _(SPDX verified)_

**Model / data licence:** NOT verified — baseline checkpoints are downloaded separately. The Wikipedia evidence corpus is CC-BY-SA.

**Restrictions:** Code permissive. CC-BY-SA on the Wikipedia evidence corpus imposes attribution and ShareAlike obligations if you redistribute a derived evidence corpus.

**Licence evidence:** https://github.com/awslabs/fever/blob/master/LICENSE

### 10. Costs

No fee. Requires substantial local disk for the Wikipedia dump and dataset, plus a Python ML stack. No paid APIs. Estimate.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

Fully local once data is downloaded; no third-party API keys required. Suitable for use on an isolated machine.

### 12. Verdict

**Reference only**

### 13. Alternatives

- AVeriTeC for a benchmark closer to real fact-checking practice — but its licence is unconfirmed
- [X-FACT](docs/projects/JAI-A4-08.md) for multilingual claim classification evaluation
- Building your own gold set from your newsroom's published fact-checks, using FEVER's annotation platform

### 14. Evidence

Verified **2026-11-17** · confidence **high** · assessment depth `metadata-verified`

- https://github.com/awslabs/fever
- https://fever.ai/
- https://github.com/awslabs/fever/blob/master/LICENSE

## 325. Maltego — 59/100

### 1. Purpose

Commercial link-analysis platform with a graph interface and a transform ecosystem that queries data sources — infrastructure, corporate, social, breach and commercial intelligence — and expands entities into a visual graph.

### Journalism / investigative use case

The commercial benchmark for graph-based investigation: start from a name, domain or company and expand through transforms to related entities, building a visual network. Many OSINT training curricula teach it, so a newsroom hiring an experienced investigator may inherit it as an expectation.

### 2. Audience

specialist investigator

### 3. Project type

application · bucket `proprietary-service`

### 4. Pros

- Transform ecosystem is the product: hundreds of integrated data sources queried through one interface, which no open tool matches for breadth of commercial data
- Graph-first interface suits investigative reasoning and is genuinely effective for exploring entity relationships interactively
- Established in the field with extensive training material, so an experienced investigator is likely to be productive immediately
- Credit-based model means light use can be genuinely cheap, including a free Community Edition tier

### 5. Cons

- NOT open source: proprietary software with a credit-metered pricing model, and the costs are substantial at professional tiers — Entry EUR3,000/year (10,000 credits/month, includes Hunchly) and Professional EUR7,500/year (20,000-40,000 credits/month, up to 5 users, billed per seat), with Enterprise quote-only (all verified on the vendor pricing page 2026-11-16)
- Every transform query discloses your target to Maltego and to the underlying data provider — for a surveillance-industry investigation that is a material exposure, and the convenience of the interface makes it easy to forget
- Community Edition is restricted to graph-only use with 200 or 1,000 credits per month, which is enough to learn the tool and not to run an investigation
- Credit consumption is hard to predict, so budgeting is awkward and an exploratory session can consume a month's allowance

### 6. Feedback (documented)

No individual user reports verified in this survey. Pricing verified on the vendor page 2026-11-16 and recorded in sources/recovered/cat/pricing.tsv: Basic free forever (200 credits/month) or Basic+ (1,000 credits/month), Community Edition graph only; Entry EUR3,000/year including Hunchly; Professional EUR7,500/year, up to 5 users, billed per seat; Enterprise custom quote for 5+ users. Maltego's prominence in OSINT training is well documented.

### 7. Assessment

Reference only for your profile, and deliberately so: the open chain in this catalogue (subfinder, httpx, asn, certstream, NetworkX, Gephi) covers most of what Maltego's infrastructure transforms do, at no licence cost and without disclosing your targets to a commercial platform. The case for buying it is an experienced investigator who is already fast in it, or a specific commercial data source you cannot otherwise reach. If you do, budget per-seat annually and treat every transform as a disclosure.

### 8. Maintenance

**Actively maintained** — Commercial product under continuous vendor development; pricing page verified live 2026-11-16 with current tier structure. No repository to assess — maintenance is inferred from the operating commercial service and active vendor documentation, which is the only evidence available for proprietary software.

### 9. Licensing

**Licence:** Proprietary commercial licence; Community Edition is a restricted free tier _(SPDX not verified — resolved from the licence file or project documentation)_

**Model / data licence:** Transform data comes from many providers under their own terms, several of which restrict redistribution of results.

**Restrictions:** Proprietary throughout. Data-provider terms restrict republication of transform results, which matters if a graph is the basis of a published graphic.

**Licence evidence:** https://www.maltego.com/pricing/

### 10. Costs

Verified 2026-11-16 from the vendor pricing page: Basic free forever (200 credits/month) or Basic+ (1,000 credits/month), Community Edition graph only; Entry EUR3,000/year (10,000 credits/month, includes Hunchly); Professional EUR7,500/year (20,000-40,000 credits/month, up to 5 users, billed per seat); Enterprise custom quote (5+ users). Credits are consumed per transform, so operating cost scales with investigation intensity and is hard to forecast.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

The weakest point for investigative use: every transform discloses your target entity to Maltego and to the underlying data provider, continuously through an investigation. For work on a surveillance vendor or a state actor, that is an exposure the open alternatives avoid.

**Reference only**

## 327. PhotoHolmes — 59/100

`JAI-A4-17` · A4 · Fact-checking support and media verification · Image forensics harness · **library** · bucket `verified-oss` · maintainer photoholmes (Universidad de la República, Uruguay)
[Project page](docs/projects/JAI-A4-17.md) · [repository](https://github.com/photoholmes/photoholmes) · [docs](https://github.com/photoholmes/photoholmes#readme)

**Scores** — relevance 3/5 · capability 3/5 · maintenance 3/5 · privacy 4/5 · usability 2/5 · licence+cost 2/5 → **weighted 59/100** (pillar rank 123, segment rank 11)

### 1. Purpose

Python library that packages multiple published image-forgery detection and localisation methods behind a common interface, with preprocessing, benchmarking and a plugin structure for adding methods.

### Journalism / investigative use case

Lets an engineer embedded in a verification team run several published localisation methods over one contested image and compare heatmaps, rather than trusting a single model — and, just as usefully, benchmark honestly how badly each method degrades on recompressed social-media copies.

### 2. Audience

engineer, specialist investigator

### 3. Project type

library · bucket `verified-oss`

### 4. Pros

- Method ensembling with a common interface is the correct epistemic approach to image forensics: agreement across independent methods is informative, a single heatmap is not
- The benchmarking capability lets you measure degradation on platform-recompressed images, which is the condition that actually matters and which papers rarely report
- Apache-2.0 for the harness, and the README explicitly flags that bundled methods carry their own terms — honest licence signposting that is rare in research code

### 5. Cons

- Apache-2.0 covers the harness only: individual methods carry their own, sometimes non-commercial licences, and the README specifically flags TruFor as restricted to non-profit use — so the ensemble as a whole may not be commercially usable
- Outputs are probabilistic localisation maps and scores from research models, NOT conclusive proof of manipulation; heatmaps are highly suggestive to non-experts and easy to over-read
- Low activity (pushed 2026-01-05, no releases, 53 stars) and a small academic team — you would own maintenance
- Per-method pretrained weights are fetched from third-party hosts (HuggingFace, authors' links), which is a supply-chain and availability risk

### 6. Feedback (documented)

No individual user reports verified. Documented: the README's own licence warnings about bundled methods (including TruFor's non-profit restriction); 53 stars with 3 open issues; last push 2026-01-05.

### 7. Assessment

The right structure for forensic work and worth adopting if you have an engineer who can own it — the per-method licence audit is the task to do first, method by method, before anything reaches publication. For your profile the pragmatic configuration is to enable only the permissively licensed methods and accept a smaller ensemble, since a non-commercial method's output in a commercially published story is a licence breach. Every output is a lead requiring non-forensic corroboration.

### 8. Maintenance

**Stable with low activity** — GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-01-05, no releases or tags, 53 stars, 3 open issues. Ten months since last push; small academic project with a complete initial release. Not classified declining because the harness is functionally complete and the issue count is low, but there is no evidence of ongoing work.

### 9. Licensing

**Licence:** Apache-2.0 (base library only) _(SPDX verified)_

**Model / data licence:** Varies per bundled method; the README flags TruFor as restricted to non-profit use. Several bundled methods carry non-OSI academic terms.

**Restrictions:** Material: the harness is permissive but the methods inside it are not uniformly so. A commercial newsroom must audit and selectively disable methods. Do not treat the Apache-2.0 badge as covering the ensemble.

**Licence evidence:** https://github.com/photoholmes/photoholmes/blob/main/LICENSE

### 10. Costs

No fee. GPU helpful for some methods; per-method weights downloaded from third-party hosts. Cost is engineer time for the licence audit and integration. Estimate.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

Inference is local, so case images need not leave the newsroom — a significant advantage over the InVID plugin's forensics panels. Weight downloads from third-party hosts are the only external touchpoint and can be pre-staged.

### 12. Verdict

**Pilot**

### Material blockers

_Tracked separately from the score._

- Bundled methods carry mixed and partly non-commercial licences — per-method audit required before commercial publication

## 329. Bellingcat smart-image-sorter — 59/100

`OSINT-C2-15` · C2 · Image/video verification, geolocation, satellite, aviation and maritime · Image triage · **cli** · bucket `verified-oss` · maintainer Bellingcat

**Scores** — relevance 3/5 · capability 2/5 · maintenance 1/5 · privacy 4/5 · usability 4/5 · licence+cost 5/5 → **weighted 59/100** (pillar rank 130, segment rank 48)

### 1. Purpose

CLI that classifies images into user-defined categories using zero-shot vision-language models, sorting a directory of images into labelled folders.

### Journalism / investigative use case

Triage a large unsorted image dump by describing the categories you care about in plain words — 'military vehicle', 'street protest', 'document scan' — and letting the model bucket images for review, turning an unreviewable folder into a prioritised queue.

### 2. Audience

newsroom analyst, engineer

### 3. Project type

cli · bucket `verified-oss`

### 4. Pros

- Zero-shot labels mean no training data and no annotation, so an analyst can define investigation-specific categories in minutes
- Runs locally after weight download with no paid API, so a sensitive image dump is not uploaded anywhere
- Apache-2.0 and simple enough to adapt; built by Bellingcat for practising investigators
- GPU helpful but not required, so it works on an analyst workstation

### 5. Cons

- Zero-shot classification is an unreliable triage aid, not a labelling authority: accuracy varies sharply with label wording and it fails on fine-grained military or technical distinctions — exactly the distinctions investigations often need

- Model weights are GB-scale downloads, which is a practical constraint on a field machine

No individual user reports verified — 68 stars means minimal community signal. Documented: no releases, last push 2024-08-14, Apache-2.0. The accuracy limitations of zero-shot classification on fine-grained categories are a documented property of the method rather than a defect of this implementation.

### 7. Assessment

The idea is right and the implementation is stale. For your profile I would reimplement the same pattern against a current vision-language model — it is a short script — and gain substantially better accuracy, since zero-shot classification has improved markedly since 2024. Keep the core discipline either way: the model produces a review order, never a label you act on, and fine-grained technical identification (which munition, which uniform) must be done by a human expert.

### 8. Maintenance

**Dormant** — GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2024-08-14, no releases or tags, 68 stars, 0 open issues. Over two years without activity; because the value depends on the underlying model, staleness here means using a model generation behind what is available.

**Restrictions:** Code permissive. The imported risk is the model licence — verify the specific checkpoint before commercial use.

**Licence evidence:** https://github.com/bellingcat/smart-image-sorter/blob/main/LICENSE

### 10. Costs

No fee and no paid API. GB-scale model weight download; GPU helpful but not required. Estimate.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

Local inference after weights download; images are not uploaded if run locally, which is the property that makes it usable on a sensitive dump.

## 331. UniversalFakeDetect — 59/100

`JAI-A4-20` · A4 · Fact-checking support and media verification · Synthetic image detection · **prototype** · bucket `verified-oss` · maintainer Wisconsin AI Vision lab
[Project page](docs/projects/JAI-A4-20.md) · [repository](https://github.com/WisconsinAIVision/UniversalFakeDetect) · [docs](https://github.com/WisconsinAIVision/UniversalFakeDetect#readme)

**Scores** — relevance 2/5 · capability 3/5 · maintenance 3/5 · privacy 4/5 · usability 2/5 · licence+cost 5/5 → **weighted 59/100** (pillar rank 124, segment rank 12)

### 1. Purpose

Method and reference implementation showing that a linear classifier on frozen CLIP features generalises across image generators better than purpose-trained detectors, with evaluation sets across many generator families.

### Journalism / investigative use case

A baseline for teams testing whether any synthetic-image detector holds up on their own case material — valuable mainly as the honest yardstick for cross-generator generalisation claims, which is the axis on which vendor detectors fail.

### 2. Audience

engineer

### 3. Project type

prototype · bucket `verified-oss`

### 4. Pros

- The finding itself is the value: a simple CLIP-feature classifier generalising better than specialised detectors is a strong reason to distrust vendor claims about bespoke detection models
- MIT licensed with author-distributed weights, so it can be run and cited freely
- Evaluation across many generator families makes it a usable generalisation test rather than a single-generator demo

### 5. Cons

- A score is a probabilistic signal, NOT evidence or proof that an image was AI-generated — and because the method is simple, non-experts over-trust it
- The repository notes that its released diffusion evaluation set is reduced to 1k real / 1k fake per domain versus 10k in the paper, so published numbers are not reproducible from the release as distributed
- Predates the current generation of image models, so its own generalisation claims need re-testing against 2025-2026 generators
- Requires CLIP weights and author-hosted datasets of roughly 72GB across 20 categories — a substantial download; 24 open issues, no releases

### 6. Feedback (documented)

No individual user reports verified. Documented from the repository itself: the reduced released evaluation set versus the paper (1k versus 10k per domain), which is an honest disclosure by the authors and a real reproducibility limit. 381 stars, 24 open issues, last push 2026-08-19.

### 7. Assessment

Use it as a measuring stick, not a detector. Concretely, for your work: when someone offers an AI-image detector, test it and this baseline on the same set of images from generators neither has seen, and expect both to degrade sharply. The Deepfake-Eval-2024 finding (roughly 45-50% AUC drops in the wild) is the number to keep in mind. Never publish a synthetic-media claim on detector output alone.

### 8. Maintenance

**Stable with low activity** — GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-08-19, no releases or tags, 381 stars, 24 open issues. Three months since last push; a research release receiving light maintenance.

### 9. Licensing

**Licence:** MIT _(SPDX verified)_

**Model / data licence:** Not separately stated; weights distributed by the authors under the repository terms. Evaluation datasets aggregate third-party generator outputs whose own terms may vary.

**Restrictions:** Code MIT. Residual uncertainty on the aggregated evaluation datasets, which include outputs from generators with their own terms of service.

**Licence evidence:** https://github.com/WisconsinAIVision/UniversalFakeDetect/blob/main/LICENSE

### 10. Costs

No fee. Roughly 72GB of dataset downloads plus CLIP weights; GPU for evaluation. Bandwidth and storage are the notable costs. Estimate.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

Dataset and CLIP weight downloads from third-party hosts; classification runs locally, so case images stay in the newsroom.

### 12. Verdict

**Reference only**

### 13. Alternatives

- [Community Forensics](docs/projects/JAI-A4-21.md) for a broader-training-distribution open baseline with MIT weights
- [Deepfake-Eval-2024](docs/projects/JAI-A4-31.md) for the in-the-wild degradation figures to cite
- Non-forensic verification — provenance, reverse search, source contact — which remains more reliable than any detector

### 14. Evidence

Verified **2026-11-17** · confidence **high** · assessment depth `metadata-verified`

- https://github.com/WisconsinAIVision/UniversalFakeDetect
- https://github.com/WisconsinAIVision/UniversalFakeDetect/blob/main/LICENSE

### 1. Purpose

Unified benchmark and training framework implementing many published face-manipulation detectors with standardised preprocessing, training and cross-dataset evaluation.

### Journalism / investigative use case

The practical way a technically staffed newsroom or research partner can run several published detectors over the same suspect video and see whether they agree, instead of trusting one black-box score — and the reference for how badly detectors generalise outside their training data.

### 2. Audience

engineer

prototype · bucket `source-available-restricted`
