Use it through a research partner rather than in-house if your outlet is commercial — the NC licence plus the dataset rights questions make direct use legally untidy. Its real value to you is the published finding rather than the software: detector agreement is informative, detector scores are not, and in-the-wild performance is far below reported figures. For an editor conversation, DeepfakeBench plus Deepfake-Eval-2024 together make the case for not publishing on detector output.

## 333. AASIST — 58/100

`JAI-A4-29` · A4 · Fact-checking support and media verification · Audio spoofing detection · **prototype** · bucket `verified-oss` · maintainer Clova AI Research (clovaai)
[Project page](docs/projects/JAI-A4-29.md) · [repository](https://github.com/clovaai/aasist) · [docs](https://github.com/clovaai/aasist#readme)

**Scores** — relevance 3/5 · capability 2/5 · maintenance 1/5 · privacy 5/5 · usability 2/5 · licence+cost 5/5 → **weighted 58/100** (pillar rank 126, segment rank 14)

### 1. Purpose

Graph-attention-based anti-spoofing model for speech, detecting synthetic and converted voice using integrated spectro-temporal graph attention over raw audio.

### Journalism / investigative use case

Screening suspect voice notes, leaked 'audio recordings' of politicians and robocall clips for synthesis or voice-conversion artefacts — the audio half of verification, where there is far less tooling available than for video and where fabricated audio has already been used in elections.

### 2. Audience

engineer, specialist investigator

### 3. Project type

prototype · bucket `verified-oss`

### 4. Pros

- Addresses a genuine and growing gap: synthetic audio is cheaper to produce and harder to verify than video, and there are very few open tools
- MIT code with pretrained models shipped in-repository under the same licence — unusually clean licensing for this field, and the main reason to prefer it over the academic-licensed alternatives
- Fully local inference with no API keys, so a suspect recording stays in the newsroom
- Compact model that runs without heavy infrastructure

### 5. Cons

- Outputs a probabilistic spoofing score, NOT proof that audio is synthetic — and in a field where a false accusation against a politician is catastrophic, that distinction is everything
- The headline sub-1% EER figures are on ASVspoof 2019 logical access, a clean studio-condition benchmark; published in-the-wild performance is far worse, so the impressive number does not transfer
- Dormant: last push 2023-06-25, no releases or tags, 314 stars, 4 open issues — three years inactive, and the synthesis methods it was trained against are now superseded
- Requires the ASVspoof 2019 LA dataset (separate terms) for training or re-evaluation

### 6. Feedback (documented)

No individual user reports verified. Documented: MIT licence for code and in-repo pretrained models; dormancy since June 2023; the benchmark-versus-in-the-wild performance gap, which is consistent with the Deepfake-Eval-2024 finding of roughly 48% AUC degradation for audio models moved to in-the-wild data.

### 7. Assessment

The best-licensed option in a weak field, and worth having precisely because audio verification has so few alternatives — but its training predates current voice-cloning systems, so treat a negative result as nearly meaningless and a positive result as a lead. For your profile the practical posture on suspect audio is: run AASIST, run forced alignment or spectral inspection, and above all pursue provenance — who first posted it, what the earliest copy's metadata says, whether the purported speaker's circumstances fit. Detection alone should never carry a story.

### 8. Maintenance

**Dormant** — GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2023-06-25, no releases or tags, 314 stars, 4 open issues. Three years inactive. Material here because the threat model (voice synthesis methods) has changed substantially since.

### 9. Licensing

**Licence:** MIT _(SPDX verified)_

**Model / data licence:** MIT — pretrained models shipped in-repository under the same licence.

**Restrictions:** None material. The ASVspoof 2019 LA dataset used for training/evaluation has its own separate terms.

**Licence evidence:** https://github.com/clovaai/aasist/blob/main/LICENSE

### 10. Costs

No fee. Modest GPU or even CPU for inference on short clips. ASVspoof dataset obtained separately for any retraining. Estimate.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

Fully local inference with no API keys — the suspect recording never leaves your machine, which matters because the audio itself may identify a source.

### 12. Verdict

**Pilot**

### Material blockers

_Tracked separately from the score._

- Dormant since 2023; trained against pre-2024 synthesis methods

### 13. Alternatives

- [ASVspoof 2021 baseline systems](docs/projects/JAI-A4-30.md) for the official scoring code to compute your own EER — but licence unconfirmed
- Commercial audio-detection services, which upload the clip and whose accuracy claims deserve the same scepticism
- Provenance investigation and spectral/forced-alignment analysis as the primary approach

### 14. Evidence

**Scores** — relevance 4/5 · capability 3/5 · maintenance 2/5 · privacy 1/5 · usability 4/5 · licence+cost 2/5 → **weighted 57/100** (pillar rank 128, segment rank 16)

> **Provisional assessment** — the evidence does not support a firm score; see Evidence below.

### 1. Purpose

Hosted API with a Claim Search endpoint for querying fact-checks published worldwide as ClaimReview structured data, plus a write API for submitting your own ClaimReview markup.

### Journalism / investigative use case

Check whether a circulating claim has already been fact-checked by any publisher worldwide before spending desk time on it, and publish your own fact-checks as structured ClaimReview so they are discoverable by others — the two halves of not duplicating work.

### 2. Audience

journalist, newsroom analyst, engineer

### 3. Project type

platform · bucket `proprietary-service`

### 4. Pros

- By far the broadest coverage of published fact-checks available through one interface, because it aggregates ClaimReview markup globally
- The write side matters strategically: emitting ClaimReview makes your own fact-checks discoverable and citable by other desks and by search surfaces
- No infrastructure to operate, and the lookup is fast enough for live use during a breaking story

### 5. Cons

- NOT open source: a hosted service under Google's API Terms, with deprecation and quota risk entirely outside your control — the same class of dependency that killed CooRnet
- Coverage is limited to publishers emitting valid ClaimReview markup, which skews toward larger and English-language organisations and silently under-represents smaller and non-Western fact-checkers
- Queries and submitted markup go to Google, so your checking activity on a sensitive subject is visible to a third party
- Licence and current pricing/quota terms were not verified in this survey — treat both as unconfirmed here

### 6. Feedback (documented)

No individual user reports verified. Documented from the project's own documentation: API users must inform their own users that results come from the Fact Check Tools API, and coverage depends on publisher ClaimReview emission. Quota and pricing details were not verified in this survey.

### 7. Assessment

Use it, with eyes open about what it is: a convenience layer over other people's structured markup, operated by a company that has retired APIs before. For your profile the asymmetry is worth noting — the write side (publishing ClaimReview) has lasting value independent of Google, because the markup is a standard; the read side is a dependency. I would emit ClaimReview regardless and treat the lookup as a useful but replaceable step, with a manual search fallback documented.

### 8. Maintenance

**Uncertain** — No repository to inspect. The service was live and documented at developers.google.com/fact-check/tools/api as of this survey, but I did not verify current quota, pricing or deprecation status from the vendor in this session. Classified Uncertain deliberately: a hosted API's maintenance cannot be evidenced the way a repository's can, and Google's API deprecation record justifies caution rather than an assumption of continuity.

### 9. Licensing

**Licence:** Not applicable (hosted service under Google API Terms of Service); specific terms not verified in this survey _(SPDX not verified — resolved from the licence file or project documentation)_

**Model / data licence:** n/a. Note that the underlying ClaimReview content belongs to the publishing fact-checkers.

**Restrictions:** Service terms rather than a software licence. Documentation states an attribution obligation to end users. Republishing aggregated fact-check content raises the publishers' own rights, separate from Google's terms.

**Licence evidence:** https://developers.google.com/fact-check/tools/api

### 10. Costs

Pricing and quota NOT verified in this survey — treat as not publicly confirmed here and check the current terms before relying on it. Historically free within quota; a Google API key is required, and Search Console verification is required for the ClaimReview write API.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

Queries and submitted ClaimReview markup go to Google. Your lookup activity discloses which claims you are examining, which is a consideration if the subject is sensitive or if the target might observe published queries indirectly.

### 12. Verdict

**Integrate**

### Material blockers

model · bucket `source-available-restricted`

Reference only, but the design is worth stealing. ### Journalism / investigative use case

Verification of image-plus-text claims as they actually circulate on social media, where the claim is a photo with a caption. Its distinguishing output is a tool-by-tool evidence trail a journalist can audit, rather than a bare label.

### 2. Audience

engineer

prototype · bucket `verified-oss`

The most interesting architecture in this subcategory and the one I would study before building anything similar — tool-orchestration with an auditable trail is the right pattern for verification automation. ### Journalism / investigative use case

The citation to reach for when an editor or vendor claims a detector is '98% accurate'. Its central finding is that open-source state-of-the-art detector AUC drops by roughly 50% for video, 48% for audio and 45% for image models when moved from academic benchmarks to in-the-wild media.

- Directly actionable editorially: it justifies a policy of not publishing synthetic-media claims on detector output

No individual user reports verified. The documented central finding — roughly 50% video, 48% audio and 45% image AUC degradation moving from academic benchmarks to in-the-wild media — is the project's own reported result, recorded in session 1 and retained here as a project claim rather than an independently replicated measurement. The licence absence was verified by inspection.

### 7. Assessment

Low as software, high as evidence — and I would score it provisionally for that reason. For your work its value is to settle an argument: it gives you a citable basis for telling an editor that detector output is a lead and not a finding, which protects the newsroom from publishing a false synthetic-media claim. Cite it as a project-reported result, note the licence uncertainty, and do not redistribute the dataset.

- Facebook/Instagram only, so it never covered the platforms where much coordination now occurs
- Its fate is a general warning: tools built on a single proprietary platform API inherit that API's lifespan

No individual user reports verified. The documented decisive facts: archived=true per the GitHub API on 2026-11-17, and the alignment of its final push (2024-08-14) with the discontinuation of the CrowdTangle data source it depended on.

### 7. Assessment

Reference only, and a useful cautionary case for your planning: the single most consequential dependency in social-media research is not the library but the data source, and proprietary research APIs have been withdrawn repeatedly. Use CooRTweet, which is data-source agnostic, and design any monitoring you build so the collection layer can be replaced without rewriting the analysis.

### 8. Maintenance

**Archived or discontinued** — GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=true, pushed_at 2024-08-14, no releases, 75 stars, 0 open issues. Archived by the maintainer; the underlying CrowdTangle API was discontinued, so the data layer is gone as well as the code being frozen.

## 359. pagodo — 36/100

`OSINT-C1-07` · C1 · Web and social research, archives and evidence capture · Search dorking · **cli** · bucket `verified-oss` · maintainer opsdisk
[Project page](docs/projects/OSINT-C1-07.md) · [repository](https://github.com/opsdisk/pagodo) · [docs](https://github.com/opsdisk/pagodo#readme)

**Scores** — relevance 2/5 · capability 1/5 · maintenance 0/5 · privacy 2/5 · usability 3/5 · licence+cost 4/5 → **weighted 36/100** (pillar rank 137, segment rank 45)

### 1. Purpose

Tool that scraped the Google Hacking Database for dork patterns and ran them against Google to find exposed files, directories and interfaces on a target domain.

### Journalism / investigative use case

Reference implementation of bulk dorking workflows; its GHDB scraper still documents dork syntax that remains useful for manual searching — for example finding exposed procurement spreadsheets or misconfigured document directories on a target's domain.

### 2. Audience

engineer, specialist investigator

### 3. Project type

cli · bucket `verified-oss`

### 4. Pros

- The GHDB dork catalogue it scrapes remains a genuinely useful reference for manual search syntax, independent of the automation
- Clean, readable implementation of the dorking workflow, with GPL-3.0 licensing
- Had a long run as the standard tool in this niche, so understanding it explains most dorking tooling you will encounter

### 5. Cons

- ARCHIVED: the GitHub API confirms archived=true as of this survey, with the final release v2.8.0 on 2026-11-01 — the maintainer wound it down rather than abandoning it quietly
- Automated Google dorking is broadly non-functional as of late 2026 because of Google's anti-scraping measures, so the core capability no longer works regardless of code quality
- Dork queries issued directly to Google from your IP are a visible, attributable pattern — and in an investigation that pattern can be linked to you
- Depends on GHDB (Offensive Security), a third-party catalogue whose availability and terms you do not control

### 6. Feedback (documented)

No individual user reports verified. Decisive documented facts: archived=true per the GitHub API on 2026-11-17 with a final release v2.8.0 (2026-11-01); 3,418 stars with 0 open issues. The practical collapse of automated Google dorking in 2026 is corroborated by the same pattern in dorks_hunter and Whoogle.

### 7. Assessment

Reference only. The honest conclusion for your work is that dorking is now a manual technique: keep the GHDB syntax patterns to hand and run them by hand through SearXNG or directly, accepting low volume. Do not build a pipeline on automated dorking — it will fail and, worse, will fail intermittently in ways that look like 'nothing found'. If exposed-file discovery matters, katana or a targeted crawl of the domain is the reliable substitute.

### 8. Maintenance

**Archived or discontinued** — GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=true, pushed_at 2026-11-01, latest release v2.8.0 (2026-11-01), 3,418 stars, 0 open issues. Archived with a final release — an orderly wind-down. The upstream capability (Google scraping) is independently blocked.

### 9. Licensing

**Licence:** GPL-3.0 _(SPDX verified)_

**Model / data licence:** The GHDB dork catalogue is maintained by Offensive Security under its own terms, not covered by pagodo's licence.

**Restrictions:** GPL-3.0 on the code. GHDB content terms are separate. Automated querying breaches Google's terms of service — a terms rather than licence issue, but a real one.

**Licence evidence:** https://github.com/opsdisk/pagodo/blob/master/LICENSE

### 10. Costs

No fee. Not operable for its primary purpose.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

Dork queries were issued directly to Google from your IP — a highly visible and attributable pattern. Anyone reviving this approach should consider that the search provider can profile the campaign.

### 12. Verdict

**Reference only**

### Material blockers

_Tracked separately from the score._

- Archived; automated Google dorking is non-functional as of late 2026

### 13. Alternatives

- Manual dorking through SearXNG at low volume
- [katana](docs/projects/OSINT-C1-15.md) for crawling a target domain to enumerate files and paths directly
- [uncover](docs/projects/OSINT-C1-10.md) for exposed-infrastructure discovery via scan databases (paid API keys)

### 14. Evidence

## 360. NewsDiffs — 34/100

`SUR-B1-26` · B1 · Monitoring public information, narratives, disinformation, censorship and harassment · Stealth-edit tracking · **prototype** · bucket `verified-oss` · maintainer Eric Price (ecprice) and collaborators
[Project page](docs/projects/SUR-B1-26.md) · [repository](https://github.com/ecprice/newsdiffs) · [docs](http://www.newsdiffs.org/)

**Scores** — relevance 2/5 · capability 1/5 · maintenance 1/5 · privacy 3/5 · usability 1/5 · licence+cost 2/5 → **weighted 34/100** (pillar rank 80, segment rank 27)

### 1. Purpose

Django application that scrapes news articles from configured sites on a schedule, stores every version, and publishes a public archive of detected post-publication edits.

### Journalism / investigative use case

The canonical prior art for stealth-edit tracking and a useful reference for how to structure per-site parsers and a public diff archive — not a tool to deploy today, but the project that established the practice of holding news organisations accountable for silent revisions.

### 2. Audience

engineer

### 3. Project type

prototype · bucket `verified-oss`

### 4. Pros

- Historically important: it demonstrated that systematic post-publication edit tracking is feasible and newsworthy, and the public-archive model shaped later work
- Per-site parser architecture is a reasonable design for the problem, and reading it saves you rediscovering the same structure
- 506 stars reflect genuine historical influence in this space

### 5. Cons

- Effectively abandoned: the last default-branch commit dates to 2018 and the stack targets Python 2.6+ with old Django versions — an end-of-life runtime that cannot be deployed safely
- GitHub reports SPDX NOASSERTION, and session-1 inspection found mixed per-file licensing, so reuse needs file-by-file review
- The README itself notes you must be a programmer to add a parser for each new site, so it never scaled beyond its curators
- 36 open issues, no releases; the public site's continuity is outside your control

### 6. Feedback (documented)

No individual user reports verified. Documented: last default-branch commit 2018 (with a 2026-04-13 push reflecting incidental repository activity rather than development), Python 2.6+ requirement, mixed per-file licensing and SPDX NOASSERTION, 506 stars with 36 open issues.

### 7. Assessment

Reference only, and specifically a cautionary one: per-site scrapers are a maintenance treadmill, which is why this project stopped. For your profile the lesson is to prefer feed- or sitemap-driven detection and generic diffing over bespoke parsers, and to accept lower coverage in exchange for a system that survives. If post-publication edit tracking matters to your beat, build it on webchanges or shot-scraper with a sitemap crawl rather than reviving this.

### 8. Maintenance

**Dormant** — GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-04-13 but the default-branch development history ends in 2018; no releases, SPDX NOASSERTION, 506 stars, 36 open issues. Python 2.6+ and old Django make it non-deployable. The recent push date is misleading and is the reason push recency alone is not used for classification in this catalogue.

### 9. Licensing

**Licence:** MIT per session-1 inspection, but mixed per-file licensing was found and GitHub reports NOASSERTION — reuse requires file-by-file review _(SPDX not verified — resolved from the licence file or project documentation)_

**Model / data licence:** n/a

**Restrictions:** Unclear in aggregate. Do not vendor code from it without reviewing each file's header.

**Licence evidence:** https://github.com/ecprice/newsdiffs

### 10. Costs

No fee. Not deployable on a supported runtime without substantial porting work.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

Self-hosted; the original project published detected diffs publicly on its own website. A revival would need an explicit decision about publication.

### 12. Verdict

**Reference only**

### Material blockers

_Tracked separately from the score._

- Python 2.6-era stack, abandoned since 2018, mixed per-file licensing

### 13. Alternatives

- [webchanges](docs/projects/SUR-B1-17.md) or changedetection.io for maintained monitoring
- [shot-scraper](docs/projects/SUR-B1-23.md) plus git for a version history of specific articles
- [EDGI web-monitoring-db](docs/projects/SUR-B1-20.md) for a platform with analyst triage

## 361. ClaimsKG extractor — 29/100

`JAI-A4-09` · A4 · Fact-checking support and media verification · Fact-check aggregation · **cli** · bucket `uncertain` · maintainer ClaimsKG project (academic consortium)

> **Provisional assessment** — the evidence does not support a firm score; see Evidence below.

### 1. Purpose

Scraper and knowledge-graph builder that extracts published fact-checks from fact-checking websites and emits a structured RDF knowledge graph of claims, verdicts and entities.

### Journalism / investigative use case

Build a cross-organisation database of already-published fact-checks (Full Fact, Snopes, PolitiFact, Africa Check, AFP Fact Check, EUvsDisinfo) so a desk can check whether a circulating claim has already been debunked before spending reporter time on it.

### 2. Audience

engineer

### 3. Project type

cli · bucket `uncertain`

### 4. Pros

- Produces a structured, queryable knowledge graph rather than a flat list, so you can ask cross-cutting questions (which claims about a given entity have been checked, by whom, with what verdict)
- Covers a useful spread of fact-checking organisations including non-Western ones (Africa Check), which the Google Fact Check API under-represents
- Self-hosted scraping means you are not dependent on a vendor API's quota or deprecation

### 5. Cons

- Licence could NOT be confirmed: the GitHub licence API returns 404 and no LICENSE file is detected; the code is also a fork of vwoloszyn/fake_news_extractor, which compounds provenance uncertainty — reuse is legally unresolved
- Dormant: last push 2022-09-01, tag v0.2, 21 stars, 0 open issues — four years inactive, and web scrapers decay faster than almost any other code because target sites change
- Scrapes third-party fact-checker websites directly, so your crawling traffic is visible to them and may breach their terms
- English-dominant coverage despite the multi-organisation ambition

### 6. Feedback (documented)

No individual user reports verified. Documented: the licence gap (GitHub licence API 404, no LICENSE file) and the fork provenance, both recorded in session 1 and retained; last push 2022-09-01.

### 7. Assessment

Not usable as-is: a four-year-old scraper against sites that have certainly changed, with no licence. The idea is sound and worth reimplementing if cross-organisation fact-check lookup matters to you — but build it against ClaimReview markup (which publishers emit deliberately) rather than by scraping, and consider the Google Fact Check Tools API for coverage with the trade-off that queries go to Google.

### 8. Maintenance

**Dormant** — GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2022-09-01, latest tag v0.2, no releases, no detected licence, 21 stars, 0 open issues. Four years inactive. For a web scraper this is effectively non-functional, since target site structures will have changed.

### 9. Licensing

**Licence:** NOT CONFIRMED — GitHub licence API returns 404 and no LICENSE file detected; code is a fork of vwoloszyn/fake_news_extractor, compounding provenance uncertainty _(SPDX not verified — resolved from the licence file or project documentation)_

**Model / data licence:** n/a

**Restrictions:** Unresolved. Do not redistribute or build a product on it. Separately, scraping fact-checkers' sites may breach their terms of use regardless of the code licence.

**Licence evidence:** https://github.com/claimskg/claimskg-extractor

### 10. Costs

No fee. Operating cost would be scraper maintenance, which is the dominant and recurring cost of this approach.

### 11. Privacy and data flows

Scrapes third-party fact-checker websites directly; your crawling pattern and IP are visible to those sites. No credentials required.

### 12. Verdict

**Avoid for new deployment**

### Material blockers

_Tracked separately from the score._
